# Preface.

The fact that these accounts constitute history and are indispensable for a complete knowledge of the same can hardly be unknown or seem doubtful to anyone. However, their particular usefulness and excellent significance are not recognized and observed even among Protestants in the manner that should rightly occur. Therefore, it will not be unserviceable to take the various types of such utility into closer consideration and to present them in such a way that both the obligation toward a more general dissemination and a more careful investigation of said history is recognized, and the dutiful use and advantageous application of the same is promoted.

This particular utility can be most conveniently divided into five main types, under which at least everything can be included that rightfully belongs here.

Firstly, the knowledge of this history is useful both for the necessary insight into the true form of the Papacy <note>original: "Papstums"</note>, as well as for the answering and parrying of many prejudices, evasions, and accusations which the Roman Church employs against us. This, accordingly, constitutes a threefold use.

1. Since the true form of the Papacy is little known in Protestant lands, even in such places where congregations devoted to this Church are found; indeed, it remains hidden from many members of the same who have had no opportunity to see firsthand the prevailing coercion of conscience <term>Gewissenszwang: the practice of forcing individuals to act against their religious beliefs or forcing them into a specific faith</term> and spirit of persecution <note>original: "Verfolgungsgeist"</note> by which it distinguishes itself from all other worshiping parties of Christendom: thus, the discovery of this unchristian, indeed inhuman cruelty, and the countless blood-guilt <note>original: "Blutschulden"</note> which this Church has loaded upon itself, is of all the more importance, the more diligently

<meta>catchword: itself</meta>

<summary>The author argues that Protestants often overlook the historical importance of documenting the Papacy's actions and outlines five reasons why studying this history is essential for defending the faith and understanding religious coercion.</summary>
<keywords>Papacy, Protestantism, religious persecution, coercion of conscience, blood-guilt, church history, polemics</keywords>

--- Page 27 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface, specifically addressing the historical violence of the Roman Church and the emergence of dissenting groups.</meta>

# Preface

Many defenders of the same strive to conceal this anti-Christian <note>original: "antichriſtiſche"</note> form, appealing to the milder conduct of modern times; regardless of the fact that this does not flow from any changed principles, but is rather to be thanked to the enlightened and restored lawful power of the secular authorities—even in Roman Catholic lands—brought about by the Reformation <term>Reformation: the 16th-century religious movement that led to the establishment of Protestant churches</term>. The history of the Papal Church <note>original: "päpſtlichen Kirche"</note> opens such a terrifying theater of bloodshed and the cruelest devastation of entire countries, as well as violent executions and otherwise unheard-of tortures of innocent people, that the modern writers of this party would gladly draw a curtain over it, or at least seek to shift the guilt for it onto their oppressed opponents.

Although this bloodthirsty cruelty extends further, and even raged in the most un-Christian manner against unbelieving or non-Christian peoples during the Crusades <note>original: "Kreuzzügen"</note> undertaken against them: nevertheless, the fates of those churches separated from this party during the Middle Ages are the most lamentable scenes of this tragedy. # Preface

The right of prescription <note>original: "Recht der Verjährung"; a legal concept where a claim becomes valid simply because it has existed for a long time</note> derived from this, used against all opposition, would be quite irrelevant and unfit for deciding our disputes with them, no matter how demonstrable that opposition might be. Meanwhile, the most demonstrable inaccuracy of their entire claim is revealed through this history in a threefold way.

First, the opposition of such a great multitude of people—mostly common folk, or at least people lacking in other sciences and insights beyond a simple knowledge of the main contents of Holy Scripture and the worship founded therein—against the specific distinguishing features of the aforementioned party's system of doctrine <note>original: "Lehrbegrif"</note> and worship, discovers and proves the recent origin of those very features. This refusal to join can be derived in a comprehensible way solely from the then-unquestionable noticeability of such innovations in worship.

Next, most of these new distinguishing features of the system of doctrine and worship, which initially only crept in little by little, were only confirmed through solemn church ordinances <note>original: "Kirchenverordnungen"</note> after conscientious people had refused to accept them or confirm them by their joining. It happened in such a way that through every discovery of such opposition and conscientious hesitation to allow human decrees and errors of worship to be forced upon them, the most intentional worsening followed instead of an improvement. This occurred through the supposed transformation of these errors into articles of faith <note>original: "Glaubenslehren"</note> by means of a subsequent decree of the Church.

# Preface.

The gracious hand of God—to whom we owe the Reformation that occurred in the 16th century, or rather the restoration of the pure doctrine of Holy Scripture and the worship founded therein, along with the liberation from the unbearable yoke and coercion of conscience under the Papacy—cannot be more clearly or fruitfully recognized than by comparing its progress. One must consider both its rapid and unexpected advancement and its powerful preservation, as well as the resulting complete and precise agreement of doctrine and worship with Holy Scripture. This was intended for the soul-saving cultivation of spirits <note>original: "Selen" (souls)</note> and the advancement of the divine work of grace within them. This stands in contrast to previous attempts at similar restorations of the obscured light of divine truth and the order of salvation, which either failed to reach the same pure, bright, widespread, and lasting radiance, or lost it again quite soon—a radiance of which divine mercy has deemed us worthy. This excellence of divine blessings can and must be recognized without diminishing or disadvantageously belittling the older witnesses and confessors of the truth, who were faithful to their own measure of insight, and without boasting or self-exaltation. For all the advantages arising from this are not only to be attributed to God—indeed, they cannot be denied or carelessly overlooked without offending Him—but they are also enjoyed only in proportion to their faithful use and serve for true benefit; in the absence of which, they only increase one's accountability and punishment.

Just as the deficient and confused knowledge of this history has very frequently been misused to contest Christianity, and has had to provide its adversaries with examples to prove their usual prejudices in a way that is—according to their claims—very clear and irrefutable: namely, that religion in general, and the Christian religion in particular, is to blame for most disturbances, wars, confusion, and the disruption of commonwealths; that it rests upon cunning deceit and superior violence; and that it is an invention of the craftiness of self-interested priests as well as power-hungry authorities who seized upon the simplicity and credulity of the common people and used them for the benefit of their own intentions; that this religion, like other similar customs established by whim, has undergone a multitude of changes and produced contradictory parties as well as their innumerable disputes; and that, therefore, a prevailing indifference toward it—even a forgetting and ignorance of it—is to be desired for the preservation of public peace and the promotion of human happiness: so it is indeed indisputable that the mere investigation and precise, as well as correct, knowledge of this very history can demonstrate the opposite of all these things, which is otherwise also provable by other means.

In this manner, purified from human falsifications, it restored itself to the external freedom of public observation and practice, to the no small advantage of the welfare of the commonweal. By this very means, the public was liberated from an intolerable yoke and a multitude of dangerous disruptions caused by the unbearable encroachments of a foreign and unauthorized jurisdiction <note>This likely refers to the legal and political overreach of the Roman Catholic Church prior to the Reformation</note>.

It is therefore the publisher's intention to make some of the best history books of this kind better known and more convenient for general use—partly through new editions, partly through translation, and partly through the publication of previously unprinted writings and documents. This intention should be acknowledged with much gratitude and promoted with all possible encouragement by lovers of history, theology <term>Gottesgelersamkeit: the study of divinity or scholarly theology</term>, and true edification. # Preface.

Regarding this history of the Waldensians: although Léger is neither the only nor the most recent, he is indisputably the most detailed and useful historian of this ancient and respectable church. Not to mention the shorter and incidental—and in part hostile—accounts found either in larger treatises on general church history and martyrologies, or in the polemical writings of their adversaries, or in the at least highly suspicious narratives of Tillet, Varillas, Bossuet, and Benoist <note>These authors were often Catholic apologists or historians critical of the Waldensian movement</note>: nevertheless, those works provided by the authors of the two smaller Waldensian chronicles (which have appeared in several languages) retain their fair value. This includes what Jean Paul Perrin, Pierre Gilles (or Aegidius), Samuel Morland, Pierre Boyer, Pierre Allix, and Thomas Bray have provided in their own historical books. To these, Balthasar Lydius’s *Waldensia* cannot be added; although this is otherwise a very useful writing, it was given an incorrect title, as its entire content belongs to the history of the older Bohemian churches <note>Lydius likely confused the Waldensians with the Bohemian Brethren or Hussites</note>. Meanwhile, the history prepared by Léger deserves the undisputed preference: for he not only made useful use of all the other aforementioned actual history books (except for the last three, which were published later), but he also possessed sufficient resources and reliable as well as significant original documents. From these, he was able to correct, supplement, and expand their reports in such a way that his additions far surpass the information borrowed from those others. Therefore, by using this work, one can dispense with the others without disadvantage, whereas their lack cannot be compensated for by all the others taken together. Boyer’s writing, on the other hand, is a mere extract of Léger’s with a short continuation. Notwithstanding that Allix, in the work *Some remarks upon the ecclesiastical history of the ancient churches of Piedmont*, which appeared in London in 1690 in quarto, as well as in the *Remarks upon the ecclesiastical history of the ancient churches of the* <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword indicates the next word is "Albigenses"</note> published in the same place in 1692 in quarto—

# Preface.

The Albigensians <note>original: "Albigenses"; a medieval religious group in Southern France often associated with the Waldensians</note> have been the subject of many new investigations, and some fortunate discoveries have been made which clarify this history and can be used very profitably by learned readers. The work undertaken by the zealous and untiring Dr. Bray <note>Thomas Bray (1658–1730), an English clergyman and founder of the SPCK</note> is of a nearly similar nature: the last two parts of that remarkable writing, which came to light in London in 1712 in large folio format, bears the following title: *Papal usurpation and persecution, as it has been exercised in ancient and modern times, with respect both to Princes and People; a fair warning to all Protestants, to guard themselves with the utmost caution against the encroachments and invasions of Popery, as they value their estates, lives and liberties, but above all, as they would preserve their consciences free from the sorest of all tyrannies and oppressions etc.* These consist of a mere collection, not of his own, but of foreign reports concerning the Waldensians. The second part contains an English translation of Perrin’s work <note>Jean Paul Perrin, a 17th-century historian of the Waldensians</note>, while the third contains the explanation and continuation of the same from the writings of Morland, Leger, Allix, and Boyer. In this selection, Perrin was preferred merely for the sake of brevity, with the express admission of the otherwise superior quality of Leger’s work; the separate edition of which in the English language he regarded as one of the most useful writings and wished to promote.

Truth and Justice are, according to the divine pronouncements that we hear from the mouths of the King and Prophet **David**, of **Isaiah**, and **Zechariah**, virtues so closely bound to one another: that the latter cannot possibly be upheld as it should be without the former. # Humble Presentation

so that he never decided anything, never received a proposal, and could never issue a decree without looking upon this beautiful symbol of his duty. It served to remind him how necessary it is to obtain the most precise knowledge of matters beforehand, before he would venture to issue a judgment, let alone put such a thing into effect. It is undoubtedly for this very reason that those to whom the **Eternal**, our **Justice**, has given the **Sword** into their hands to exercise justice against those who do evil, wish to impress these thoughts all the better upon the mind: when Justice is presented to them under the image of a completely naked woman, and when she is shown holding the **Scales** in one hand and the **Sword** in the other. This indicates that, just as one would examine the weight of accusations and offenses in vain if one did not intend to determine and exercise justice according to that measure, so too would one boast of the exercise of justice in vain if one did not first carefully weigh and examine all matters, as it were.

God, unquestionably for this reason, when He granted the High Priests a judicial authority among His people under the Old Covenant <note>The "Old Covenant" refers to the era of the Old Testament/Hebrew Bible.</note>, commanded them to wear the **Urim** and **Thummim** <note>Sacred devices used by ancient Hebrew priests to determine the will of God.</note> upon the breastplate, on which the names of all the tribes of **Israel** were engraved upon twelve precious stones. Since **Urim** signifies the light of truth, so **Thummim** shall indicate the most perfect justice; and **Thummim** is never spoken of without **Urim** preceding it: to show that he would never be able to handle justice in a perfect manner if he were not first sufficiently enlightened by the light of truth.

Since Holy Scripture places a **curse** as much upon him who **punishes the innocent** as upon him who **acquits the guilty**, it is absolutely necessary—if a judge wishes to escape such a harmful curse—that he gathers all care to be able to distinguish the innocent from the guilty; so that, after sufficient insight into both the nature of the matter and what is right concerning it, he may pass a right judgment, not from another's con- <note>original: "non ex aliena con..." likely "non ex aliena conscientia," meaning "not from another's conscience."</note>

Your Royal Highness’s upright subjects in the Valleys have very often been maliciously accused, both before your Highness and before your illustrious ancestors of most glorious memory, for these two reasons: that they are both heretics and rebels.

The first point is certainly significant; for, if they are heretics, they then deny the right faith and the true Evangelical doctrine <note>The term "Evangelical" here refers to the Protestant faith based on the Gospels</note>, they oppose the true religion, and must be regarded as a plague upon the State and the Church; but if this is not the case, then they must be regarded as upright subjects as well as true members of the latter.

This investigation concerns the cause of God and the eternal salvation or damnation of souls; it is also beyond doubt that Princes, as truly God’s viceroys on earth, are bound—both for the sake of their own soul’s salvation and to dutifully care for the welfare of their subjects—to proceed in this investigation as earnestly and carefully as is ever possible for them, and therein to follow solely and alone the light of the Holy Scriptures: since, according to Saint Paul, faith comes from the hearing of the Word of God. And Joshua was no sooner raised to be the head and leader of the people, as one sees in the 1st Chapter of his book, than God commanded him: let the book of this law not depart out of thy mouth, but meditate therein day and night, that thou mayest observe and do in all things according to that—

# Preface

Several learned and distinguished men, who were also concerned with the honor of God, suggested when their advice was sought that I should begin this history with the year 1655. They proposed I should turn immediately to describing the streams of blood of these honest confessors of the truth <note>The "confessors of the truth" refers to the Waldensians, a medieval Christian movement that predated the Reformation</note> which flowed so abundantly in that year. The cruel persecutions which our poor Waldensians endured in the said year had caused a sensation and compassion throughout all of Europe; however, they were also described quite differently by certain biased authors. Therefore, a book which presented the matter according to its true nature would have found its readers and admirers, and many would have purchased it merely for the sake of the histories contained therein.

But all of this does not satisfy me; and to be read by many merely out of curiosity was the very least intention of my labor. I therefore deemed it more useful to begin the work in question in its natural order, and through a thorough description of the matters occurring therein, to place everything that follows into a more complete light from the very start. My aim, once and for all, was to deal quite thoroughly with the actual origin and descent of the Waldensians or "Valley-people" <note>original: "Thalleute." The name Waldensian was often locally associated with the word for valleys (vallis), though historically it is also linked to Peter Waldo</note> (for this is how people used to name the regions where these people lived, whereas nowadays by "Waldensians" one understands people who are opposed to the Roman Church).

Should I achieve this goal, I had to show quite irrefutably, above all else, what these people—now known to us under the name of Waldensians—have taught since ancient times, and also what they still believe today, before I could speak of the persecutions they had to suffer for the sake of this doctrine and their faith. Regarding the fundamental doctrines necessary for salvation, they remain the same as those they profess today through the grace of the great GOD, who has given them power "to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the devil" and the Anti-Christ, according to the promise of our dear Savior in Luke chapter 10. However, because these valleys are located in the Duchy of Piedmont, I must first provide some information regarding the location and size of this Duchy.

->§. II.<-

# I. B. 1. Chapter: On the Location, Size, and Fertility

<margin>Hannibal's crossing of the Alps</margin>
The Carthaginians <note>referring to Hannibal during the Second Punic War</note> had a path made through these immense and unclimbable rocks in a very peculiar way: they first softened the stone with vinegar and afterwards hewed it out with iron tools, so that he was able to pass over unhindered with his entire great army. It is also said that King Francis I <note>King of France, reigned 1515–1547</note> had it tunneled through, thereby paving a way for himself into Italy. Although the French have since discovered a much shorter and more comfortable way to reach Italy by opening the passage over Mount Genèvre, and thus no longer find it necessary to crawl through this hole, it is nevertheless true that one can still see it today. Presumably, it will remain visible as long as the world stands, as it is hewn almost entirely through living rock. It takes nearly two hours to pass through it, which can be done quite easily and without further inconvenience with loaded mules, except that one is compelled to provide oneself with good torches because of the terrible darkness found on this unusual highway. One can find this mountain, as well as the path through it just described, marked on the attached map.

->§. III.<-

The second main river that waters Piedmont is the Tanaro; the third is the Stura, from which the large surrounding valley is also called the Valley of Stura; the fourth is the Dora <note>original: "Doria"</note>. In addition to these four main rivers, there are over twenty-eight other significant streams and brooks that water these valleys throughout and make them so fertile that, although Italy is generally considered the most beautiful country in the world, an old and very well-known proverb says: **"If Italy were a ram, Piedmont would necessarily be the kidneys."** <note>A historical metaphor suggesting Piedmont is the choicest, most nourishing part of the "body" of Italy.</note>

### §. IV.

Toward the north, Piedmont is, as it were, bordered by various beautiful valleys: for there is the aforementioned *Stura* Valley, the *Susa* Valley, and several others. Toward the west lie those which are the actual subject of this discussion, and which are commonly called the Piedmontese Valleys, the Valleys of *Angrogna*, or even simply "the Valleys"; these include the Valleys of *Luserna*, *Perosa*, and *San Martino*. To these one can also add the Valley of *Chisone*, or *Pragela*, which, although they are under the King of France, are nevertheless situated on this side of the Alps and within Piedmont. <note>The author is distinguishing between political borders and geographical/cultural regions; though under French rule at the time, Pragela was considered part of the Waldensian heartland.</note>

### §. V.

<margin>Coat of arms and parishes of the Luserna Valley.</margin>
<margin>Size.</margin>
The Valley of *Luserna* has from time immemorial carried in its coat of arms a burning torch surrounded on all sides by darkness, with the inscription: *The Light shines in the Darkness* <note>original Latin: "Lux lucet in Tenebris"</note>. From this torch—which was perhaps a foreshadowing of that Light which God would one day kindle and preserve in this region—the great valley likely received the name *Lucerna* <note>Latin for lamp/lantern</note>, rather than from the small stream *Luserna* which originates near *Rora*. It is 15 Piedmontese miles in length and comprises the communities or parishes <term>Kirchspiele: ecclesiastical districts that functioned as local administrative units</term> of *Garzigliana*, *Campiglione*, *Fenile*, *Bibiana*, *Luserna*, *Rora*, *San Giovanni*, *Angrogna*, *La Torre*, *Villar*, and *Bobbio*. To the west, it is separated from the Valley of *Queyras* by the so-called Cross Hill <note>Col de la Croix</note>, where the river *Pellice* rises, which waters nearly the entire valley. The width, however, both here and in the other valleys, is not uniform. The first five parishes just mentioned lie almost entirely in the plain toward *Turin* and *Saluzzo*, from whence in the year 1655 the poor Evangelical <note>Protestant/Waldensian</note> inhabitants were at that time through the most horri—

### §. VI.

<margin>The Community of Rora.</margin>
Rora is the smallest community of all and lies toward the south of Luserna: it extends toward Mount Bisol and ends at the Alps near Frioland and Sea Bianca. It lies in a true valley, the entire width of which is occupied by the Luserna stream, which falls here from the Alps. It is uncommonly mountainous and full of rocks; nevertheless, it is incomparably fertile, so that between the rocks—and especially in the lowest regions—one can produce wine and other fruits and cultivate the fields with profit. From the middle of these mountains, the length (or rather height) of which extends for four French miles <note>A French league or "lieue," roughly 4 kilometers or 2.5 miles</note>, up to a considerable height, one finds a great abundance of chestnuts, grain, and meadows for hay; on the highest peaks, however, the cattle are grazed for eight to ten weeks in the summer once the snow has melted.

### §. VII.

<margin>San Giovanni.</margin>
The community of San Giovanni <note>Today known as San Giovanni Pellice</note> could rightly be called a small earthly paradise, were it not situated so very close to Turin and surrounded on both the east and south by nothing but Roman Catholic neighbors and monasteries. These neighbors open their doors and gates to the community's enemies and persecutors at all times, and they themselves never cease to afflict the inhabitants to the utmost degree. Toward the south, a charming plain reveals itself with the most beautiful meadows, which border the Pellice River and are watered and made fertile by it. The rest is a single field, but so arranged that viticulture and agriculture exist there together: for here the grapevines grow very high, and with

### §. VIII.

<margin>Angrogne.</margin> The community of Angrogne begins where the aforementioned height of St. Jean ends, and climbs ever higher toward the North, until it finally ends at the high Alpine mountains of Vachera, Sian, Cella, Cella Veglia, and Infernet.

### §. IX.

<margin>The natural fortification of this region.</margin>
The Lord our God, who wished to make His wonders known here in a special way and to make this place, so to speak, the resting place for His Ark <note>A biblical metaphor comparing the Waldensian territory to the safety of Noah's Ark or the Ark of the Covenant</note>, has Himself fortified this region in a singular and miraculous manner. From below, one can reach this community from only two places: namely from the South, in the direction of Lucerna <note>original: "Lucerne"; modern Luserna San Giovanni</note>, and from the East, from the side of Bricherasio <note>original: "Bricheras"</note>. In these two places, there have been only two entrances since ancient times, which required only a few people to be stationed and guarded. Even if these gates had been taken through the violence, treachery, or cunning of the enemy, these poor people would only have had to retreat half a mile higher up. Indeed, in the area of the Barricade <note>A famous narrow pass in the Val d'Angrogna</note>, they found a secure valley provided by nature with only a single, and moreover very narrow, entrance. This path is further intersected by many rocks, rendering the place almost inaccessible. Indeed, where even the rocks no longer offer protection, one sees a terrifyingly strong wall—built without lime or sand and thus able to truly withstand wind and weather—surrounding this place, leaving open as if only a single door to enter.

Even assuming the enemy occasionally found means to take this entrance, the poor believers still found a secure and wondrous refuge on Mount Vachera. This mountain forms the exact center point of these three valleys and is of such a nature that even the most powerful enemies and cruelest persecutors could do them no harm there in the year 1655, as these accounts will better demonstrate below. Indeed, it was so far from failure that, instead, the poor fugitives of this place often ambushed the enemy from there—with the help of the Lord and the terror of the God of Jacob—in such a way...

so that they were able to retake the entire valleys from them, which they had already completely lost through the treachery of the Marquis de Pianeza <note>original: "Marquis de Pinesse"; a commander notorious for his role in the 1655 massacres</note>. Even if this place could finally no longer be held, they would still have had a retreat to the *Pré du Tour*, or the Tower-Meadow, where nature, so to speak, united all her forces to preserve these poor people when their need reached the utmost extremity. Thus, in the years 1560 and 1561, this was their only refuge when the Pope and the King of Spain united a fearsome power with that of the Duke of Savoy, Emmanuel Philibert, in order to exterminate these poorest people root and branch <note>literally "with stocking and stalk"</note> under the leadership of the Count de la Trinité. This place, however, is a large hollow between the highest and almost impassable mountains, toward the evening side <note>the West</note> of the Vachera mountains; and although one cannot reach it except with the greatest difficulty—as the passage along the bank of the Angrogne river is occupied through and through with the cruelest rocks, and this is the only access—it nevertheless has space within its district for a great multitude of people. Here, even in the thickest darkness and at the time of the harshest persecutions, the old so-called *Barbes* <note>term for Waldensian pastors, from the local word for "uncle"</note>, or Valley-Preachers, preached unhindered and maintained their colleges for the instruction of those they prepared for the ministry. From here, until the time of the Reformation, they sent out most of the teachers who had to preach the Gospel of the Lord even in the most remote lands and gather congregations for Him here and there. Indeed, young people were even sent here from other places to study, as we shall see, God willing, in the next and following chapters.

->§. X.<-

<margin>La Tour.</margin>The community of La Tour <note>Now known as Torre Pellice, the historic center of the Waldensian church.</note> follows that of St. Jean and lies along the Pelice River. It takes its name from a high and strong tower that was formerly located on a height at the mouth of the Pelice and Angrogne rivers, but was torn down again by King Francis I <note>King of France from 1515 to 1547.</note>. In this place, the Duke of Savoy built a strong fortress after the massacre of the year 1655 <note>Refers to the "Piedmontese Easter," a notorious period of state-sponsored violence against the Waldensian Protestants.</note>, so that he might have the opportunity to visit these poor people whenever he pleased and, if it were possible, to root them out entirely, as indeed almost came to pass in the years 1663 and 1664. In this community, as well as in the entire community of Villar, which likewise lies lengthwise along the aforementioned river, there is little flat ground, but very fertile fields for wine and all kinds of other fruits. Toward the south, there are indeed only chestnuts and fodder for the cattle, because the mountains that enclose them are very high and hang far over, thus causing almost nothing but shadow. On the other hand, on the hills toward the north, although they are likewise very high and rugged, wine grows in abundance, or where it is too cold for this crop, there is the finest grain and meadow-growth.

# and other circumstances of the Piedmontese Valleys.

The community of Bobbio <note>original: "Bobi"; modern Bobbio Pellice</note> is rich in wine and other fruits in its lower reaches, though cultivated with somewhat more effort; the middle elevations abound with chestnuts, and the upper regions with beautiful cattle pastures. It contains many fine and large districts, which are like so many distinct valleys, each forming its own separate community. These include, at the very top, the communities of Prali, Rodoretto, Macello, and Salza <note>original: "Prals, Roderet, Macel und Salsa"</note>; further down are Maneille, Chiabrano, and Saint Martin; Bouvils toward the north; and finally Faet and Riclaret toward the south.

<margin>Its strength etc.</margin>
In terms of natural strength, this valley surpasses all others. To say nothing of the immense mountains that surround it on all sides—which are covered with snow for at least eight to ten months of the year and are therefore impassable—one can only reach it through a single opening called the Tower Bridge <note>original: "die Thurmbrücke" or "le Pont de la Tour"</note>, which is cut through a rock. This passage is no wider than the breadth of the river running through it, the Germanasca, which is more accurately called a wild mountain stream. Over this stream stands an extraordinarily high bridge, which meets terrifying cliffs and mountains on both sides. Through these rocks, a very narrow path has been carved with the greatest effort, being no wider than is necessary to lead a horse or mule through. If this bridge is removed—which can be done with little effort and as often as one wishes—it is impossible to cross. One only needs to prevent the bridge from being rebuilt; even the women could accomplish this simply by rolling down stones, and anyone attempting the passage would very soon be forced back.

The aforementioned Alps, which enclose this valley on all sides except for the very bottom toward the east <note>original: "gegen Morgen," literally "toward the morning"</note>, are named Sea, Bianca, Chalanchia, Balma, Julian, and Bodelcol.

->§. XIV.<-

In all these valleys, especially in that of Saint Martin <note>likely the Val San Martino or a similar Alpine region</note>, there are here and there between the highest mountains and impassable rocks, great forests and thickets that could never be cleared or cultivated. From these, much turpentine, pitch, and resin are extracted. There are also found many white hares, which do not turn gray even in summer as is customary in other lands; they are also much smaller and not as good in taste as the gray ones. Likewise, there are foxes, exceedingly large pheasants, and both gray and white partridges. No less common are many wolves and bears. The former do great damage to the livestock and sometimes even to the shepherds themselves; the latter, however, damage the barley, oats, and legumes that are sown near such pastures. These animals are particularly dangerous in the month of March, when they first emerge from their dens—where they have slept all winter—and can find nothing yet to eat. For then they often come right into the stables and slaughter the poor peasants' cows, because these are scattered here and there in the woods, or they guard the rest of the livestock in places where there is the most pasture or where manuring is most necessary. They also tend to pursue the bees remarkably well and often do them great damage even in the villages, as they not only ruin the beehives but consume the wax and honey without distinction; indeed, they often climb the highest trees for the sake of this sweet fodder, and there is almost no place to which they will not make a path for themselves. ->§. XV.<-

<margin>Marmots.</margin>
On the very highest Alps, and in those places where no wood grows and there is only some pasture—at least enough for sheep to graze, which can often be tended there in summer for six or even eight weeks—one finds animals that are somewhat larger than rabbits, which are called <term>Marmots</term> <note>original: "Murmel-Thiere"</note> (<term>Marmottes</term>). Their color is a mixture of gray and reddish; the meat is good to eat and tastes almost like pork. They can whistle very loudly and are accustomed to sleeping in their burrows for eight to nine months of the year, namely as long as these mountains are covered in snow. Indeed, they sleep so soundly then that if they are pulled out of their holes during that time by those who know the location of their dens, they cannot be awakened except by great heat or very hot water. When they go out into the fields in summer, they usually stay together in groups; one must always stand sentinel on a height and give the others a signal by whistling as soon as any danger is present, whereupon they retreat most hastily back into their holes.

<margin>Their Skillfulness.</margin>
I have many times watched with pleasure the love and loyalty these little animals show one another—if I may call it such—and I could not sufficiently admire their industry and skill which they demonstrate at the time of their harvest. For when they wish to gather the provisions they need, either for the preparation of their bedding or for fodder during the winter before sleep overcomes them, they help one another bite off the grass with their teeth, dry...

<margin>A strange kind of mountain goat.</margin>
Likewise, there are many wild goats and bucks here called Chamois <term>Gemse: a goat-antelope species native to European mountains</term>, of which I will mention nothing further here, as they are well enough known in other countries. If someone is frozen stiff from the cold or has a frostbitten limb, they are accustomed to giving him only a few drops of the blood in warm wine or broth and then placing him in bed; a strong sweat then follows, and the patient soon becomes healthy again. ->§. XVI.<-

<margin>Jumarts.</margin>
<note>original: "Jumarren." A legendary hybrid animal of the Alps, long believed by locals to be a cross between a bull and a mare or jenny.</note>
These, then, are the wild animals, of which I find no mention elsewhere. Among the domestic animals, I know of only one which is entirely unknown in these northern lands, but is quite common there under the name of **Jumarts**. It is sired either by a bull and a mare, or by a bull and a female donkey: the former is somewhat smaller and is called a **Bif**, while the latter is much larger and is called a **Bas**. This last variety has a shorter upper jaw than the lower, almost like a pig, yet in such a way that the upper teeth stand one or two inches further back than the lower ones. The first variety, however, has much longer upper jaws, almost in the manner of hares and rabbits, yet so that the lower teeth likewise stand much further forward. Consequently, neither variety can graze unless the grass is long enough that they can crop it with their tongues. The head and tail resemble an ox, and they even have small humps in the places where horns grow on that animal; otherwise, however, they are shaped in all respects either like a donkey or like a horse. They possess an incomprehensible strength, though they are not even as large as a mule; they eat very little and are very fast in running, so much so that I once—specifically on the 30th of September—traveled 18 miles in a single day over nothing but mountains on one

### §. XVII.

<margin>Curiosities of these mountains.</margin>
People come from far-off places in both Italy and France to these mountains to collect many flowers and herbs for medicine, which are either difficult and rare to find elsewhere, or are not nearly comparable to these in their strength and effect. In particular, people fetch the herb *Lunaria* <note>Moonwort; historically believed to have magical and medicinal properties</note> here, which is said to grow here frequently. There are also many edible berries up to high altitudes, and certain small fruits called blueberries (*Hereles noires* <note>original: "Hereles noires" - likely a regional French dialect variant for myrtilles noires</note>), round and the size of a pea, which grow on small low shrubs. They are very good to eat and are effective against dysentery <note>original: "Ruhr" - a common intestinal infection in the early modern period</note>.

<margin>A special kind of thistle.</margin>
But what I have admired most is a certain kind of thistle, which is not unlike artichokes but does not grow as high. The fruit is like a turnip, but the leaves with which it is bordered are full of sharp spines; they can be eaten both fresh and preserved, and are also a proven remedy against the plague. The peasants—which one cannot wonder at enough—use this instead of an infallible calendar, not only when it is still fresh and green, but also when it has already been harvested and brought into their houses. Namely, they hang it entirely as it is on the wall. No matter how dry it may be, even several years old, it is nonetheless something infallible—as I myself have experienced a thousand times—that the leaves which enclose the fruit contract like a pouch and hide it as if in a hand one or two days before it rains; whereas it is again completely exposed and spread out when the weather intends to clear up again.

All these valleys, hills, and mountains are provided throughout with the most beautiful springs and the resulting streams, which carry nothing but the finest trout and perch.

### §. XVIII.

However, so that one may also know that not only the so-called Tower Meadow <note>original: "Thurm-Wieſe," referring to the Pra del Tor, a famous natural fortress of the Waldensians</note>, which we discussed above, nor the community of Angrogna, have been the only refuge for the churches of God in these valleys since time immemorial, but that the Most High has also provided the other valleys here and there with similar hidden and naturally fortified places: it should be noted that in the Lucerna Valley, the entire community of Rora—which still has a church today—as well as that of La Tour <note>Torre Pellice</note>, the entire high region from the so-called Margaret Bridge up to the top, and especially the valleys of Tuillaret, Bonnet, and Chabriol, are of the same character. <margin>Wonderful Cave.</margin> A marvelous token of such a secure dwelling, which the Almighty Creator himself prepared for his poor flock in times of extreme tribulation, can be seen in this very community, on the peak of Mount Vandelin; they have frequently used it to their greatest advantage. This is a large cave in a gap of the aforementioned mountain or rock, partly natural and partly hollowed out by art <note>meaning man-made craftsmanship</note>, vaulted at the top almost like a baking oven, and so large that three to four hundred people can stay inside. Through several cracks in the rock, light falls in, and at the same time, watch can be kept on what is happening outside. Inside, however, there are various chambers, a spring of living water, even several trees, and an oven; one also finds there the remains of a very old kneading trough and cupboards. One can only climb in from above through a single hole, which is no larger than what a single man can crawl through, such that a single person, provided with a good pike, can protect this entire fortress from an enemy invasion.

->§. XIX.<-

Just as such large caves and holes are found here and there in these valleys, in which these poor people hid themselves during times of persecution—especially their wives and children, like the dove in the Song of Solomon <note>A reference to Song of Solomon 2:14: "O my dove, that art in the clefts of the rock."</note> hidden in the rocks and crevices of the stone—their preachers visited and comforted them there, and even preached and administered the Holy Sacraments. They were often forced to do this in the thickest bushes and most hidden corners. Consequently, their enemies took the opportunity to accuse them of committing the most shameful indecencies with one another in those places, which we wish to note here in passing.

In the parish of Villar, the locations of the Guichard and La Combe valleys; in Bobi, almost all locations, especially those called the Coal Pits, Julian, Ville, Neuve, and the hills of Sarrena, Le Poy, Pontet, and others; and in the Perosa Valley <note>original: "Perouser-Thal"</note>, the great Diblon, Taluc, Balmats, Costabella, and Pevi, all possessed similar advantageous caves.

->§. XX.<-

In the parish of St. Martin, almost all the valleys lying up toward the bridge of Rabious are provided with such hiding places; especially the area of Macel, Salse, Rodoret, and Prali <note>original: "Prals"</note>, where even today one still finds the remains of such antiquities, as well as at Duchira and in the valley of Faet. The Court at Turin has always been well aware of this. Therefore, Duke Emmanuel Philibert—through the very same edict by which he granted them the freedom to live throughout all of Piedmont following the bloody persecutions of the years 1660 and 1661, though without the public exercise of their worship—nevertheless permitted such worship in the aforementioned places, and indeed in the entire region of

### §. XXI.

Before the unfortunate massacre and the conflagration of the year 1655 <note>This refers to the "Piedmontese Easter," a notorious period of state-sponsored violence against the Waldensians</note>, I possessed in my own library the Acts of the old Synods. From these, it could be seen that there were formerly many more preachers in the said valleys. They mentioned the clergy of Rodoret, Macel, and Faet in the Valley of St. Martin; those of Taluc or Great Diblon, St. Germain or Balmas in the Valley of Perouse; those of Revangie, Taillaret or Bonnet, Bezze, from the Valley of Guichard, and in the Coal Mines <note>original: "Kohlgruben"</note>, or Lucerne Valley. All these places have now been annexed to the parishes which shall be discussed in the following pages. This is presumably attributable to the extreme poverty of the inhabitants there, who have been rendered unable to support more preachers due to the excessive taxes <note>original: "Schatzungen"</note> imposed upon them.

In this chapter, nothing remains but to refute the claim of Giovanni Botero Benese <note>Giovanni Botero (c. 1544–1617) was an Italian thinker and priest; "Benese" refers to his birthplace, Bene Vagienna.</note> regarding the number of inhabitants in these Piedmontese valleys. This is a deception intended to serve a "good purpose" and gain religious merit, a tactic which is brought up quite often in this history. It is certain, however, that the number of people in this entire valley never rose so high, not by a long shot, nor did the Protestants ever make up more than half of them. In the valleys of Perosa <note>original: "Peirouse"</note> and Saint Martin, there were also at most never more than in the Valley of Lucerna, or no more than seven or eight thousand Protestants. # I. B. 2. Chapter: On the Actual Origin

...lived toward the end of the eighth century, as we shall show in detail in the 20th chapter of this book, were already known in these valleys. This Waldo possessed something quite extraordinary in: 1. his calling, 2. his doctrine, 3. his life, and 4. in the blessed fruitfulness of his preaching ministry.

->§. IV<-

<margin>1. In his calling.</margin>
1. Regarding his remarkable calling, historians relate of him that once, while he was enjoying himself with other good friends after supper, it happened that one of the company profaned the name of God in a careless manner, and immediately fell down and died. This tragic accident so moved Waldo that he resolved from that moment on to begin a different life, to care for his salvation, and no longer to strive for what is on earth, but for what is above. Thus, he intended to spend his remaining time as a fellow citizen of Israel <note>A biblical metaphor for a member of the community of faith</note> and as a faithful servant of his God, thereby becoming a worthy successor of the holy Apostles. <margin>2. In doctrine.</margin> 2. In order to reach this set goal more quickly, he devoted himself entirely to the Holy Scriptures and the reading of spiritual books. He had several of these translated into the French language, or rather did so himself; for even then he is said to have possessed a considerable knowledge of languages. To these writings, he especially added many testimonies from the Church Fathers <note>Early influential Christian theologians and writers</note>. In this work, he was greatly assisted by the books of the Albigensians <note>A medieval Christian sect, also known as Cathars, primarily in Southern France</note> from Provence, which actually originated from Piedmont and had already formed significant congregations there long before him. Their doctrine had already spread here and there in France, but mainly in Lyon, as we shall prove in what follows.

# Concerning the Name of the Waldensians

->§. V.<-

Once he had acquired great enlightenment through these means, both regarding the understanding of the Bible and the writings of the ancient Church Fathers from the first and pure age, he now began to teach these things publicly. At the same time, he turned his house into a Bethel <note>Hebrew: "House of God"</note> and a Bethlehem <note>Hebrew: "House of Bread"</note>. In this house of God, many pious souls gradually gathered, and those who hungered and thirsted for righteousness found the most precious nourishment for their souls in this house of bread. Thus, their numbers grew so rapidly in a short time that the house became too narrow, and he himself was compelled to preach in public squares. These squares were thereby transformed into churches, often containing a greater number of listeners than the largest churches in the city. Here, he no longer hesitated to teach publicly and to prove from the Bible that the Roman Church had completely fallen away from faith in Christ. He argued that she was therefore to be regarded as the Great Whore spoken of in the Revelation of John <note>original: "Offenbarung Johannis"</note>, and that she was the barren fig tree which the **Lord Jesus** cursed. Furthermore, he taught that the Pope was not to be considered the head of the Church, and that the society of monks was nothing other than a rotten and stinking carcass. He claimed that the "Mark of the Beast" could be discerned from their vows, and that purgatory, the masses, the invocation of saints, praying for the deceased, and so forth, were merely devised by Satan and the insatiable greed of the clergy <note>term: "Clerisey" - the body of ordained ministers or priests</note>.

Thus, one can still many times to this hour gather the fruit thereof in the beautiful church at Quevilli (St. Romain), which location was granted to the Reformed <note>Protestants</note> in the region of Lyon by the edicts for the exercise of their divine service.

# Of the Name Waldenses.

They turned their backs on their native city so that they might follow the Lamb <note>A biblical reference to Jesus Christ, signifying a life of pure discipleship.</note> wherever he might go, without hindrance. Thus, they preferred the Cross of Christ far above all earthly advantages, and their flight became a means of making the Gospel known far and wide—just as, in ancient times, this was the blessed fruit of the persecution that befell the faithful Christians after the stoning of Stephen. Just as the rejection of the Jews was once the wealth of the world, so one might well say that this scattering of the "Poor of Lyon" <note>original: "Armen von Lion" — the early name for Waldo’s followers who embraced voluntary poverty.</note> brought the greatest blessing to Picardy, the Netherlands, Germany, England, Poland, Moravia, and Bohemia. It was in this last country that Waldo finally reached the end of his pilgrimage, after having stayed for some time in the Netherlands and Germany. Through this dispersion, the already planted churches in Languedoc and Provence grew significantly, while those in the valleys of Dauphiné and Piedmont increased so much that they were able to spread further into Apulia, Calabria, and other regions in Italy.

### §. X.

<margin>Waldensians before Waldo.</margin>
I will, therefore, as a good and native Waldensian <note>The author identifies as a member of the Waldensian church, a medieval proto-Protestant group</note>, publicly set forth what I know of this name, while leaving the reader full freedom to judge the origin of this name as it seems most probable to them. I am at least certain that everyone must agree with me in this: even if the lands that received the divine treasure of the Gospel from this Waldo <note>Peter Waldo (c. 1140 – c. 1205), a wealthy merchant from Lyon who founded the "Poor Men of Lyon"</note>, or from his disciples, had named themselves Waldensians after him; this nevertheless does not prevent us from believing that not only had his doctrine already existed and flourished in these valleys and elsewhere, but also that those who adhered to such doctrine were generally and commonly called Waldensians.

<margin>Proof from Nicolas Vigner.</margin>
Indeed, they must have been known by this name before Waldo's time, because they had been persecuted as Waldensians and condemned to death long before. Thus, among others, Nicolas Vigner <note>A 16th-century French chronicler and physician</note> relates in his Church History, under the year 1214, that in this year seven Waldensians from Provence were burned, not to mention the others from Agenois, Périgueux, Limousin, Quercy, Rouergue, etc., and that a hundred years earlier, the heretics called Albigensians <note>A religious group in Southern France, also known as Cathars, targeted by the Albigensian Crusade</note> had descended from them. From which it must necessarily follow that the doctrine of the Waldensians was already known in the eleventh century, and its followers were labeled with the name of Waldensians, since the so-called heresy of the Albigensians had already sprung from the same at the beginning of the twelfth, namely in the year 1114, and had already

->§. XI.<-

<margin>Peter, a Monk of Vaux-de-Cernay <note>original: "Petro Monacho Vallis Sernens." Peter was a Cistercian monk and chronicler of the Albigensian Crusade.</note></margin>
Peter, a monk from the Valley of Cernay, not only confirms this observation but, in the preface of his history, makes it a hundred years older still. Namely, when he wishes to greatly extol Count Simon de Montfort—the arch-enemy and persecutor of the Waldensians and Albigensians in Provence, who, as he reports, was descended from Almaric, a natural son of King Robert of France—he gives him, among other things, the testimony that he opposed with his utmost strength the harmful sect and heresy which had already manifested itself at Orleans since 1017, and endeavored to root it out. According to this famous monk, the doctrine of the Waldensians must have been diligently planted and well-known as early as the tenth century, since by the beginning of the eleventh, namely 1017—and thus a hundred and fifty years before the time of this Waldo—it had taken root in the very heart of the Kingdom of France.

# I. B. 2. Chapter: On the True Origin

The previously cited writings, in which they are called Waldensians both before the time of the one Waldo and the other <note>The author likely refers to Peter Waldo and perhaps an earlier legendary figure or namesake</note>, add the following observation for careful consideration: why these Waldensians, whom we shall treat in this work, were given this name since ancient times as the most original, natural, and appropriate designation—namely, that they were called "Valley-People," or the inhabitants of the valleys.

->§. XX.<-

<margin>Derived from the word *Vaux*, or from the Latin and Italian names for valleys.</margin>
In the particular Waldensian language <note>Occitan or the specific Alpine dialect used by the inhabitants</note> which these people have used since antiquity and still use today, those places which we French call *Vallées* (valleys) are called *Vaux*. This designation has not only been common among these valley-inhabitants at all times, but one also finds sufficient evidence in the writings of the very oldest French authors that they labeled valleys, or those regions situated between mountains, with this very name. Among many others, the writings of Marot and Beza <note>Clément Marot and Theodore Beza, famous for their French metrical psalter</note>, which were considered exceptional models of eloquence in their time, can testify to this. As languages changed over time and much was borrowed from the Latin or Italian languages, the new word *Valli*, or even more briefly *Val* with the usual addition of *di*, gradually arose from the old word *Vaux*. This addition is specifically used by them to indicate the distinction between one *Val* or valley and another; hence it is called: *Val di San Martin*, *Val di Peirouse*, *Val di Lucerne*, and so forth.

Just as the valleys were called *Vaux* by the ancients in this manner, so too were their inhabitants called *Vaudois*. However, those who later preferred the Latin or Italian pronunciation, and accordingly the word *Val*, consequently called these people *Valdesi*,

# I. B. 2. Chapter: Concerning the True Origin

...because nothing is more common than the naming of peoples after the lands in which they dwell. Since this is to be understood not only of entire countries—just as the Italians and Germans, etc., are named after *Italy* and *Germany*—but also of smaller districts and provinces, such as *Piedmont*, *Dauphiné*, *Normandy*, and the like, from which people take their names; why then should our Valley-people <note>original: "Thals-Leute"; referring to the inhabitants of the Alpine valleys</note> not also be named after their valleys? Especially since *Thuanus* <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a famous French historian</note> and others do not only call them "Mountain-dwellers" (*Montagnards*) generally after their mountains, but have also bestowed upon them the specific names of Alpine-dwellers, *Alpinos* <note>Latin: inhabitants of the Alps</note>, and inhabitants both on this side, the far side, and within the Alps themselves: *Cisalpinos*, *Transalpinos*, *Inalpinos* <note>Latin terms for those living on the Italian side, the French side, and inside the mountain range respectively</note>.

->§. XXII.<-

<margin>
How it came to pass that this name subsequently designated a specific sect.
</margin>
How it subsequently came to pass that the name "Waldensians" came to signify the doctrine—or as those of the Roman Church speak, the "sect"—to which these people profess, is not at all difficult to guess. It is quite common, and provable from countless examples, that when one names the inhabitants of a land, one simultaneously intends the faith which they hold. If one speaks of Turks, one simultaneously understands followers of *Mahomet* <note>Muhammad</note>; if one speaks of the inhabitants of *China* and *Japan*, it is also well known that they are heathens. And when one hears of an Italian, there is no doubt that he professes the faith of the Roman Church. Thus, conversely, in *Italy*, *Spain*, and other Catholic countries, it is the same whether one calls a Swiss person from *Geneva* a heretic, a *Calvinist*, or a Protestant. After it pleased the Most High to choose *Zion* <note>A biblical metaphor here referring to the centers of the Reformation</note> for His dwelling, and to set up there the golden lampstand, from which so many other churches subsequently [lit] their lamps...

# Of the Name Waldenses.

...fires were lit. Thus, after many of our Valley-people <note>The author refers to the inhabitants of the Alpine valleys, the Vaudois or Waldenses</note> traveled to Albi, the capital of Languedoc, and there abolished the Papal abominations and introduced the pure doctrine of the Gospel, the name **Albigenses** no longer referred—as it once had—merely to the inhabitants of that city. Instead, it was understood to mean only those who were devoted to the Gospel doctrine there. And this is still so common today that, when the Albigenses are named, there will not be one in a hundred who considers their place of residence or assumes they carry this name from the aforementioned city of Albi, as the Parisians do from the city of Paris, and so forth. Rather, it is generally understood to mean all those who adhere to the doctrine that the said Valley-people introduced in that place. And this is exactly the same situation regarding the people treated in this work. For as soon as these people—who, as mentioned above, mostly lived in valleys and were therefore called **Waldenses**—began to declare themselves publicly against the Papal See, it immediately became one and the same thing to the Roman Catholics whether one spoke of a Waldensian or a heretic <term>Ketzer: a German term for heretic, historically derived from 'Cathar'</term>.

### §. XXIII.

*The naming is determined by the more prominent part* <note>original Latin: "A potiori fit denominatio"</note>, as the Latins say; and this rule also applies here. To be sure, there are other valleys in Italy, such as those of Chiavenna and Tellina, whose inhabitants have likewise maintained the pure doctrine of the Gospel since ancient times—which is why the name **Valteline** (the Teline Valley) appears even in the oldest historians. However, since these valleys do not separate Italy and France from one another in the same way the Alps do—from which the names **Cis-alpine** and **Trans-alpine Gaul** <note>Cis-alpine meaning 'this side of the Alps' (Italy) and Trans-alpine meaning 'across the Alps' (France)</note> originated—it was specifically the inhabitants of those [Alpine] valleys who, above all others, were called the Valley-people.

### §. XXIV.

From the causes cited thus far, it finally reached the point where—after the word "Waldensian" came to signify their doctrine more than their geographical residence—this name was subsequently applied to all those who confessed to their religion. Thus, Waldensians were found in all lands, as France, Italy, Germany, England, Bohemia, and other countries must testify.

# Of the Name Waldensians.

To this end, it has contributed not a little that almost all these lands received their doctrine, either mediately or immediately, from the Waldensians. And, which is well worth noting, many from said lands who were dedicated to the spiritual estate were sent into these valleys and instructed there; so much so, that the churches there were regarded by others of their ecclesiastical communion as, so to speak, high schools <note>term: high schools <note>original: "hohe Schulen," referring here to centers of higher learning or academies</note></note>.

# Of the Name Waldensian

<margin>Various other names for the Waldensians.</margin>
...sians, Albigensians, Transmontanes, Josephists, Lollards, Frairots, Fraticelli, Picards, Lyonists, Gazari (or "the pure"), Patarines (so named because they had to suffer much), and Apostolics; yet they could never be entirely rooted out or burned away. In passing, it should be noted regarding these surnames that the names Transmontani <note>original: "Transmontani" - meaning those from beyond the mountains</note>, Fraticelli, and so on, arose because they themselves, or at least their doctrine, came from the valleys on the other side of the Alps. There, the Italians commonly called them *Fraticellos* (the little brothers) or *Frairots* in the Waldensian language, as well as Gazari, Apostolics, and Patarines. This is testified by the Grand Prior Rorenco, a distinguished man from the valleys, in his own historical accounts. They were called Lollards, however, after Lollard, an excellent teacher who was likewise a native of our valleys. He wrote a beautiful commentary on the Revelation of John and finally brought the Waldensian doctrine as far as London in England, as Aubigné and others demonstrate. They first received this name in England, where the aforementioned Lollard engraved his teaching so deeply into the stones of the tower—which to this hour is called the Lollards' Tower in perpetual memory of the many believers with whom it was formerly filled—that it could never again be erased.

<margin>They are, as it were, the high schools and mothers of all other churches, according to the testimony</margin>
The other observation we made above—namely, how in former times these valleys were regarded as the high school and mother of all other churches affiliated with them, no matter how far distant they were—requires no further proof. From here, teachers and preachers (who were also called the *Barbes* <note>term: Barbes - a Waldensian term for pastor, literally meaning "uncle" to distinguish them from Catholic "fathers"</note>) were sent out into all other lands. Conversely, most of those from other countries who were dedicated to the spiritual estate were sent here to school. This is evident if one only considers what the Roman Inquisition itself says about it...

Having the freedom to proceed directly to the next point, in which they will find everything—and perhaps even more—than what they sought: I have therefore resolved, after having sufficiently explained the name and origin of the Waldensians, to now further demonstrate the nature of their doctrine and way of life. ...having been bound together with several other sermons, I have placed these in the custody of the Library of Geneva, but had the following certificate issued to me by the librarian at that time, Mr. Gerard:

> I, the undersigned, hereby testify that Mr. Léger, former preacher in the Valleys <note>The "Valleys" refers to the Waldensian ancestral lands in the Cottian Alps</note>, has actually delivered the following items to me and handed them over for necessary use into the custody of the local City Library: 1) A book written on parchment in octavo <note>A book size where the sheet is folded into eight leaves</note>, containing various works concerning the doctrines of the ancient Waldensians in their own language: 2) A bundle of records or writings, in which many important matters of the said people of the Valleys are contained, partly in the Italian and partly in the French language. In witness whereof, given at Geneva on November 10, 1662. Signed: Gerard, first preacher at the Collegiate Church and Librarian.

Yet another list of such writings was found, particularly in the Valley of Pragelas <note>A valley in the Piedmont region</note>, which belongs to the King, and where the frequently dispatched "murder-burners" <note>original: "Mordbrenner" — a term for arsonists or those sent to destroy by fire during religious persecutions</note> could not penetrate as often as into the other valleys under Savoyard jurisdiction. This list was sent by the assembly of the Valley clergy to Mr. Perrin, a clergyman in Dauphiné. That he actually received it, and drew most of the material for his *History of the Waldensians and Albigensians* (published in Geneva in 1619) from it, he himself acknowledges on page 57 in the seventh chapter of that book. He cites there not only the most important pieces contained in this list, but also various other works besides. Mr. Perrin’s own words regarding this are as follows: "We have," (he says in the place just cited) "first of all, another New Testament in our hands, which, although in the ancient Waldensian language, is nevertheless very neatly written on parchment."

# and printed documents.

All these books are written in the Waldensian language <note>A Romance dialect related to Occitan, used by the Waldensian community in the Middle Ages</note>, partly as it is spoken in Provence and partly as it is spoken in the Piedmontese regions. They are perfectly sufficient to guide those who read them both toward true faith and a godly life. The doctrine contained therein agrees perfectly with that which the Reformed Church confesses today. This has been confirmed to us, among others, by Mr. Theodore Tronchin <note>original: "Theodorus Fronschine"</note>, preacher and professor of theology at Geneva, through irreproachable testimony dated November 17, 1656, after he had most carefully reviewed and examined all the writings sent to him by the aforementioned Mr. Perrin.

From all of this, the conclusion follows naturally: a doctrine which has remained intact to this day—despite all the human cunning and artifice employed against it from time to time—contains nothing "new," except in the eyes of those buried in ignorance, whose ancestors denied it only because they were unable to recognize its inner worth. The Lord of St. Ferriol, a preacher at Orange, collected many of these books out of a holy curiosity and showed them to the Lord of St. Aldegonde. The latter subsequently mentions them in his first *Tableau* <note>referring to Philippe de Marnix, Lord of Saint-Aldegonde's work "Tableau des différends de la religion"</note> on page 153, along with many others written in very ancient script, which are held in the famous library of Mr. Joseph de l'Escale <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger, a renowned French religious scholar</note>.

Regarding the ancient Waldensian Bible, to which I shall refer in the continuation of this work, I found it by chance in the mountains of the Valley of Cluson, and I still have it in my possession.

## The Fourth Chapter,

->Contains within it the first specimen of Waldensian doctrine, from the so-called "Noble Lesson" from the year 1100.<-

Since we shall cite various testimonies from members of the Roman religion, both here and in the course of this book, in order to maintain the antiquity of the Waldensian churches and their unadulterated, true propagation since the times of the Apostles: the reader will at the same time learn to clearly recognize the content of their doctrine from time to time. This will become particularly evident to him from the conclusion of the eighth century onwards, at which time the excellent and courageous Archbishop Claudius <note>Claudius of Turin (died c. 827), a bishop famous for his opposition to the veneration of images, often claimed by later Protestants as a precursor</note> departed with them from the communion of the Church of Rome,

# From the Noble Lesson of the Year 1100.

since they would by no means agree to, nor confess, the veneration of images and other superstitious practices that were being introduced into the Church at that time. However, it is only fair that we first hear them speak for themselves. They themselves know best what they believe; thus, they can best give an account and answer for it themselves. We are, for that very reason, also bound to give credit to them above all others in this matter. I have therefore collected in this work many beautiful writings of their ancient doctrine, and have drawn them with all faithfulness and care from the first manuscripts—which we mentioned in the preceding chapter—and which are preserved in the famous book collections at Cambridge and Geneva. I therefore have no doubt that this will be all the more pleasant to my readers, as these writings are so rarely to be found; for their enemies spared neither cunning, nor diligence, nor money to root out their memory from the world. And they were occupied in this not only during public persecutions, but also at times when everything appeared outwardly peaceful. Indeed, it affected me personally: while I had given every possible effort since the year 1640 to seek out and collect the antiquities of the Waldenses <note>The Waldenses were a medieval Christian movement often persecuted as heretics by the Roman Catholic Church.</note> here and there, all of them together were stolen from me by the murderers sent into my fatherland in the year 1655. As they themselves later confessed to me, these were carried away with the rest of my book-stock to Turin and Saluzzo, without a single leaf remaining to me. One can easily imagine that it must have cost me incredible effort to seek out these remnants anew in the neighboring valleys, which stood under the French scepter and were therefore not quite so exposed to the consuming fire of the Roman See <note>The "Roman See" refers to the Papacy or the central authority of the Roman Catholic Church.</note>. I have retained and set down the most important of these in their own language <note>original: "in ihrer eigenen Sprache" — referring to the Occitan/Waldensian dialect</note> without violating a single syllable, partly to give the curious reader all the more pleasure

# I. B. Chapter 4: The First Proof of Waldensian Doctrine

All Cardinals, Bishops, and clergy together,
Do not have the power to absolve in such a way, or to grant forgiveness
For mortal sins to any creature.
<margin>Only GOD alone.</margin> Only GOD alone forgives sin, and no one else.
On the other hand, it is the duty of teachers <note>The original German uses "Lehrer" (teachers), referring to the Waldensian pastors or "Barbes."</note>,
To preach to the people, and to pray,
To diligently lead them to the pasture of the divine Word.
To punish sinners with good discipline,
And to exhort them to repentance through good examples,
So that they may follow the Lord Jesus, and do His will,
Holding fast to His commandments,
<margin>To flee the Anti-Christ.</margin> And that they may know how they should flee the Anti-Christ,
Without allowing themselves to be misled by his words or works.
For the Scripture says, there are already many Anti-Christs,
For all those are Anti-Christs who are contrary to the Lord Christ.

<column-break/>

And all the Cardinals, and all the Bishops, and all the Abbots, all these together,
Have not so much power of duty to absolve that they can pardon,
Any creature for even one mortal sin.
Only God pardons: for another cannot do it.
But this they ought to do, those who are Pastors,
They ought to preach to the people and remain in prayer,
And feed them often with divine doctrine.
And chastise the sinning, giving them discipline,
That is, true admonition so that they may have repentance,
But in following Jesus Christ, and doing His pleasure,
And keeping firmly that which He has commanded,
And being very well-advised to flee the Anti-Christ,
That we believe not in his deed, nor in his word.
For according to the Scripture now there are many Anti-Christs,
For Anti-Christs were all those who are contrary to Christ.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Noble Lesson" (La Nobla Leçon), a foundational Waldensian text dated here to the year 1100. It outlines the comprehensive scope of the work, which serves as a biblical compendium and a critique of Roman Catholic practices.</meta>

### From the Noble Lesson of the Year 1100.

This sample may suffice from this noble teaching, since the entire manuscript is too extensive to be included here in its entirety. For it contains: 1) a beautiful summary of the history of Creation; 2) an account of the nature of the first world up until the times of the Great Flood. Following this, it 3) continues further until Abraham; 4) from him further until Moses, giving us a brief overview of the moral, civil, and liturgical Law <note>The author refers to the tripartite division of Mosaic Law: moral, civil, and ceremonial.</note>. Then it describes 5) the sins of the Israelite people and the judgments of God which they drew upon themselves, along with various beautiful lessons for our edification; 6) it treats David and other pious kings and prophets; 7) the Babylonian captivity; 8) the return from said captivity. Following this, 9) the coming of Christ in the flesh is treated, wherein one finds a brief summary of the entire teaching of the Gospel and an exceptionally beautiful comparison of the Law with the Gospel. 10) The sending of the Apostles, the condition of the first Christians, and the outpouring of the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost. Finally, 11) the author gives us an excellent antidote against the grossest errors of the Papacy, proceeding in the same manner as the sample we heard above, against the money-grubbing of the priests <note>original: "Geldschneiderey der Pfaffen"</note>, auricular confession, soul-masses <note>Masses said for the souls of the dead in Purgatory.</note>, deceptions regarding absolution, and the misuse of the "Keys" <note>The "Power of the Keys" refers to the authority to forgive or retain sins.</note> by the Antichrist. Accordingly, this spiritual poem is rightly to be regarded as a *Summa* <note>A comprehensive summary or compendium of a subject.</note> of both the history and the doctrine of the entire Old and New Testaments; since not only the asserted dogmas but also the controversies regarding faith, customs, and life are found here. Therefore, these wise teachers, with good deliberation, placed this heavenly treasure in verse and in the common tongue

# Concerning the Doctrine of the Waldenses

Through the fear of the Lord, one finds the joys of Paradise. For the love of God and of one's neighbor is charity <note>The original uses "charità" and "Liebe," referring to the theological concept of selfless, divine love</note>. And he who has charity has God. And where he has God, he departs from worldly things; and he who loves God fears the pains of Hell and desires the joys of Paradise, to which he hopes to arrive, and where there is no fear of death nor fear of enemies. There is Life without Death. Therefore, through the love of God and of one's neighbor, eternal life is acquired. And Saint Paul says: *The love of God and of the neighbor works no evil.* <note>original: "l’amor de Dio e del proyme non obra mal"</note> And he who does these things shall not fall into sin. But he who inclines himself toward temporal things distances himself from the love of God, for the riches of this world cannot be acquired without sin. For if one does not lose, the other cannot gain; and he who gains rejoices, while he who loses is saddened. But there are many who hope to give alms from the sweat of others, and they despoil one to clothe another. But alms made with iniquity are despised

<column-break/>

Through the fear of God, one finds the joy of Paradise. For friendship with God and one's neighbor is love; but whoever dwells in love, he dwells in God, and whoever is in God, he rids himself of worldly things. He who loves God fears Hell and wishes for the joy of Paradise, where he also hopes with certainty to arrive, in order to remain there eternally: for then the fear of death and of all enemies will have an end. For there is life without death. And thus one obtains eternal life through love toward God and toward one's neighbor. So also says Paul: **Love for God and the neighbor does nothing evil,** and whoever stands in the same shall not fall into sin. Whoever, on the <margin>an obstacle.</margin> contrary, hangs with his heart upon temporal things, he removes himself from this love; since the treasures of the world are hardly acquired without sin. If one is to win here, the other must lose, and the latter will grieve over it, while the former rejoices over his gain. Many a man gives from the [sweat of] strangers <note>The text cuts off, referring to the practice of giving alms using wealth stolen or extorted from others</note>
