It emphasizes that charity and the fear of God are the paths to the eternal joys of Paradise.</summary>

# Book 1, Chapter 5: The Second Test

...the sweat of his brow as his alms, and takes the garment from one to cover the nakedness of another. Such an alms, however, which is mixed with injustice, is an abomination to the Lord. Therefore, Saint Augustine says:

<margin>The right kind of alms.</margin>
That is a right gift, pleasing to God, which you give from your own property, not that which you give from robbery or usury <note>Usury: the practice of lending money at unreasonably high interest rates, historically considered a sin.</note>. For giving alms from stolen goods or usury is not a work of mercy, but rather a nourishment of sin.

<margin>Greed is a root of all evil.</margin>
O my brothers, what shall we say of those rich men who gather treasures and do not know for whom? Abuse of divine mercy.

<column-break/>

For, what thing is more to you: to have your soul, or your children, who shall be strangers to you after death?

Also, he lives badly who departs from the mercy of God, even though He Himself is pious, patient, and merciful, and waits for us to amend ourselves. For He does not only give pardon to the repentant; but promises to them the reward, and to those persevering He gives the Crown. We have an example in the thief <note>original: "leiron"</note>, who was converted on the Cross, and earned the right to hear:
> I say truly to you, that you shall be today <note>original: "encoy" — a specific Romansh/Occitan term for "today".</note> with me in Paradise.

Therefore, that man is always prepared. For the Lord will come in the hour which we do not know. Therefore let us work while we have time. And let us not wish to delight in this world, which is full of iniquity, in which our life is full of temptations.

# 88 I. B. 6. Chapter: The Third Trial

<margin>The 1st Reason.</margin> The Savior himself strengthens His own, and says: Do not fear those who kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul. <note>Matthew 10:28</note> All who persecute you are like madmen who do not see or know themselves; after they have cut a corner of another's garment away, they thrust the sword into their own bodies. For what the garment is to the body, such is the body to the soul.

<margin>The 2nd Reason.</margin> If the righteous man suffers much here in time for the Lord’s sake, his reward for it shall be great in eternity. Consider what the Savior has endured for you: you need not suffer so much evil for the love of God; nor would you take as much upon yourself for His love as He has taken upon Himself for yours.

<margin>The 3rd Reason.</margin> Furthermore, your enemy has no more power over you than God permits him: so look not so much at this power which God permits the wicked, but rather at the reward which God has promised you in return.

<margin>The 4th Reason.</margin> Hear, therefore, what He Himself says of this glorious reward of grace in His Word.

<column-break/>

The Lord comforts the good men, saying: *Do not wish to fear those who kill the body, but cannot kill the soul.* <note>original: "non vollia temer aquilli lical aucion lo Cors, ma non pon aucir l'Arma."</note> All those who oppose you are raving, for they do not see, nor do they know themselves, but they act as if a madman held the sword in his hand and cut the tunic of another, and afterwards struck himself in the belly. For just as the tunic is the clothing of the body, so the body is the clothing of the soul. And if the just man shall suffer any evil thing in this world for the love of God, his reward <term>guiardon: a recompense or prize</term> shall endure without [end].

Look upon the evils which the Lord has sustained for you: you will never suffer as many evils for the love of God as the Lord has sustained for you. You will never be placed on such a cross as the Lord was placed.

Do not wish to believe that your enemy has power over you, except that which God grants: and do not think of the power that God grants to wicked men, but think of the reward that God promises to you.

Hear what the Scripture says regarding the reward which God promises to you.

Now, whoever does not want to suffer with Christ, he also does not want to be a member of his body; and whoever will not bear his cross here, he also cannot come to him there.

<margin>Distress from childhood onward.</margin>

Therefore Saint Peter praised the life of Lot: for he had suffered tribulation among evil men. And Saint Paul says: "perils among false brothers."

# I. B. 6. Chapter: The Third Proof

The olive that is pressed the most gives the finest oil and the best wine <note>The author likely refers to the "must" or essence of the fruit here</note>. The better the grain is tossed, the better it is cleansed from the chaff: and whoever wishes to be truly purified must only endure and remain still patiently before his adversaries. And the wise man says that whoever is truly patient has a certain hope of one day being received into the brotherhood of the angels.

A patient person does not become angry, and nothing is more certain than that God loves the one who hates the world out of love for Him. The pious person should rejoice despite all his toil, labor, and poverty, and comfort himself with the eternal life that God has promised him in return: whereas the godless person, despite all the joy, pleasure, and abundance he possesses, has cause to mourn constantly. For in exchange for such earthly joy, pleasure, and wealth, God will one day send him eternal pain.

God Himself takes pleasure in the one who carries his cross patiently. Saint Sixtus writes: Do not kill yourself, but if someone wishes to kill you, so

The olive, when it is most pressed, the dregs go to one side and the oil remains clear. Just as the wheat, when it is most threshed, the straw goes to one side and the grain to the other. But if you wish to be good while you are in this life, suffer the evil men near you in patience. And the wise man says, the truly patient one hopes to have the brotherhood of the angels.

The truly patient one does not become angry. For it is a certain thing that God loves those who will hate the world for the love of Him. The good man ought to rejoice in pain, and in his labor, and in his poverty. For God promises him eternal life. And the wicked man ought to weep in his joy, and in his delight, and in his riches. For through such joy and through such riches, God grants to him eternal pain.

God is pleased by that one who carries in patience all the evils which are done to him. And Saint Sixtus says: do not kill yourself, but if anyone shall kill you, do not let it displease you.

# I. B. 7. Chapter: The Fourth Proof

Only believe, and He will give it to you.

<margin>It is easy.</margin>
Prayer is also nothing difficult. In all places and at all times one can lift up holy hands. Even if you are not in a position to say much, simply send your thoughts and your desires to GOD: for this too is called praying. David says: **The LORD hears the desire of the miserable.** <note>Psalm 10:17. The German "Elenden" here refers to the afflicted or those in spiritual poverty.</note> That is to say, the desire of the lowly, who are so poor that they can do or bring nothing more than sighs and prayers: God gladly hears such a prayer of the heart: **The LORD hears the desire of the miserable.** Thus, prayer is and remains something high, something useful, and also something easy. We see this also with the disciples in the Gospel. These knew well that they could learn nothing better: therefore, as good students, they turn to the best Master and ask that He should teach them to pray: **Lord**, they say, **teach us to pray!** Jesus answers hereupon: **When you pray, you shall not babble much: For—**

Believe that you shall receive it and it shall be done for you.

It <note>original: "Illi" referring to prayer (oraison)</note> is most easy, for a man can pray in every place and at every time, nor is it necessary to seek anything outside of oneself; for only to think well and to desire well is to pray, whence the Lord grants the desire of the poor, that is, of the humble; or the poor are the infirm, those who cannot speak nor do anything, but can only pray with desire, and God is ready to grant the prayer of their desire, even as David said: the Lord grants the desire of the poor: therefore praying is a work so honorable, so profitable, and so easy, and for this reason, as it is said in the Gospel, the Apostles asked Christ, as good Disciples of a good Master, that He should teach them to pray: for they knew that they could not learn a better lesson, and they said to Him: O Lord, teach us to pray: to which He responding said, when you pray, do not wish to speak many—

The first petition is: Hallowed be Thy name. We pray herewith for the deliverance from all sins, but especially from intemperance <note>German: Unmäßigkeit; here implying both lack of moderation and impurity</note>, and for the gift of purity. We are indeed called Christians after Christ, that is, disciples, servants, and children of Jesus Christ: but this name is defiled, held in low esteem, and blasphemed by us when we live in all kinds of impurity and intemperance; whereas it is hallowed when we abstain from all defilement in thoughts, words, and deeds, and cleanse ourselves from our former sinful way of life through righteous repentance. For in this way true Christians are cleansed, that is, have been sanctified. For holy is he who is without stain or reproach. But the sin of intemperance is such a defilement. For just as a stain takes away the natural color from cloth or wool: so it also happens to us with this sin. It robs us of the innocence that we obtained through baptism, and of all virtues. Just as often as the color [stains] a cloth from within and

# I. B. 7. Chapter: The Fourth Test

The first kind of poverty, of which *David* <note>The author likely refers to the Wisdom literature traditionally associated with Davidic tradition, specifically Proverbs 28:19</note> says, "whoever follows idleness shall have poverty enough," we should flee; the second we should patiently endure, and the third we should take upon ourselves with joy; thus we shall become truly poor in spirit. Of this poverty *James* speaks when he says: "Has not God chosen the poor of this world, who are rich in faith and heirs of the Kingdom which He has promised to those who love Him?" <note>James 2:5</note> And *Augustine* speaks of it in the person of *Christ* thus: "I sell: and what then? The Kingdom of God, Heaven, the Kingdom of Heaven. And how dear? Merely for poverty: for here is rest for labor, life for death: in a word, the Kingdom of Heaven is for the poor." Therefore, whoever wishes to be saved must become poor in spirit, and follow in the footsteps of Jesus with the Apostles and all true Christians, and despise temporal things. To this end, the works of mercy serve, when one, like *Zacchaeus*, gives half of his goods to the poor, and if one has <meta>de-</meta>

<column-break/>

we must patiently sustain the needy state, and embrace the voluntary state with all our heart; in this way we are made poor in spirit. Of this poverty Saint James says: "Did God not choose the poor in this world, rich in faith, heirs of the Kingdom, which God has promised to those who love Him?" And Saint Augustine says in the person of Christ: "I have something to sell, I have something to sell; and what? The Kingdom of God, the Heavens, the Kingdom of the Heavens." In what manner is it bought? Through poverty; rest for labor; life for death; the Kingdom of the Heavens belongs to the poor. Therefore it is necessary for it to be acquired through poverty, just as the Holy Apostles did, and those who followed them; that is, all the religious men <note>original: "baron Religios" - a term used in Occitan to denote noble or distinguished men of faith</note> who leave all temporal things and follow Christ through poverty; furthermore, it is necessary for it to be bought from the poor through works of mercy given to the poor; just as Zacchaeus did, who gave to the poor half of his goods, and if he had defrauded anyone, he returned it fourfold; and in this <meta>way</meta>

<margin>Value of the Kingdom of Heaven.</margin>
No one can excuse themselves from the purchase of this Kingdom; for as Gregory <note>Saint Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a Church Father frequently cited by the Waldensians.</note> says, the Kingdom of God is worth as much as you have. To the holy Apostles, it was worth a ship and their nets; to Zacchaeus, it was worth half of his goods; to a poor widow, it was worth two small coins <term>mites: small copper coins of negligible value</term> which she placed upon the altar of God; and to another, it was worth a cup of cold water.

As Gregory says: Furthermore, nothing is cheaper when it is bought, nor dearer when it is possessed. But if you say that you cannot even have a cup of cold water to give to the poor, you still cannot excuse yourself from the purchase of the Heavenly Kingdom: for if you have nothing else, a good will is sufficient for you, which God accounts to you as the deed itself. For as the Apostle says, the will is accepted according to what it has, and not according to what it does not have. <note>Reference to 2 Corinthians 8:12.</note>

"Thy kingdom come" means, therefore, just as much as: make us, O God, truly poor in spirit, so that we may become capable of inheriting your kingdom; make us pious and compassionate, so that we, as the poor, may attain the possession of your kingdom. Conversely, deliver us from greed and all evil desires. For the kingdom of heaven will be closed to all who are greedy and lustful for money.

### The Third Petition.

<margin>
Against
negligence.

The third petition: "Thy will be done," contains the longing for divine assistance against negligence and laziness. Idleness and laziness is a mother of lust and intemperance, a seed of discord and disunity, and a tinder for envy against those who are diligent in doing good. Commonly, man is so disposed that, even when he does some good, he does it only negligently, coldly, and with reluctance, and therefore instead of the blessing, the curse

# I. B. 7. Chapter: The Fourth Trial

The soul can never be idle: it is occupied either with something good or with something evil. Idleness is therefore called a pit <note>original: "Grube"</note> in which all vices run together; and just as in the lowest part of a ship, because of its impurity, all kinds of adders and vermin easily breed: so also in an idle soul, all kinds of evil thoughts, consents, and pleasures arise. Therefore Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great, c. 540–604 AD</note> says: After Solomon turned his heart away from the wisdom of God, he also no longer gave ear to discipline outwardly. Therefore, man has great need to stand diligently on guard, and to care carefully for his heart, so that the enemy may never find this fortress empty, but always well-fortified with good thoughts, words, or works. Jerome <note>St. Jerome, c. 347–420 AD, known for his Bible translation</note> says to that end: always practice something good, so the devil will never find you idle. We thus wish to be freed from this so dangerous sin of laziness <note>original: "Faulheit"</note> when we pray, "Thy will be done": and on the other hand, we pray for the virtue
->of<-

<column-break/>

if it is not occupied in good, it is occupied in evil. And therefore it is said, that idleness <note>original: "oççiofità"</note> is the bilge <note>original: "fentina," the lowest part of a ship where waste collects</note> of all evils; the bilge is the lowest place in the ship, and serpents and reptiles are easily born there. In the same way, it often happens that in the idle soul are born evil thoughts, consents, and delights. And Gregory says: the heart of Solomon abandoned altogether the wisdom of God, and therefore no discipline guarded him from without. Therefore it behooves man to watch over the guarding of himself, and to guard curiously <note>meaning "with great care" or "meticulously"</note> the castle of the heart and of the soul, and to occupy himself always in some good thought, or speech, or work; just as Jerome says, always do some thing of good, so that the Devil finds you occupied. Therefore we ask to be removed from us this most dangerous sin of sloth <term>acidia: a state of spiritual apathy or "spiritual sloth," considered one of the seven deadly sins</term>, when we say, "Thy will be done." And we ask here to be given the virtue of devotion and of true love, and of good work; but

# Concerning the Doctrine of the Ancient Waldensians.

<column-break/>

The devout man, inflamed with Divine love, never wishes to be idle, but studies always to occupy himself in doing the will of God on Earth, even as the saints who are in Heaven have done and continue to do.

But we cannot do this without Divine grace <note>original: "Devina gracia"</note>; therefore we must ask: *Thy Will be done, even as it is done in Heaven, so let it be done on earth;* for the Will of God is done in Heaven without intermission, without sadness, without murmuring or contradiction: in this same way all good Christians study to do on earth. As Gregory <note>Pope Gregory the Great (c. 540–604), a favorite authority for medieval reformers</note> says: *the proof of the work is the fulfillment of love; and the love of God is never idle, for it works great things, if it exists; but if it refuses to work, it is not love.* And Saint Bernard <note>Bernard of Clairvaux (1090–1153), a Cistercian abbot and influential mystic</note> says: *O good Jesus, thy love is never idle; those who love thee do not grow sluggish; to speak of thee is perfect consolation, to speak of thee is full refreshment,*

<column-break/>

of devotion, of love, and the exercise of good works. For whoever is devout, and loves God from the heart, is never idle, but is always mindful that the will of the Most High may be done by him on Earth, just as it is by all the saints in Heaven.

<margin>Necessary assistance of Grace.</margin>
Because, however, we are capable of nothing without the grace of God, we certainly have cause to pray to Him: *Thy will be done on earth as it is in heaven.* Just as the will of God happens in heaven without ceasing, with a joyful heart, without murmuring or contradiction; even so an upright Christian strives that it may happen through him on earth in the same way. Therefore Gregory says: *Love is the touchstone of works: for true love for God is never idle, but always occupied in something great: where no good works are to be found, there is also no love.* Bernard: *O good JESUS, thy love is not idle, it is also active in the hearts of Thine own:*

It cites Church Fathers like Gregory and Bernard to support the necessity of divine grace in fulfilling God's will.</summary>
<keywords>Waldensians, Divine Grace, Good Works, Love of God, Lord's Prayer, Saint Gregory, Saint Bernard, Devotion</keywords>

<margin>Matthew</margin>
"Therefore, Chrysostom <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407), an influential Early Church Father known for his eloquent preaching.</note> says that even the evil which a man allows to rule over him is his god. If you ask, 'How can I know what I love more: God, or that which God has forbidden me to love?' then simply take note of the following: That which a man regards the least in an extreme case of necessity is the loss that weighs least heavily upon him; conversely, that for which he provides the most in such a case is what he loves the most. Thus, a merchant, in the face of the apparent danger of an inevitable shipwreck, throws all his goods into the water and cares only for his life: for life is dearer to him than all his possessions. The test will now be easy to make. If you are certainly assured that you would rather suffer the greatest temporal damage to your fortune, in your household, to your livestock, yes, even to your kin and your own body, than do anything that could cause you to forfeit the grace of God: then you have a sure testimony that you love God more than anything in the world. On the contrary, if you would rather offend God than abandon something temporal, you thereby make it known that you love earthly things more than God; consequently, you are an idolater <term>Götzen-Diener: literally a servant of idols</term>. <margin>Luke 14:26</margin> This is what the Savior says:

> *"If anyone comes to me and does not hate his father, mother, wife, children, brothers, sisters, and even his own life, he cannot be my disciple."*

If they were truly earnest about honoring the invisible Creator in his visible creatures, they would only need to do good to their poor neighbor, whom God himself made according to his own image. The image of God is in all people: but only those are like him who have a pure heart and a loving soul. If you wish, therefore, to honor your God in deed and in truth, you must give place to the truth and do good to those who actually bear the image of God upon themselves. One honors God in his image by feeding the hungry, giving drink to the thirsty, and clothing the naked. But fall down before your stone image as much as you like, pray to your wooden god ever so fervently, make images for yourself and adorn them ever so beautifully; they remain merely images without life, in which nothing is to be found that has anything divine about it, while you overlook your fellow Christian <note>original: "Neben-Christen"</note> who actually bears the image of the Lord upon himself; and tell me afterwards whether, in all of that, even the slightest honor is rendered by you to the true God? *Chrysostom* <note>John Chrysostom (c. 347–407 AD), an influential Early Church Father and Archbishop of Constantinople known for his eloquence.</note> says in his explanation of the Gospel of *Matthew*: It is not gold, but man who is made according to the image of God. Imperial coins are made of gold and silver, but the coin upon which the Most High has stamped his image is man. For this reason, even in the most ancient Law, the Jews were commanded to abolish all images and figures of men, animals, and other things, and to honor only the true God alone; therefore *Samuel* also had to say to the whole house of *Israel*:
<margin>1 Samuel 7:3</margin>
"If you return to the Lord with all your hearts, then put away the foreign gods and the *Ashtaroth* <note>Astaroth or Ashtoreth: ancient Canaanite goddesses whose worship was forbidden to the Israelites.</note> from among you, and direct your hearts to the Lord, and serve him only, and he will deliver you out of the hand of the *Philistines*." How much more should a Christian now tear his heart away from all such things, and lift it up only to where *Christ* is, sitting at the right hand of his Father?"

### I. B. 9. C. Interpretation of the Waldensians

### Explanation of the Third Commandment.
->You shall not misuse the name of the Lord, your God, etc.<-

<margin>The ultimate purpose of this commandment.</margin>
In this commandment, all false, deceitful, and useless swearing <note>original: "Schweren"; refers to the taking of oaths</note> is forbidden, as we also find in the third book of Moses <note>The Book of Leviticus</note> in the 19th chapter; and in the Proverbs <note>The author likely refers here to the Wisdom of Sirach/Ecclesiasticus 23:11, often cited in this context</note> it is said: He who swears often, sins often, and the plague shall not depart from his house. An oath appeals to the omniscience of God and is an end to strife, consequently it is a form of divine service <term>Gottesdienst: worship or religious service</term> that belongs to God alone. Therefore, whoever swears by the elements or other things sins against God; for this reason, the Savior himself forbids it and says: I say to you, that you shall not swear at all, neither by heaven, nor by the earth, nor by Jerusalem, nor shall you swear by your head, but let your speech be yes, yes; no, no; whatever is more than these comes from evil; and James says: above all things, my brothers, do not swear, neither by heaven, nor by the earth, nor by any other oath: but let your word be yes, that is yes, and no, that is no, so that you do not fall into hypocrisy.

### Explanation of the Fourth Commandment.
->Remember the Sabbath day, to keep it holy, etc.<-

<margin>Four things that belong to the Sabbath celebration.</margin>
One hallows the Christian Sabbath day, or Sunday, and celebrates it when one pays attention to four points. First, that one rests entirely from all kinds of labor on that day; second, that one commits no sin at all on this day; third, that one is diligent in good works; and finally, that one does something that brings a spiritual advantage and benefit to the soul.

<margin>1. To do no work at all.</margin>
Regarding the first kind of this celebration, it is said: Six days
you shall

## Explanation of the Sixth Commandment.
->You shall not kill.<-

<margin>The purpose of this commandment.</margin>
To be sure, in this commandment, killing is specifically forbidden, but at the same time, so is every insult and harm to one's neighbor in general, no matter what form it may take. To this belong all slanders, insults, and abusive words, as well as all physical injuries through blows and the like. Of the first kind of such insult, which is included here under the word "kill," the Savior speaks when he says in Matthew chapter 5: Whoever is angry with his brother is in danger of the judgment. Likewise James chapter 1: Man's anger does not produce what is right before God. And Paul to the Ephesians in the 4th chapter: Do not let the sun go down on your anger. Whoever is angry with his brother without cause is in danger of the judgment; for a righteous zeal is by no means forbidden here. It would certainly bring little advantage to the doctrine of truth if one were not allowed to be zealous for the sake of the faith; and how would it look for the administration of justice and the punishment of evil if one wanted to banish all anger from the world? A righteous anger is rather a mother of discipline <term>Zucht: refers to moral upbringing, order, and corrective discipline</term>, and those sin who remain silent when they should speak with zeal. An untimely patience is the seed from which much evil grows; it nourishes unrestrained freedom and causes both the good and the evil to forget their duty. If evil is...

"We are alienated from the life that is from God. Salvation and all blessedness are far removed from the sinner, but the knowledge of sin leads to repentance: for no one is truly known to himself. ## The Tenth Chapter.

The seventh proof of the faith of the Waldensians <note>A medieval Christian movement that predated the Reformation, often persecuted for their beliefs</note>, containing their formula of confession as they have maintained it from olden times, and as it is found in their own language in the book *The New Comfort* <note>original: "lo Novel Confert" - a significant Waldensian religious text</note>, which is mentioned on page 23 of the *Book of Martyrs*. The beginning of it reads as follows:

->O God of Kings, and Lord of lords, I confess to You, for I<-
->am that sinner who has greatly offended You, etc.<-
<note>original: "O Diou de li Rey, e segnor delli segnor, yo me confesso à Tu, car yo fey aquel peccador que t'ay mot offendà, &c." translated from the original Occitan/Waldensian dialect.</note>

"O You God of Kings, and Lord of all lords, before You I confess, as a poor sinner who through ingratitude has grievously sinned against You, all my misdeeds. I have no excuse before me, for You Yourself have shown me what was good or evil. Your omnipotence has not remained hidden from me, Your wisdom I have recognized, Your justice has become manifest to me, and Your goodness I have been able to perceive only too clearly. Nevertheless, I have done evil, and my own corruption has been to blame for it. Forgive me, O Lord, and awaken in me a true repentance. I have [sinned] against You..."

# I. B. 10. C. Confession Formula of the Waldensians

> "...despised through my pride, I have not believed in your wisdom,
> and have not believed your commandments, but have transgressed them in manifold ways. All of this bows me down before you, and awakens an inner grief within me. I have not feared your justice and your judgments, but have done evil from my youth onward. Your goodness has not been as dear to me as it well should have been. In this wretched state, I have all too lightheartedly given ear to the Devil; I have turned my face toward haughtiness <note>original: "Hoffart," an archaic term for extreme pride or arrogance</note>, but turned my back upon humility.
> This evil desire is so firmly rooted within me that I must be eternally lost and damned, unless you are willing to be gracious. I cling to avarice, love vain glory, and am ungrateful toward those who do good to me.

**The Barba** <note>original: "Lo Barba." A term used by the Waldensians for their pastors or uncles/elders.</note>
If you were asked, who are you? Answer.

**The Child.** A creature of God, rational and mortal.

**The Barba.** Why has God created you?

**The Child.** So that I may know Him, and worship Him, and having His grace, may be saved.

**Question.** In what does your salvation consist?

# 148 I. B. II. C. The Waldensian Doctrine of Christianity

Question: How many kinds of faith are there?
Answer: Two kinds: the living and the dead faith.

<margin>Is living.</margin> Question: What is the living faith?
Answer: That which is active through love. <note>original: "per Carità" / "durch die Liebe"</note>

<margin>or dead.</margin> Question: What is a dead faith?
Answer: James says: Faith without works is dead: therefore faith without works is nothing; or, a dead faith is when one believes that there is a God, and believes one thing or another about this God, but does not believe *in* Him. <note>The distinction here is between intellectual assent (believing *that*) and relational trust (believing *in*).</note>

Question: Of what faith are you?
Answer: I profess the true Catholic and Apostolic faith. <note>The term "Catholic" here is used in its original sense of "universal," rather than specifically referring to the Roman Catholic Church.</note>

Question: What kind of faith is that?
Answer: It is the very one that is summarized in the Apostolic Creed in twelve main articles.

Question: How does this Creed go?
<margin>Of the Apostolic Creed.</margin> Answer: I believe in God the Father, etc.

Question: How do you know that you believe in God?
Answer: When I apply myself

<column-break/>

Question: In how many manners is Faith?
Answer: In two manners, that is, living and dead.

Question: What thing is living Faith?
Answer: It is that which works through Charity.

Question: What thing is dead Faith?
Answer: According to Saint James, Faith, if it has no works, is dead, and likewise, Faith is idle without works. Or dead Faith is to believe God exists, to believe about God, and not to believe in God.

Question: Of which Faith are you?
Answer: Of the true Catholic and Apostolic Faith.

Question: Which is that?
Answer: It is that which, by the counsel of the Apostles, is divided into twelve Articles.

Question: Which is that?
Answer: I believe in God the Father almighty, etc.

Question: By what thing can you know that you believe in God?
Answer: By this: because I know and keep—

Q. You believe God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit to be three in Persons. Therefore, do you have three Gods?

A. I do not have three.

Q. Why then have you named three?

A. This is by reason of the difference of the Persons: but not by reason of the Essence of the Divinity. For although He is three in Persons, nevertheless, He is one in Essence.

Q. That God in whom you believe, in what manner do you adore and worship Him?

A. I adore Him by the adoration of <term>Latria</term> <note>From the Greek 'latreia', referring to the highest form of worship and devotion reserved for God alone, as opposed to 'dulia' or 'hyperdulia' offered to saints or Mary.</note> exterior and interior. Exteriorly by the bowing of knees, lifting of hands, by bowing, by hymns, by spiritual songs, by fasts, by invocations; but interiorly by pious affection, by a will prepared for all things pleasing to Him; and I worship Him through Faith, through Hope, and through Charity in His commandments.

ity, and equal God with the Father and the Son.

<margin>Of the Holy Trinity.</margin>
Q. You believe in three Persons, God the Father, God the Son, and God the Holy Spirit. So then, do you have three Gods?

Ans. No, I do not have three.

Q. Why then do you name three names?

Ans. To indicate thereby the distinction of the Persons, but not of the divine Essence. For although there are three Persons, yet there is only one single divine Essence.

Q. How do you honor the God in whom you believe, and how do you serve Him?

<margin>How to honor Him.</margin>
Ans. Through an outward and inward service of God. Outwardly through the bowing of the knees, lifting up of the hands, reverent gestures, songs and spiritual hymns, fasting and prayer: but inwardly through a holy desire and longing to do His will, and to serve Him faithfully according to His commandments in faith, hope, and love.

# I. B. II. C. The Waldensian Doctrine of Christianity

...been concluded. According to its administration, the Church consists of the community of the servants of God, and of the people subject to them, who make use of their office in faith, hope, and love.

<margin>And its characteristics.</margin>
**Question:** By what is the Church of Christ recognized?

**Answer:** By the upright teachers, and by those who truly participate in their service.

<margin>Concerning the teachers.</margin>
**Question:** But by what does one recognize the teachers?

**Answer:** By the true sense of faith, by sound doctrine, by a good way of life, by the pure preaching of the Gospel, and by the uncorrupted administration of the Sacraments. <note>The Waldensians emphasized that the validity of a religious leader was tied to their moral conduct and adherence to scripture.</note>

**Question:** By what does one know the false teachers?

**Answer:** By their fruits, such as error, an evil life, perverse doctrine, and the unlawful handling of the holy Sacraments.

**Question:** By what is their error recognized?

<margin>Their pure doctrine, and the sincere administration of the Sacraments.</margin>
**Answer:** Because they neither know nor understand the truth belonging to salvation, they carry on with

**Question:** By what thing ought you to know the church of Christ?

**Answer:** By the suitable Ministers and the people participating in truth in the ministry.

**Question:** But by what thing do you know the Ministers?

**Answer:** By the true sense of the Faith, and by sound doctrine, and by a life of good example, and by Evangelization, and by the due administration of the sacraments.

**Question:** By what thing do you know the false Ministers?

**Answer:** By their fruits, by blindness <note>original: "l'encequerà," referring to spiritual blindness or error</note>, by evil works, by perverse Doctrine, by the undue administration of the sacraments.

# I. B. 11. C. The Waldensian Doctrine of Christianity

<margin>
Signs of the false church: evil living and erroneous doctrine.
</margin>

**Question.** By what does one recognize the people who do not truly belong to the Church?

**Answer.** By their manifest sins and erroneous doctrines. One should flee such people, so as not to be infected by them.

**Question.** Through what shall you have fellowship in the Church?

**Answer.** In essence, through faith, hope, love, the observation of the commandments of the **Lord**, and perseverance in good until the end.

**Question.** How many parts properly belong to the office <note>The "ministerial things" or functions</note> of the Church?

**Answer.** Two parts: the Word and the **Sacraments**.

**Question.** How many **Sacraments** are there?

**Answer.** Two: Baptism and the Lord's Supper.

<margin>
Concerning Hope.
</margin>

**Question.** What is the name of the third virtue that one must possess if one wishes to be saved?

**Answer.** Hope.

**Question.** What is hope?

**Answer.** A confident assurance of the grace of **God**, and of future salvation.

<column-break/>

**Question.** By what thing is the people known, who are not in truth in the Church?

**Answer.** By public sins, and by erroneous Faith. For one must flee from such, so that their filth does not come upon oneself.

**Question.** By what thing ought you to commune with the holy church?

**Answer.** I ought to commune with the church by reason of substance through Faith, through hope, through charity <note>original: "carità"</note>, and by the observance of the commandments, and by final perseverance in good.

**Question.** How many are the ministerial things?

**Answer.** Two: the Word, and the sacraments.

**Question.** How many are the sacraments?

**Answer.** Two: that is, **Baptism** and the **Eucharist**.

**Question.** What thing is the third virtue necessary for salvation?

**Answer.** **Hope**.

**Question.** What thing is **Hope**?

**Answer.** It is a certain expectation of grace, and of the glory to come.

It emphasizes that the true Church is defined by the Word, the two sacraments, and the virtues of faith, hope, and love.</summary>

# I. B. 12. C. The Doctrine of the Waldenses

The nature of the communion among them, however, consists in the pure and clear teaching of the Word, the unadulterated administration of the Sacraments <note>The Waldenses emphasized simplicity in these rites compared to the Roman Church of the time.</note>, and in prayer. I believe in both the one and the other kind of such communion: namely, the one spiritual in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; the other bodily in the Christian Church.

**Question:** In what then does eternal life consist?
**Answer:** In a living and active faith, and in persevering in the same until the end. For so says the Savior in John 17: **This is eternal life, that they might know thee, who alone art the true God, and him whom thou hast sent, Jesus Christ**; and, **he who perseveres until the end shall be saved.** Amen!

# Of the Sacraments.

taught concerning the holy Sacraments, he need only read the following writing with impartial eyes:

->The Sacrament according to the saying of *St. Augustine* etc.<- <note>original: "Sagrament second lo dire de S. Augustin &c." This is likely a citation from Augustine's "City of God."</note>

<margin>The difference between the signs and the thing signified.</margin>
> "According to the testimony of *Augustine* in his book *The City of God*, a Sacrament is an invisible grace presented under a visible thing: or, the Sacrament is a sign of something that is holy. Thus, there is a great distinction between the sign and the thing signified in the Sacrament. The thing contained in the Sacrament, or signified by it, is the grace of God and the merit of the crucified Redeemer and Savior *Jesus Christ*, through whom those who had fallen have been restored. This resides solely and alone in a powerful, actual, glorious, and meritorious manner in God and in His Son *Jesus Christ*, who through His bloody suffering and death has re-acquired the lost grace and righteousness for His believers. The signified matter of the Sacrament is in the souls of the believers who partake of it, as *Paul* says: we have become partakers of *Christ* <note>A reference to Hebrews 3:14.</note>; just as it is also present through the proclamation or revelation in the preaching of the *Gospel*, and finally in a sacramental manner in the Sacraments. The dearest Savior gave such external assistance of the Sacraments to His Church for the purpose of better aiding its weakness, and to strengthen and ground it all the more in faith, namely, when the doctrine of the *Gospel* is, as it were, sealed by such external signs.
>
> "There are, however, two such Sacraments: one consists of water, the other of food, namely of bread and wine."

### Concerning Baptism.

<margin>Baptism.</margin>
The first is called Baptism, that is, a washing
"with water, whether it be from a river or a foun-
"tain, and it is performed in the name of the Father, the Son, and
"the Holy Spirit. By this, however, it is signified in what
"manner—through the grace of God the Father, in consideration
"of His Son, through participation in Him as
"our Redeemer, and through the renewal of the Holy Spirit,
"who works the right and true faith in our hearts—
"we are simultaneously washed and cleansed from our sins,
"received and accepted again into grace by God, and if
"we persevere in the same until the end, we shall also one day
"be eternally blessed in Christ Jesus.

"And this is precisely the baptism with which Jesus Christ,

"fill all righteousness: just as He also, for that same end,
"allowed Himself to be circumcised, and it is the very same [baptism] which He com-

"This baptism is visible and physical, and in and of

# Concerning the Sacraments.

Outside of what is necessary regarding the administration of Baptism are the exorcisms <note>original: "exorciſmi"; the ritual expulsion of evil spirits</note>, the breathing upon the candidate, the sign of the cross on the chest and on the forehead, the putting of salt in the mouth, the anointing with spittle on the ears and on the nose, the anointing of the chest, the hood, the anointing with the chrism <note>original: "creſma"; a consecrated oil used in Catholic and Orthodox liturgy</note> on the crown of the head, and similar things consecrated by the bishop, the placing of candles in the hands, the putting on of the white garment, the blessing of the water, the three-fold immersion, and the requirements of the godparents <note>original: "Pairin"</note>. All these things regarding the administration of this sacrament are outside of necessity; that is, they are not of the necessity nor of the substance required for the sacrament of Baptism. Many take from these things an occasion for greater error and superstition rather than edification for salvation, and according to some Doctors <note>referring to learned theologians or Church Fathers</note>, they are of no virtue or profit.

<column-break/>

<margin>Unnecessary actions of the Roman Church during Baptism.</margin>
To that which is not necessary in Baptism belongs the adjuration of the evil spirit, the blowing upon the candidate, the sign of the cross on the breast and on the forehead, the salt which is given in the mouth, the wetting with saliva in the ears and in the nose, the smearing of the head with chrism, and whatever other such things there are which a bishop has previously consecrated, the giving of a candle into the hands, the putting on of a white garment, the consecration of the water, the three-fold dipping of the child into the same, and the petitioning of the godparents <note>original: "Paten"</note>. All these things are superfluous in the performance of baptism, because they belong neither to the essence nor to the effect of the same, but rather give occasion for error and superstition instead of edification for salvation, and therefore, according to the own testimony of many teachers, have neither power nor benefit.

I. B. 12. C. The Doctrine of the Waldensians

Christ, as the true model for the entire Church, never allowed himself to be given Confirmation, and for his baptism he used no chrism <note>original: "Chrisam"; a consecrated oil used in Catholic rituals</note>, but only plain water. From which it follows that such a sacrament is by no means required for salvation; through it, God is blasphemed, and it has been instituted through devilish inspiration so that the common man might be deceived and deprived of the faith that comes from the Word of God, and might remain dependent only upon outward pomp and the necessity of bishops.

### Concerning Extreme Unction

The seventh sacrament of the Roman Church is the Extreme Unction of the sick. To be sure, one seeks to prove this from the words of the Apostle James: however, nowhere does one find any traces that Christ or his apostles instituted it. If this bodily anointing were a sacrament, as it is claimed to be, then certainly the Savior or His disciples would not have remained silent regarding its practice. When one considers this well, there remains nothing left that has even the appearance of belief, much—

<column-break/>

—in this manner, nor baptismal chrism in this manner, but only water. Therefore, such a sacrament is not seen to be a necessity for salvation, in which God is blasphemed, and it is introduced by Diabolical movement, so that the people may be mocked in the Faith of the church, and more belief is given to the solemnity or necessity of the Bishops.

The seventh sacrament of the Roman church is the Extreme Unction of the sick, which they forcibly attempt to found upon the saying of Saint James the Apostle. It is not seen to be ordained by Christ, nor by his Apostles. For if this bodily anointing were a sacrament, in the way it is feigned to be; Christ or his Apostles would not have been silent about the required manifestation of its execution. Thinking on these things, one ought not dare to hold, nor confess it as an Article of Faith,

# The Thirteenth Chapter.
## The tenth proof of the doctrine of the Waldenses, concerning Fasting and Visiting the Sick.

<note>The text below is presented in parallel columns: the left in Occitan (the native Waldensian Romance language) and the right in German.</note>

Now follows Fasting, which is twofold: that is, spiritual and corporal. Spiritual fasting is to abstain from sins; corporal fasting is to abstain from food. But a Christian has the liberty to eat at all times, as all days are fit for fasting, not observing [days] superstitiously as if by the virtue of continence.

Note that there are some Fasts which are not to be kept nor praised by the faithful, but rather are to be excommunicated <note>meaning "shunned" or "rejected"</note> and fled from. Such as are the Fasts of the scribes and Pharisees, and those ordained by the Anti-Christ <note>A common Waldensian term for the corrupt Roman Church hierarchy</note> involving idolatry.
<column-break/>
<margin>Fasting.</margin>
Now follows fasting. This is of two kinds: spiritual and physical. One fasts spiritually when one abstains from sins, and physically when one abstains from food. A Christian has the freedom to eat or to fast without looking at the distinction of days; only he must not be superstitious in this, or represent his abstinence from food as a meritorious work <note>The Waldenses argued that fasting does not "earn" salvation, but is a discipline of faith</note>.

It is, however, well to note that there are certain types of fasting that a Christian should neither keep nor agree with, but rather should abhor and avoid. Such is the fasting of the Scribes and Pharisees, as well as those idolatrous fasts—

It shall be shown to him how, in such confidence, he may comfortingly abandon himself to the merciful love of his heavenly Father, and leave it entirely to Him to deal with him as He knows will be most useful for him, and most blessed for body and soul. Furthermore, he is to be exhorted with all emphasis to behave toward his neighbor as he would wish the neighbor to do toward him, to banish all resentment from his heart, and to arrange matters so that his kin, after his death, may live together kindly and peacefully without any strife or quarreling.

> "Thereupon, let it further be shown to him how he should ground all hope for salvation solely and alone upon the Mediator between God and men, Jesus Christ, and how outside of Him no other way to heaven is to be found: so that, when he recognizes himself as a wretched sinner worthy of eternal death, he may seek grace from God. If one perceives in him a fear of the judgment seat of God and of His wrath, then one should present to him the comforting promises of the Lord Jesus, which all those are entitled to partake in who approach Him with their whole heart and seek forgiveness of sins from the Father in His name. Thus shall an upright teacher <note>In this context, "teacher" refers to a pastor or spiritual leader</note> conduct himself if he wishes to lead the sick person to the Lord Jesus even upon his deathbed.

## The eleventh proof of the doctrine of the Waldensians, from which their opinion of the Antichrist can be seen: and the reasons why they separated themselves from the Roman Church.

Because the content of this chapter concerns a matter that is still disputed here and there to this day, it will hopefully not be unpleasant for many to be able to read what our Waldensians believed about it here in their own language, alongside the translation. We have taken this from an old book written on parchment, which contains various speeches of their ancient preachers. The assembly of the godless is, on the contrary, passed off as the mother of the genuine children of God. Lies are publicly taught and promoted instead of the truth, wickedness instead of good, injustice instead of justice, errors instead of the true faith, and vices instead of virtues.

**Question:** What kind of works arise from these first works?

**Answer:** The following: The first work is that the service <note>original: "Dienſt" / "coltivament de Latrie." By this we understand men, deceased saints, their images, bodies, or other remains <note>relics</note>, the sacraments, especially the sacrament of the Lord's Supper <note>the Eucharist</note>, which must be honored and worshipped in a truly divine manner, indeed as God Himself; likewise all consecrated things, and so forth. Who does not see from this that the commandment is explicitly abolished: One should serve God alone?

# Of the Antichrist, and why they have separated themselves.

<margin>Why the Waldensians do not hold with the Antichrist.</margin>
...also rightly, in both a physical and spiritual manner, depart from him. We hold him to be the true Antichrist <note>The Waldensians, like many later Reformers, identified the institutional Roman Church and the Papacy with the "Antichrist" described in the New Testament.</note>, and have therefore, out of sincere conviction, voluntarily and without compulsion, united and bound ourselves together to the end that we might strive purely and simply to please the Lord in all things, and to be saved through Him. In this, we rely upon His assistance, and intend to hold fast to His truth and to His bride, the Church, as far as it is possible to achieve in this state of human weakness.

<note>original: "Doncnos ordonnèn notar quals sian las causas del nostre departiment..." This paragraph is in Occitan (Old Provençal), the native language of the Waldensian valleys.</note> Therefore, we have ordained to note what the causes of our departure are, and also of our congregation, so that if the Lord should grant someone to have this same truth, he may bear love for it together with us. And if by chance he is not well enlightened, he may receive help through this service, the Lord providing the dew <note>A metaphor for divine grace or inspiration.</note>. And if more is given to anyone, and more highly, we desire to be taught more humbly, and to learn better from him, and to be corrected in our defects. Therefore, these things that follow are the causes of our departure.

<column-break/>

<margin>The causes thereof are set forth piece by piece in the following.</margin>
And so we have resolved to discover the causes that moved us to go out from this Babel <note>A common biblical allusion to Babylon, representing a state of spiritual confusion or corruption.</note>: but no less also to indicate the true nature of our assembly, so that those to whom the Lord wishes to grant the knowledge of this same truth may come to love it just as we do. Should this not yet be sufficient to enlighten others enough, may the Lord Himself make up for this deficiency through His Spirit and Word. But if someone has progressed further in this knowledge, it shall be pleasing to us to learn from him, and we shall not be ashamed to improve the defects still clinging to us through better instruction. # I. B. 14. C. The Doctrine of the Waldensians

Be it known and recognized hereby to all in general, and to each one in particular, that we have separated ourselves from the Roman Church for this reason: so that the true essence of faith might be maintained among us, as well as the inner knowledge of the true God, who is one in three persons—which, certainly, flesh and blood cannot reveal to us. We have separated ourselves so that we may serve this one true God as is fitting, and may hallow and revere His name above all things; so that a living hope in God through Christ may be established in us; that rebirth and renewal may be wrought through faith, love, and hope; that the merit of Jesus Christ and the grace and righteousness springing therefrom may be attributed to us; and that we, with all the elect, may partake in the forgiveness of sins, and finally arrive with them at the enjoyment of most blessed perfection. The creature worships, adores, and honors him in many ways: through songs, prefaces <note>original: "Proemis"</note>, through solemnities and the celebration of Masses, Vespers, and Compline <note>The final prayer service of the day in the traditional Christian liturgy</note> dedicated to themselves; through set hours, vigils, and feast days. They seek the acquisition of grace through these things, even though grace exists essentially in God alone, is merited through Jesus Christ, and is acquired only through faith by the Holy Spirit.

For idolatry is nothing other than a false opinion regarding Grace, Truth, authority, invocation, and intercession—all of which the Antichrist himself has separated from God and attributed instead to the ministry, to the works of his own hands, to the saints, and to Purgatory. And this iniquity of the Antichrist is directly contrary to the first Article of Faith and the first commandment of the Law.

Similarly, the disordered love of the world belonging to the Antichrist is that from which germinates—

<column-break/>

—manner, with songs, long-winded chatter <note>original: "Geschwätze," likely referring to repetitive or empty prayers</note>, public pomp, the reading of Masses, evening services, prayers set at specific hours, early soul-masses, feast days, and the acquisition of grace. Yet this grace is to be sought only and uniquely from God through the merit of Christ, to be obtained through faith, and to be made one's own through the Holy Spirit.

<margin>The first source of idolatry.</margin>
It is certain that nothing is more to blame for this idolatry than the false opinion concerning grace and truth, the testimonies of the Scriptures, invocation, and intercessions. All of these have been robbed from God and dedicated instead to outward ceremonies, human prestige, the works of one's own hands, the saints, and Purgatory. This Antichristian injustice, however, runs expressly against the first main article of the Christian faith and against the first commandment in the Law.

The twelfth proof of the Waldensian doctrine of faith, containing their opinion on Purgatory: drawn from the same book from the year 1120 in which the Antichrist was discussed. <note>The Waldensians often identified the Papacy with the Antichrist, a common theme in their 12th-century polemics.</note>

### Concerning the Purgatory that exists only in Dreams and Fantasy.

<margin>The Papists' doctrine of Purgatory.</margin>
What the priests and monks dream up regarding a Purgatory hatched in their own brains, and which they teach as an article of faith, can be seen from the following. They say that after this life, and after the ascension of Christ, the souls of the deceased—especially those who are to attain eternal life but could not make sufficient satisfaction for their sins in this life—pass immediately after death into Purgatory. There, they must endure the most sensitive pains and allow themselves to be purified from their sins; from which, however, after the completion of purification, they would emerge again, some sooner, some later, some only at the general Last Judgment, and some even before it. # Opinions concerning Purgatory.

The Bride of Christ <note>The Church or the individual soul</note> is washed in His blood: and this is a testimony in Heaven for those who have followed the law itself, that is, that purity in practice, of which it is said in the Apocalypse <note>original: "Apocalyps"; the Book of Revelation</note>: "These are they who came out of the great tribulation, and have washed their robes, and made them white in the blood of the Lamb; therefore they are before the throne of the Lamb and serve Him." Behold how many ways are gathered from the Faith of the Scripture, by which those making the journey in this Life are purged in the present of their sins.

We suppose thirdly, that it is a most certain thing, that each person should live in such a way in the present Life, that he has no need afterwards of any purgation. For it is better to do good in the present Life, than to hope for uncertain help afterwards. And a more secure life is that the good, which one hopes to be done by others after his death, he should do for himself.
*Waldensian History, Part I.*

<column-break/>

This cleansing of the Bride in the blood of her Bridegroom does not only speak for her here in this life: but this blood also bears witness of it in Heaven. For so it says in the Revelation: These are they, who have come out of great tribulation, and have washed their clothes, and have made their clothes bright in the blood of the Lamb; therefore they are before the throne of God, and serve Him day and night. See, the Holy Scripture shows us so many kinds of cleansing for those who are engaged here on their earthly pilgrimage.

<margin>After death no further help takes place.</margin>
We assume thirdly, that it is safest of all to live here in this time in such a way that after death one no longer requires any cleansing in Purgatory <note>original: "Fegefeuer"</note>. At the very least, it is much safer to apply oneself to piety here in time, than to want to hope for uncertain help there in eternity: it is also much more useful and beneficial to do that during one's life oneself, which one wished that others—

# Opinion regarding Purgatory.

The first part is this: regarding the Scripture, such a thing <note>the existence of Purgatory</note> is not deducible according to the Law itself; this appears manifested clearly. For in reviewing the entire Law binding the Christians, it is not seen that there is any express Scripture of the Law by which it is a necessity for the faithful to believe, as an article of Faith, that after this life there is such a place as Purgatory, as some say. Nor is there given any primary significance of this from any part of the Holy Scripture, nor can any proof be made of any soul that has entered into the said Purgatory and has departed from it.

Therefore, it is not to be believed, nor held as Faith. In confirmation of this, Augustine, in the book which is called *A Thousand Discourses* <note>original: "Mil Parlament"; likely referring to a collection of sayings or a specific pseudo-Augustinian work</note>, writes thus: For we believe by Catholic Faith and by Divine authority that the Kingdom of the Heavens is the first place to which Baptism is received. The second is the punishment where those excommunicated and estranged from the Faith of Christ shall suffer eternal torment. The third place we are entirely ignorant of, nor do we find it in the Holy Scripture.

# Opinions concerning Purgatory.

<column-break/>

Who does not now see sufficiently from all this that, after the Ascension of Christ, no more than two places are revealed to us where departed souls shall go, and that the Holy Scripture knows nothing at all of a third place?

<margin>The early church did not believe in Purgatory.</margin>
Since neither God in His Law, nor the Apostles in their writings, make any mention of a Purgatory; and since the early Church <note>original: "Gleifa primitiva"</note>, which was planted by the disciples of Christ themselves, neither knew nor taught anything of it, but rather Pope Pelagius <note>Pelagius I, reigned 556–561 AD</note> first ordered, 558 years after Christ lived on earth, that one should remember the deceased in the Masses: it certainly follows from this that, as God's Word is expressly silent on the matter, one is in no way bound to establish such a Purgatory for departed souls, nor to believe in it as an article of Faith.

<margin>Against prayers for the dead.</margin>
One must therefore rightly wonder how it has come to pass that in these modern times the living are so concerned with providing aid to the dead, as in all the Sa—

<column-break/>

See how these authorities sound forth that there are only two certain places after the Ascension of Christ into Heaven, after this life for the souls separated from the body, and the third is not at all to be found in the Scriptures.

Therefore, as in no place in the Law is there any express mention made of such a place as Purgatory, nor have the Apostles left us any express teaching; nor did the primitive Church, living according to the Gospel of which the Apostles were the governors, hand down to us anything by ordinance or commandment: but Pope Pelagius, after the year of the Lord 558, is read to have ordered that in the Mass there should be a remembrance of the dead. It remains that from the Scripture brought expressly from the Law of God, it is not a necessity to believe as an article of Faith that there is such a place as Purgatory after this life.

But the doubt runs <note>i.e., the question arises</note> why modern men have such affection for the assistance of the dead, as in all the Ho—

# On the Invocation of Saints

We suppose thirdly that the saints are not left to us for worship <note>original: "coltivament" / "verehren"; implying religious cult or adoration</note>, but for imitation <note>original: "resimillament" / "Vorbild"</note>.

Saint Paul says: O Brothers, be imitators of me, even as I am of Christ, and watch those who walk according to the pattern you have in us.

Saint Peter did not allow himself to be adored by Cornelius, nor did the Angel allow it of John the Evangelist. And for this reason, Augustine wrote in *Of True Religion*: O religious ones, let the worship of dead men not be among you; for if they lived holily, they did not do so in order to seek such honor, but they wish Him to be worshiped by us, through whose enlightenment they rejoice that we are fellow-servants with them. Therefore, they are to be honored by imitation, not to be adored through religion.

These few things above we say, so that any man—

<column-break/>

<margin>One should follow the saints, but not worship them.</margin>
We further presuppose that the saints should serve us so that we view them as our models and walk in their footsteps, but by no means so that we should worship them.

Paul says it expressly: Dear brothers, be my followers, just as I am of Christ; follow me, and look to those who walk as you have us for an example.

<margin>Example.</margin>
So also Peter did not want to be worshiped by Cornelius, nor the Angel by John; therefore Augustine also, in a letter sent to his friend who was likewise a lover of the truth, expressed himself thus: You clergy, do not let the evil desire <note>The German "böse Lust" here interprets the Occitan "cootiva" (worship/cult) as a misplaced passion or desire for the dead</note> of the dead rule in you; who, if they lived holily, would not allow themselves to be honored for it, but rather that He should be honored through whose enlightenment they and we have attained such holiness. The conclusion therefore always remains this: one should honor the saints through imitation, not through invocation.

<margin>Christ alone to be worshiped.</margin>
All this now having been presupposed, we believe and confess,

<margin>Other additional causes.</margin>
And oh, how many have already been deceived by the vain hope of obtaining other help! God is indeed a righteous God; since we, as sinners, are unable to help ourselves, He Himself forgives us all our sins. For He gave Himself up for our redemption and sacrificed Himself for our sins. God did not spare His own Son, but sent Him into the world so that poor sinners should not despair in their sins. Oh, let us then hasten to this Advocate, who represents us day and night before His heavenly Father, constantly praying for us, and who is not only our Mediator and Advocate, but also our Judge. # The Seventeenth Chapter.

->Concerning the Doctrine of the Waldensians, containing various<-
->credible confessions of their faith.<-

I have now, beyond all doubt, clearly enough demonstrated what the ancient Waldensians believed, taught, and publicly confessed, both regarding the Christian faith and those points which were already regarded as new and erroneous at that time. However, so that absolutely nothing remains from which even the most extreme malice could take opportunity to object or to blaspheme their opinions, I will further add, in abundance, the most important and irrefutable testimonies from their Confession of Faith. These are the same as they frequently presented to the authorities, thereby parrying the malice of the Devil and the deceit of the slanderers, who in all ages have been intent on utterly rooting them out and blackening their doctrine as a monstrous teaching.

<margin>Confession of Faith of the Waldensians from the year 1120.</margin>
I begin this with an excellent piece which, partly because of its age and partly because of its exceptional content, is well worthy of all attention. I have taken it from the previously mentioned old manuscript book, which Perrin mentions in his history on page 225. It was written in the year 1120, and thus sixty to eighty years before the time of Waldo <note>Peter Waldo, the wealthy merchant of Lyon often credited as the founder, though the author argues the faith existed earlier</note>. ### Christ our only Intercessor.

<margin>The eighth Article. The only Intercessor.</margin>
Thus we also believe that JESUS Christ is our only Mediator and Intercessor with the Father: that the Virgin Mary was humble, gracious, and full of (divine) grace: and that all the saints in heaven await the resurrection of their bodies from the dead for judgment and for eternal life.

### Against Purgatory.

<margin>The ninth Article. Against Purgatory.</margin>
Likewise, we also believe that there are only two places for the souls of the deceased; namely, Heaven for the blessed, and Hell for the damned; and we absolutely reject the antichristian dream of Purgatory as an error running contrary to the truth.

### Against Human Ordinances.

<margin>The tenth Article. Against human ordinances.</margin>
We firmly hold that all human ordinances <note>The German "Menschen-Satzungen" refers to religious rules or traditions established by church authorities rather than by Scripture.</note> are an abomination to the Lord our GOD, and therefore among Christians one should not even know of them. Such things include the feast days, holy eves, or vigils, the so-called Consecrated—

<column-break/>

Similarly, we firmly hold that there is no other Mediator and Advocate before God the Father except Jesus Christ: but that the Virgin Mary was holy, humble, and full of grace: And likewise we believe of all the other saints, that they await in Heaven the Resurrection of their bodies at the Judgment.

Also, we believe that after this life there are only two places, one for the saved, which we call Paradise, and the other for the damned, which we call Hell; utterly denying that Purgatory dreamed up by the Anti-Christ, and invented against the Truth.

Also, we have always believed it to be an abomination, not to be spoken of before God, all those things found [invented] by men, such as are the Feasts, and the Vigils of the Saints, and the water which they call Holy <note>original: "Aigua... Benieta" (Holy Water)</note>, and abstaining on certain days from—

### More against Human Ordinances.

We abominate human inventions as Anti-Christian disturbances which trouble the soul and which prejudice the liberty of the Spirit.

<margin>The eleventh article.</margin>
We loathe human ordinances as errors of the Anti-Christ, which only serve to lead consciences astray and strive against spiritual freedom.

<margin>The twelfth article. Of the Sacraments.</margin>
We believe that the sacraments are the sign and the external form of the holy matter contained therein, and that it is necessary that the believers, when it is possible, make use of these visible forms often. We know of no other sacraments than Baptism and the Supper.

We shall honor the secular authorities with all subjection, obedience, and service, as well as with taxes and gifts.

# I.B.17.C. Wherein various Confessions of Faith differ

Another short Confession of Faith, under the title: **Brief Confession of Faith** <note>original: "Brieve Confession de foy"</note>, as prepared by the teachers and heads of households in the Piedmontese valleys—specifically at their assembly in Angrogne on December 12, 1532—and which is preserved along with other documents in the library collection at Cambridge. It begins with the following preface:

The following articles were signed by all the teachers and heads of households present at that time, and were recognized as truths perfectly consistent with Holy Scripture. They contain the essence of the entire doctrine as it has been passed down from parents to children according to the Word of God, following the example of the faithful in the times of Ezra and Nehemiah. See on this Ezra 10 and Nehemiah 9, 10.

->What is to be observed in true Divine Service.<-

1) We believe that one must serve God in spirit and in truth: For God is a Spirit, and those who worship Him must worship Him in spirit and in truth.

->Concerning Gracious Election <note>The theological doctrine of Predestination.</note><-

2) That God, even before the creation of the world, chose those who have already attained salvation and those who shall yet be saved.

->The consequences thereof.<-

3) That it is impossible for those who have once been ordained to salvation not to actually be saved.

->Concerning Free Will.<-

4) That those who believe in a free will <note>original Latin: "liberum Arbitrium"</note> abolish the grace of God and His eternal gracious election.

### Concerning Good Works.

5) That there are no other good works except those which God has commanded, and none are evil except those which He has forbidden.

### Concerning Oaths.

6) That, provided a Christian does not use the name of his God in vain, he may swear by the same without sin and without acting against the saying in Matthew 5:34—<note>original: "Ich sage euch, daß ihr allerdings nicht schweren solt" (I say to you, that you should not swear at all)</note>—"I say to you, that you should not swear at all." However, the name of God is not used in vain when the oath serves either the honor of God or the benefit of one's neighbor. Thus, one can also swear with a good conscience before the authorities <term>Obrigkeit: the established civil government or magistracy</term>, who, whether they be good or evil, are God's servants and represent His power on earth.

### Against Auricular Confession.

7) That auricular confession <note>The practice of confessing sins privately to a priest</note> was neither instituted by God nor commanded in His Word; rather, every Christian is obligated to confess and acknowledge his sins to God alone, since such an honor belongs to God alone. It is an entirely different and permitted way of confessing one's sins of which we read in Matthew and in John 5 <note>likely referring to James 5:16 or 1 John 1:9, though the text cites John 5</note>, namely when one is concerned with reconciliation with one's neighbor. Furthermore, it is no more than just that he who has given public offense must also acknowledge the same publicly.

### Concerning the Sabbath.

8) That on Sunday, partly to the honor of God and partly out of love for the servants, one should rest from all labor and occupy oneself with nothing but the Word of God.

### Against Revenge.

9) That it is not permitted for any Christian to avenge himself, in whatever manner or way it might be.

Another Confession of Faith, which was delivered to the King of Bohemia by the Waldensians in the year 1535; wherein their teachers first demonstrate why they separated themselves from the Roman Church, and afterwards the Estates and the Nobility of the land, in a separate preface, cite the reasons which moved them to profess this doctrine.

# The First Chapter.
## Concerning the Holy Scripture.

<note>original: "Principio nostri omnes unanimi consensu docent scripturas sacras, &c."</note> First, all those who adhere to us teach with one voice that the Holy Scriptures, etc.

First of all, all those who hold with us teach unanimously that all writings contained in the Bible, by which the Fathers were guided and which possess canonical authority, must be held as true without contradiction, and must be preferred in all respects over all spiritual and worldly writings. Furthermore, since all these writings are inspired by God—as Peter and Paul testify—one must also derive everything pertaining to faith and salvation from them. Consequently, they must be diligently read and explained in all our churches, especially regarding the Gospels and Epistles; and indeed, following the example of the early Church, this should be done in our common mother tongue <note>The Waldensians were pioneers in using the vernacular (common language) rather than Latin for worship</note>, so that they may and can be understood by everyone. And finally, that from these Scriptures must be drawn all grounds for doctrine, exhortations, sermons, comforts, and so forth—indeed, all the duties of a clergyman.

# The Second Main Chapter.

## Concerning their Catechism, along with a brief summary of the doctrine contained therein.

->*From this source they teach the Catechism, this Catholic and Orthodox Doctrine of the Fathers, etc.* <note>original: "Hinc Catechismum docent Catholicam hanc & Orthodoxam Doctrinam Patrum &c."</note><-

From these Holy Scriptures we have also drawn our instruction in Christianity, in which the universal and orthodox doctrine of the Fathers is contained and presented, according to the Ten Commandments of God and the Apostolic Creed—which consists of twelve articles and was accepted and confirmed by the Council of Nicaea <note>The Council of Nicaea (325 AD) was the first ecumenical council of the Christian church, which established the core tenets of the faith</note>; to this also belongs the Lord’s Prayer, along with the interpretation thereof. We believe, therefore, on this very basis, that everything contained in the aforementioned Ten Commandments of God, the Apostolic Creed, and the Lord’s Prayer must be written most diligently into all of our hearts: for the law is spiritual. Indeed, all these doctrines of faith must be believed by us from the heart and demonstrated through our works. We therefore apply ourselves with all possible diligence not only to prove these doctrines from the Word of God, but also to present their true meaning and purpose in the clearest and most distinct manner. However, so that every possible difficulty may be removed and the matter explained clearly and thoroughly, we compare Scripture against Scripture. We further believe and teach that one should worship God alone, and specifically in the name of our only Mediator Jesus Christ; one should also include in their prayers those to whom the Most High has entrusted oversight, both over His church and over the secular government <term>Regiment: the civil authorities or ruling body</term>.

The Word of God convinces man clearly and distinctly that he is a sinner: the restless, sad, and confused conscience takes possession of his soul; he can neither advise nor help himself: because of this, he becomes entirely dejected, distressed, and despondent, and sees, as it were, the wrath of God and damnation already before his eyes, just as David says of himself: **There is no soundness in my flesh because of your anger, neither is there any rest in my bones because of my sin: I am troubled; I am bowed down greatly; I go mourning all the day long.** <note>Psalm 38:3, 6</note> Nevertheless, such a terrified sinner should not despair, but rather through faith in Jesus Christ, convert to God from the heart. For although we are stripped of all righteousness, we should nevertheless implore the grace and mercy of God, that He may have compassion on us, and forgive us our sins for the sake of the merit of His beloved Son, who was made to be sin and a curse for us, so that we might become in Him the righteousness of God, and so that He might satisfy the justice of God for our sins.
