And in another place, this same Apostle writes: God has appointed Christ as the head of the Church over all things, which is his body, namely the fullness of him who fills all in all <note>Ephesians 1:22-23</note>. Thus, we also believe and teach that this is the true universal <note>original: "algemeine" – referring to the catholic or ecumenical church</note> church, where the believers—from whatever part of the world or whatever station in life they may be—unite and profess their faith in the triune God through the Word of God. For so it says in the Revelation: After this I looked, and behold, a great multitude, which no one could count <note>Revelation 7:9</note>. And the Lord Jesus himself testifies to it when he speaks: Where two or three are gathered in my name, there am I in the midst of them <note>Matthew 18:20</note>. Accordingly, wherever Jesus Christ is preached, lived according to his Word, and the holy Sacraments <term>Sacraments: specifically Baptism and the Lord's Supper as outward signs of inward grace</term> are administered and received according to his institution, there is the church and the congregation of God, whether their assembly be as large or as small as it may be. On the contrary, where Christ is not, and where his Word is rejected, there the true church cannot be, nor a congregation that could please the Lord. Now, as for the specific small congregations that gather here and there, we believe that such are only to be regarded as parts and members of that universal church, according to the testimony of Paul in 1 Corinthians 12: You are the body of Christ, and members, each according to his part.

We further teach that this universal church has the power to compel all the godless, wicked, impenitent, and stubborn—who will no longer give ear to any admonitions—through punishment, church discipline <term>Kirchen-Zucht: the practice of maintaining moral and doctrinal purity within the congregation</term>, or the like; indeed, even according to the nature of the circumstances, to exclude them from their fellowship through curse and ban <note>original: "Fluch und Bann" – referring to excommunication</note>. And this is to be done without any respect of persons against all those who live in manifest sins and works of the flesh, and who have already [ignored] all...

Finally, we teach that the Antichrist is the "man of sin," who seats himself in the temple of **God**, that is, in the Church: of whom the prophets, **Jesus Christ** himself, and also his disciples prophesied and spoke, and against whose error and seduction they so faithfully warned all believers.

## The Ninth Chapter.

### Concerning the Spiritual Orders, or concerning the Overseers and Servants of the Church.

<note>original: "Docemus, Ministros Ecclesiæ, quibus administratio Verbi & Sacramentorum Ecclesiæ demandantur, ritè institutos esse debere, &c."</note>
We teach that the Ministers of the Church, to whom the administration of the Word and the Sacraments of the Church are entrusted, ought to be rightfully instituted, etc.

We believe that those to whom the preaching of the divine Word and the administration of the holy sacraments are to be entrusted as servants of the church, must be lawfully called and ordained to this important office according to the instructions which Christ gave to his disciples in this regard: That, above all things, one should seek out faithful and blameless workers for this purpose, who are properly provided with the necessary physical and mental gifts, are of good conduct, and that these must then be chosen by the elders and confirmed in the execution of their office by the laying on of hands in a public assembly: in such a way that whoever has not been chosen and appointed in the said manner may not exercise the office of a teacher among us. Furthermore, we also teach that the duty of those who have been ordained as servants of the church in the manner just described is to watch over the flock entrusted to them with the greatest care, to present the Gospel of Christ to them purely and clearly, to administer the sacraments according to the mind of Christ, to lead all people with their own good example, and to pray fervently to **God** for their salvation.

# I. B. 17. C. Wherein various Confessions of Faith differ

## The Tenth Chapter.

### Concerning the Preaching of the Divine Word.

<note>original: "Deinde docemus, quod Verbi Dei, sive Evangelii prædicatio, est Ministerium à Christo institutum, & præceptum. Matth. 28."</note> Next, we teach that the preaching of the Word of God, or of the Gospel, is a Ministry instituted and commanded by Christ. Matthew 28.

We further teach hereafter that the **Lord Jesus** himself ordained and established the holy Office of Preaching, specifically in Matthew 28, when he says there: Go forth into all the world, and preach the Gospel to every creature. We also believe that one must rightly make a distinction between the power of the Law and of the Gospel; namely, that the Law preaches death, while the Gospel, by contrast, preaches life to the glory of Christ. For as it says in 2 Corinthians 3: The letter kills, but the Spirit gives life; and in John 5: The words that I speak, they are spirit and life. Furthermore, we believe that no one can attain true faith except through the hearing of the preaching of the Word, concerning which Paul makes the following statement: Faith comes from preaching, but preaching through the **Word of God:** and again: How shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? In accordance with this, our teachers apply all possible diligence to preach the **Word of God** purely and clearly within the congregation, guarding themselves most carefully against all human trifles <note>German: "Menschen-Tand," referring to worldly vanities or traditions not found in Scripture</note>; and we ourselves read the Gospel and the remaining books of Holy Scripture in our own familiar mother tongue.

# The Thirteenth Chapter.
## Concerning the Lord’s Supper.

->*The Lord's Supper or the Sacrament of the Eucharist is a mystery*<-
->*instituted by Christ, etc.*<- <note>original: "Dominicam Cœnam seu Eucharistiæ Sacramentum misterium esse à Christo, &c."</note>

We teach that the Holy Supper is a mystery which was instituted by Christ for the use and salvation of all true believers, continued by the Apostles, and propagated throughout the entire Christian Church, according to the testimony of the Evangelists and the Apostle Paul, whose words the whole Church employs: "I have received from the Lord that which I have delivered unto you; for the Lord Jesus, in the night in which he was betrayed, took bread," etc. and shortly thereafter: "Therefore, my dear brothers, when you come together to eat (namely, of this Supper), wait for one another." <note>References to 1 Corinthians 11:23 and 11:33.</note>

We teach no less that one should believe with the heart and confess with the mouth that the bread in the Holy Supper is the true body of Christ, which he gave for us, and the cup is his true blood, which he shed for us for the forgiveness of sins: and this according to the express words of Christ: "This is my body, this is my blood."

However, we also teach that during the administration of this sacrament, one should undertake absolutely nothing that has not been expressly commanded by Christ himself, who made himself heard in the words of institution thus: "Take, eat, this is my body." And again: "Drink all of you from it, this is my blood of the New Testament, which is shed for many for the forgiveness of sins."

In accordance with this command of the Savior, we therefore teach that

## The Fourteenth Main Chapter.

### Concerning Church Authority and the Use of the Keys.

<note>original Latin: "Et docemus, ut credatur, Claves à Christo Ecclesiæ, &c."</note> And we teach that it should be believed that the Keys [were given] by Christ to the Church, etc.

We also believe and teach that the Savior Himself entrusted the power and the use of the keys to His Church, in the words where He says to Peter, but at the same time to all the Apostles: *I will give to thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven:* and that by this is represented the administration of the Church, which is placed into the hands of all teachers who have been dedicated to its service until now and until the end of the world.

We believe that the use and the authority of this administration, according to the proper sense and intention of the Savior, consists in this: namely, that through the same, the persistently godless and impenitent shall be punished and, according to the circumstances, even excluded from the fellowship of the Church, as the Holy Scripture declares. On the other hand, however, the penitent and the faithful shall be assured of the certain forgiveness of their sins, brought to the sweet peace of conscience, thoroughly convinced of their salvation, heaven opened to them, and they shall be best equipped against all temptations. All this, however, the teachers do not do out of their own power, but merely as Christ's servants and stewards over God's mysteries; <note>The term "stewards of the mysteries" refers to the clergy's role in administering sacraments and teaching divine truths</note>

## The Fifteenth Chapter.
### Concerning Human Traditions.

->*Human traditions, rites, and customs, which are in no way contrary to piety, are to be observed in public assemblies, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Humanas Traditiones, Ritus, & consuetudines, quae nihil pietati adversantur, in publicis Conventibus servandæ &c."</note><-

Regarding human traditions and institutions that do not conflict with godliness <term>godliness: "Gottseligkeit," referring to a life lived in reverence and devotion to God</term>, we believe that such things may certainly be retained in public assemblies. However, should anyone give approval to such traditions that are detrimental to the honor of **God**, and merely serve to turn people away from the true faith, or even dare to prefer them over the Word of **God**: then we hold that such a person, who abandons the true use of the Word of **God**, must be earnestly punished and rejected.

## The Sixteenth Chapter.
### Concerning Civil Authority.

->*It is taught here among us according to the scriptures, that the sublime powers, or the secular magistrate, has been ordained by God, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Docetur hic apud nos juxtà scripturas, quòd sublimes Potestates, seu Magistratus secularis à Deo ordinatus sit &c."</note><-

Here we teach one another according to the Scripture, that civil authority is indeed a divine ordinance, through which the people should be governed in civil and temporal matters. For Paul says expressly: There is no authority except from **God**: and those authorities that exist have been instituted by **God**. <note>A reference to Romans 13:1, a foundational text for the "Divine Right of Kings" and the duty of subjects to obey the state.</note> Furthermore, authorities must also know and believe—no matter who they may be—that the office they hold is not theirs, but **God's**, who is a **Lord** of all lords, and to whom they must one day render an account of their administration.

We further teach that, according to the Word of God, everyone should be subject to the authorities in all things that do not conflict with God and His revealed will. In matters of faith, however, and in such things that concern the soul alone, one should follow only the Word of God and those who teach the same purely and clearly, according to the words of Christ: *Give to Caesar what is Caesar's, and to God what is God's.* <note>Matthew 22:21</note> Should anyone, therefore, wish to force us into things that are contrary to God and His Word, we follow in the footsteps of the Apostles and say it to the face of the authorities: *One must obey God more than men.* <note>Acts 5:29</note>

## The Seventeenth Chapter.
### Concerning the Invocation of Saints.

*In the beginning we teach that, since humans were created, none among them has ever existed, nor is now, nor ever shall be, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Initio docemus, quòd post creatos homines, nullus eorum usque extitit, nec nunc quoque est, nec aliquando futurus est, &c."</note>

Here we teach first and above all things that since the creation of the world until its end, there has not been a single mortal, nor is there now, nor ever will be, who could be called holy in and of himself. For as Job says: *What is a man, that he should be clean? and he which is born of a woman, that he should be righteous?* <note>Job 15:14</note> Rather, even the most pious must regard the good they possess merely as a gift and present from the Lord, and must acknowledge that they have only His mercy to thank if they have found any grace in His eyes.

Following this, we teach that one should by no means render to the so-called saints, or to their images, that honor which belongs to God the Most Holy alone, and who for that reason spoke through the mouth of His prophet: *I*

## The Eighteenth Chapter.
### Concerning Fasting.

*Our fasts are a certain external form of worship among the godly, to be offered to God alone, etc.* <note>original: "Jejunia nostra cultum quendam externum in piis esse, Deo soli exhibendum, &c."</note>

Regarding fasting, we believe that such is a certain external kind of divine service which we are bound to perform for God alone; and in doing so, one must always be guided by the circumstances of the people, the places, times, and matters, but above all things, one must carefully avoid all superstition and hypocrisy.

Likewise, we also teach that true fasting does not consist in abstaining from certain foods; but rather in a moderate use of the same, and in the crucifixion and mortification <note>The spiritual practice of "killing off" sinful impulses or worldly desires.</note> of the flesh and the heart before God. However, so that one may know how and in what manner one should fast in a way pleasing to God, one may read further on this in Matthew 6 and Isaiah 58.

## The Nineteenth Chapter.
### Concerning the Single State.

*Regarding Celibacy, we teach that no one is to be forced into it, nor restrained from it, etc.* <note>original: "Ad Coelibatum docemus neminem cogendum, aut ab eo retrahendum esse, &c."</note>

Concerning the single state <term>celibacy: the state of remaining unmarried, often for religious reasons</term>, we teach that no one is to be forced into it, nor held back from the same; since it concerns a matter that God has neither expressly commanded nor forbidden, but has left it free to every individual either to marry or to remain in the free single state. Furthermore, no one should prefer the single state over the married state with the intention of thereby earning forgiveness of sins and eternal life, since such cannot be acquired through any works, whatever name they may have,

## The Twentieth Chapter.
### Concerning the opportune time to seek God and to receive His grace.

<note>original Latin: "Hoc demum loco docemus, ut sciant homines tantisper, dum in vivis sunt, Tempus à Deo quod gratiae est, &c."</note> Finally, in this place we teach so that men may know that as long as they are among the living, it is the time of grace granted by God, etc.

Finally, we teach that man, while he still lives, is bound to seek God and to be converted, in order to obtain His grace, mercy, and favor for the salvation of his soul: that while it is still called "today," and the door of grace remains open, he should repent, turn to God, and seek to quiet his conscience through faith in Jesus Christ and through the ministry of preaching which He has ordained in His church; in the certain confidence that all his sins are then forgiven, and God is reconciled with him through the merit of Jesus Christ, by whose grace he is also strengthened and perseveres in good works. Whoever stands in such circumstances has no cause at all to doubt that his soul, once departed from the body, shall immediately—and without being further tormented <note>A rejection of the doctrine of Purgatory</note>—be carried by the angels into Abraham's bosom <note>A biblical metaphor for paradise or heaven</note>, and there remain in the enjoyment of the most perfect blessedness with Christ from eternity to eternity.

The following testimony is drawn from the preface of Doctor Martin Luther, which is to be found before the Confession of Faith of the Waldensians from the year 1533, wherein he praises them and their doctrine.

# I B. 17. C. In what way the Confessions of Faith differ

II. Regarding **auricular confession** <note>The practice of confessing sins privately to a priest</note>, they confessed their sins every day to GOD Himself, and prayed for forgiveness both in their public gatherings and in private; this, they claimed, was the will of GOD and the command of the Lord JESUS, contained clearly enough in the Holy Scriptures. If the priests could prove their practice of auricular confession from these same Scriptures just as well, they would not seek to withdraw themselves from it.

III. **Baptism** was accepted by them with all reverence, according to the command of the Son of GOD, and performed just as the Lord JESUS instituted it, without them venturing to add anything to it, take anything from it, or change even the slightest detail: For they also performed everything associated with it, according to the exhortation of Paul <note>original: "Vermahnung Pauli"; likely referring to 1 Corinthians 14 regarding speaking in a known tongue</note>, in a language that could be understood by everyone. If it could be demonstrated to them that the oil, salt, and similar things <note>Traditional Catholic elements used in baptismal rites at the time</note> had their foundation in the Word of GOD, they would be willing to accept it all immediately.

IV. Concerning their **burials**, they committed their dead honorably to the earth with a large procession of followers: In doing so, they sought to comfort the afflicted, but also to exhort everyone to live in such a way that they might all one day die the death of the righteous. If it could be proven to them that GOD was not displeased by the glimmer of burning candles, the ringing of bells, and other ceremonies customary within the Papacy, they would readily join in such things.

V. As for **human ordinances** and oral traditions: they gladly and willingly accepted all those aimed at good order, outward decency, and the honor due to the preaching office. However, those that aimed at some merit toward—

To the representation made to them that the Councils <note>The author refers to the Ecumenical Councils of the Catholic Church.</note> had ordained such things, they answered: that such a claim could be made by very few. All connoisseurs and lovers of a pure, clear, and thorough divinity <note>original: "Gottesgelahrtheit" — an archaic term for theology</note> must read through this confession with the most heartfelt pleasure. It is very detailed and extensive, and contains in general nothing other than what we have already read of them, and will hear further in the sequel. My readers will therefore hopefully be satisfied if I only indicate the order of it to them, and here and there cite only a few expressions which they used in the most important main sections, especially those that are still subject to some dispute.

The 1st Article deals with the Holy **Scripture**. It states therein among other things: **The books of Holy Scripture comprise within themselves everything that is necessary to know for salvation: one must perform no other service to God than that which he himself has prescribed for us therein: outside of these books, one needs no other defense nor weapons to defeat all errors, heresies, and malices of men with which the truth is contested: All upright believers therefore prize them above all else, and searching in them is much dearer to them than gold and pearls: one shall add nothing to it, nor take anything from it, etc.**

The 2nd Article deals with the Holy, highly praised **Trinity**: especially, of **God the Father.**

The 3rd of **Christ Jesus the Son of God.** After many remarks, it says here among other things in particular: **This Jesus is the sole author of eternal life: the only one who redeems us from sins, makes us righteous and holy: The sole mediator, advocate, and representative of the human race: The sole High Priest, who has no further need of any successors.**

### The 18th [Article] on the Holy Supper.

The words read as follows: We believe and confess that the Lord Jesus instituted the Supper as a thankful remembrance of His suffering and death; and that in the same, the external signs, namely, bread and wine, are distributed and received as testimonies and memorials of the body and blood of the Lord Jesus, which He sacrificed for our sins on the tree of the cross. Therefore, whoever believes from the heart that the Lord Jesus gave His body into death also for him, and shed His blood also for him, for the forgiveness of sins: he enjoys the body and the blood of the Lord truly, and is made a partaker of both in deed. And further below it says: One must not imagine, as some do, that the body of Christ with His flesh and bones is actually stuck within the bread in the Holy Supper, or that the bread is transformed into the body of Christ <note>A rejection of the doctrines of Consubstantiation and Transubstantiation</note>: for this opinion is directly contrary to the Word of God and also to the articles of our faith; in which it is expressly taught that Christ ascended into heaven, and from there shall only come again to judge the living and the dead. # I.B.17.C. Regarding Various Confessions of Faith

1. That one should follow no one except the Lord Jesus alone.
2. That the Gospel of Jesus, without the addition of human doctrines, is already sufficient to show the way to heaven to the pilgrims in this world.
3. The canonical books of Holy Scripture alone can serve as the rule and standard of faith.
4. To what extent the writings of the Church Fathers <note>Early Christian theologians from the first few centuries after Christ</note> may be accepted.
5. What the actual nature and purpose of ceremonies in the New Testament should be.
6. Regarding the doctrine of the Sacraments, one must believe what the Holy Scripture teaches, not what the Roman Church teaches.

Following this, all these main points are treated quite thoroughly. However, since this explanation comprises an entire book of 303 leaves in large octavo <note>A book size where each sheet is folded into eight leaves</note>, we cannot include it all here. Palatini Ecclesiastæ apud Dur-drechtanos Valdensia"</note>, or "Reports on the Waldensians," which was printed in Rotterdam in the year 1616, where they may find the entire work in full.

This same Johannes Crispinus cites another Confession of Faith in that same third book of his *History of Martyrs*, which the Waldensians of Mérindol and Cabrières <note>Two prominent Waldensian settlements in Provence, France</note> presented to the Parliament of Provence; and yet another, which they sent to the King of France in the year 1544, who later had it read publicly in the Parliament of Paris in the year 1551. For the sake of brevity, I shall pass over others and include only this latter one, word for word, which summarizes quite concisely everything that was stated at length in the preceding sections. It begins as follows:

### Concerning God.

I. We believe in only one God, who is a Spirit, Creator of heaven and earth, the Father of us all, who is over us all, in the midst of us all, and in us all; who must be worshiped in spirit and in truth; from whom alone we receive life, nourishment and clothing, health and sickness, prosperity and adversity, and whom we love as the source of all good; but whom we should also fear as the one who searches hearts and minds <note>original: "Hertzen und Nieren," literally "hearts and kidneys," a biblical idiom for the innermost thoughts</note>.

II. We believe that Jesus Christ is the true Son and the image of his Father, in whom all the fullness of the Godhead dwells, and through whom we must come to the knowledge of God the Father: that He is our sole mediator and advocate, and no other name under heaven is given to men whereby they must be saved. We pray to the Father only and alone in the name of this His Son, and in no other way than as it is in the Holy

### Concerning the Christian Church.

IV. All true believers must have fellowship with this Church: she prays without ceasing for everyone; she is pleasing to God and can take refuge in Him in every distress; and outside of this Church, neither health nor salvation <note>original: "Heil noch Seligkeit"</note> is to be hoped for.

### Concerning the Teachers.

V. We firmly maintain that the bishops and teachers should be blameless in doctrine and life: if not, they shall be deposed and others appointed in their places. # I. B. 17. C. Wherein various Confessions of Faith differ

### On Good Works.

X. We believe that the faithful and God-fearing should sacrifice themselves entirely to God in order to devote themselves to good works, as He has ordained that they should walk in them. Such good works, however, are love, joy, peace, patience, friendliness, goodness, faith, gentleness, chastity, and other virtues commended to us in the Word of God. On the contrary, one should be well on guard against false prophets, whose intention is only that the honor due to the true God alone be withdrawn and turned toward creatures, and that we base our trust more on the creature than on the Creator; so that one does not do what God has commanded in the Scriptures as good works, but only follows human inventions.

### On the Holy Scriptures.

XI. We recognize and hold the entire Word of God, both the Old and New Testaments, as the rule and standard of our faith.

### On the Apostles' Creed.

XII. We uphold the Apostles' Creed. Should anyone, therefore, come forward and wish to demonstrate that we believe or teach something else: we are always ready to show the contrary, provided we are permitted to do so.

# I. B. 17. C. Wherein Different Confessions of Faith

...had been handed down to them from their ancestors from ancient times, and from one century to the next.

The above-cited historian, being ignorant of in which year of the world he should seek the origin of the Waldensians <note>The Waldensians were a medieval Christian movement often viewed as precursors to the Reformation</note>, begins their history in the first book, page 35, with these words:

> The so-called Waldensians have, from time immemorial, most zealously resisted the abuses of the Roman Church; and since he mentions a few lines later that they came from Provence and from the Piedmontese valleys, where they were held dear and esteemed by the Roman Catholics as people who were particularly loving, charitable, sincere, and generally enemies of all vices, he adds: they had never given ear to the Popish superstition, and this very thing had been the cause why they were persecuted at all times by the ecclesiastical judges, etc. Furthermore, it is to be regarded as an evident miracle from God that these people were able to preserve themselves for so long a time.

When, in the years 1532 and 1538, some of them became fugitives and took their refuge with the Margrave George of Brandenburg <note>George the Pious (1484–1543), an early supporter of the Reformation</note>, they likewise presented him with their confession, which was of the same content in all respects as those already cited.

Now I should also add the beautiful and thorough writings of defense which they issued, particularly from the years 1432, 1434, and 1508: however, I shall content myself with citing only a single one, which they presented to the Duke of Savoy, and which, although it is short, nevertheless encompasses everything contained in all the others. One can rightly regard it as a sample, and judge from it the value of the other more extensive writings.

# ...contained concerning the Waldensians.

When, in the year 1603, the Duke of Savoy expelled the **Waldensians**, those from the valleys of **Meane**, **Matthie**, and the County of **Saluzzo** published the following declaration, which I have faithfully translated from the authentic Italian transcript in my possession.

<margin>Their doctrine is ancient.</margin>
Since time immemorial, our ancestors have constantly passed down from father to son that doctrine in which we were born and raised, which we have publicly confessed until now, and which we have intended to teach our children just as we received it from our parents. From this doctrine, we did not deviate by a hair’s breadth as long as the King possessed the Marquisate of **Saluzzo**. Instead, like our brothers in the valleys of **Lucerne** <note>original: "Lucern"; likely referring to Val Luserna, a historic Waldensian stronghold in the Cottian Alps</note>, who to our deepest joy received special permission through a settlement established with the high provincial authorities, we have remained stiff and firm in our adherence to it. And now His Highness—moved more by the instigation of ill-intentioned advisors than by his own impulse—has resolved to disturb our peace and, to that end, has issued a sharpened decree against us. Therefore, we hereby testify to everyone that this does not happen because of any crimes or vices, or because we have opposed the authorities or their laws, or been murderers, robbers, or the like, thereby giving cause or occasion to be treated so cruelly, to have our goods and fortunes stolen, and to be driven from house and home, etc.

<margin>Agrees with the Reformed Church.</margin>
We therefore hereby declare publicly, and before the eyes of all the world, how we are certainly and truly convinced that the doctrine and religion which the **Reformed** churches in **France**, **Switzerland**, **Germany**, **England**, **Scotland**, **Geneva**, **Denmark**, **Sweden**, **Holland**, and other kingdoms, lands, and provinces confess with one voice, and to which...

# I.B.17.C. In which different Confessions of Faith

we also, under the protection and shield of our high territorial authorities, have hitherto publicly maintained and confessed that the one true doctrine is that which God Himself commanded to be believed and taught, and which is therefore solely and alone able to make us pleasing in the eyes of God here, and eternally blessed there one day.

<margin>We wish to live and die by this.</margin>
We are therefore also firmly resolved, even at the loss of life, property and goods, honors and dignities, to uphold the same, and until the last moment of our lives to freely offer the confession of it. Should anyone nevertheless hold that this our doctrine be erroneous or false: we most obediently and urgently request the same to thoroughly demonstrate these supposed errors to us, and we are prepared to abandon such immediately, and conversely to accept something more excellent, which is able—according to our heart's desire—to make us capable of serving our God as purely and clearly as duty requires of us poor humans, if we wish to one day attain the enjoyment of eternal joy and salvation. Should anyone, however, wish to force us with violence to leave the path of life, and instead to follow the errors and false statutes of men: then we would a thousand times rather turn our backs on our houses and goods, indeed leave body and life in the lurch <note>idiom: "im Stiche lassen" - to abandon or sacrifice</note>, and we most humbly implore Your Highness, whom we recognize and revere as our lawful high authority: only not to permit that we be persecuted without cause, but rather to graciously allow that we, our children, and their descendants, may and can further render that obedience with inviolable loyalty and obedience, which we have hitherto rendered to Your Highness as most faithful and obedient subjects.

# I. B. 17. C. Wherein Various Confessions of Faith

<margin>
...confessions did not appear earlier than the year 1120.
</margin>

...led, and these are indeed held and regarded as the first and oldest among them. We believe this to be the case because it does not seem to have been necessary to produce such documents previously, or to use them as public letters of defense to carry out their cause against the storms of persecution that threatened them, and thereby to convince the world of their righteous cause; especially since, before that time, matters had never reached such an extreme for them. Prudence itself would not have permitted them to make a great deal of fuss about their faith without necessity, and thereby wake the "biting dogs" <note>A metaphor for the inquisitors or hostile church authorities</note> from their sleep. These dogs had previously so fiercely attacked their Archbishop *Claudius of Turin* <note>Claudius of Turin (died c. 827) was a bishop famous for his opposition to the veneration of images, often cited by later Protestants as a forerunner of the Reformation</note>, who had rescued them from the Roman Church when, toward the end of the eighth century, they tried to force the veneration of images upon them and thus turn them into idolaters (of which we shall treat further below); however, after that, things had become somewhat quiet again.

But after renewed efforts were made in the aforementioned year 1120 to force Roman decrees upon them, it became a matter of the highest necessity that they not only publicly state the reasons that moved them to depart from the aforementioned Church—which we shall cite hereafter—but also lay before the eyes of the whole world that which they, for their part, believed and taught.

Let us now see whether the intervening period of 550 years, which has passed since then, has been able to change even the slightest thing in this, their Confession of Faith.

To truly get to the bottom of this, we must attentively examine the following confession, which they produced in the year 1655 after various suffered "blood-baths" <note>A reference to the "Piedmontese Easter," a brutal massacre of the Waldensians by the troops of the Duke of Savoy in April 1655</note>.

## A Brief Confession of Faith of the Reformed Congregations in Piedmont, which they published in the year 1655, together with their Defense, on the occasion of the cruel persecutions directed against them.

Since we have certainly heard that our adversaries were not satisfied with having persecuted us in the most cruel manner and deprived us of all that was ours, but are furthermore striving with all their might to make us suspicious and utterly hated in all places; to that end, they do not hesitate to spread such false rumors, which are intended not only to make us personally an abomination, but also to make the holy and soul-saving doctrine to which we profess appear erroneous and suspicious: Therefore, we find ourselves compelled to convince those who might be moved by such representations and led into adverse prejudices of the contrary; and to that end, to prepare a brief statement of what we believe, profess, and teach, just as we have done before, and as we are assured is in accordance with the Word of God. Through this, as we hope, all false accusations and slanders will reveal themselves, and all who hear and see it will be able to judge with what right we are persecuted for the sake of such an innocent doctrine.

->We believe, therefore:<-

<margin>Concerning the Holy Trinity.</margin>
I. That there is only one single GOD, and that He is a Spirit, eternal, infinite, perfectly wise, merciful, and just; that in this simple and sole essence there are three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.

<margin>How GOD has made Himself known.</margin>
II. That this GOD has revealed Himself to men often and in many ways, partly through the works of creation and preservation, but partly also through His Word, which He initially revealed orally, but afterwards <note>The text breaks off here, likely continuing with the written transmission of Scripture on the following page.</note>

# I.B.17.C. Wherein different Confessions of Faith differ

...had recorded in writing; which books we collectively call the Holy Scripture.

<margin>Concerning the Holy Scripture.</margin>
III. That one must hold this Scripture to be Divine and canonical <note>The term "canonical" refers to the official list of books accepted as authoritative for Christian doctrine and practice.</note>, just as we do; that is, that one should govern oneself according to it both in doctrine and in life: that this Scripture is comprised of the books of the Old and New Testaments: that in the Old Testament only those books should be included which God Himself prescribed to the Jewish people as a rule of conduct, and which were in turn accepted and held by them as Divine, such as the five books of Moses, the book of Joshua, the book of Judges, the book of Ruth, the first and second book of Samuel, the first and second book of Kings, the first and second book of Chronicles, the book of Ezra, the book of Nehemiah, the book of Esther, the book of Job, the Psalter, the Proverbs of Solomon, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Solomon, the four major Prophets, and the twelve minor ones; to the New Testament, however, belong the four Evangelists, the Acts of the Apostles, the Epistles of Paul—namely one to the Romans, two to the Corinthians, one to the Galatians, one to the Ephesians, one to the Philippians, one to the Colossians—the Epistle to the Hebrews, one Epistle of James, two Epistles of Peter, three Epistles of John, and the Revelation of John.

<margin>How one recognizes the Divinity of the same.</margin>
IV. That one recognizes the Divinity of the Holy Scripture not through the testimony of the Church alone, but much more through the eternal and undeniable truth contained within it, as well as no less through the excellent, high, and entirely Divine Majesty which reveals itself therein; and then finally through the grace of the Holy Spirit powerfully co-operating with it, which leads us to reverently accept the testimony that the Church gives to these writings, and which also opens our eyes so that these rays of heavenly light truly enlighten them, and improves and purifies our taste in such a way that we can truly taste the sweetness of the Divine nourishment contained therein.

# ...contained within the Waldensian [confession].

<margin>On Creation.</margin>
V. That God created all things according to His free and unrestricted will, and through the infinite omnipotence of His Word, out of nothing.

<margin>On Providence. God is not the cause of sin.</margin>
VI. That He guides and governs everything according to His providence, and nothing happens in the world without His command and decree. Yet, by this we in no way make Him the author or cause of sins, but rather most carefully reject all guilt from Him in every way and manner.

<margin>On the Angels.</margin>
VII. That the angels were created pure and holy, but some of them fell into eternal ruin and damnation; the others, however, through the operation of Divine goodness—which preserved and confirmed them in what is good—remained in this blessed state.

<margin>On the Fall of Adam.</margin>
VIII. That man, who was initially created in the image of God, namely righteous and holy, lost this great happiness through his own fault and by giving ear to the deceitful speeches of the Devil.

<margin>On the corruption of the entire human race.</margin>
IX. That this man, through his disobedience and transgression of the Divine command, lost the righteousness and holiness created within him, and instead fell under the wrath of God, death, and the dominion of him who has the power of death, that is, the Devil; so much so, that his own will has become a servant and slave to sin, and now by nature all men, both Jews and Gentiles, are children of wrath, dead in sins and transgressions, and consequently are not in a position to have even the slightest good impulse toward the salvation of their souls, or a good thought, without the preceding grace of God: for the <term>imagination and striving</term> <note>original: "Tichten und Trachten," a common Lutheran-era German idiom for the inclinations of the heart</note> of the heart is evil from youth evermore.

## Testimonies from the writings of the adversaries themselves, which irrefutably prove that the doctrine of the Waldensians was indeed at all times as we have previously presented it from their own books.

If anyone has the patience to compare these testimonies with what we have recorded so far, they will find that the content of their doctrine and the foundation of their faith have always been the same.

<margin>
Testimony of Claude Seyssel.
</margin>
In the year 1500 lived Claude Seyssel <note>original: "Claudio Seissel"</note>, Bishop of Marseille. He wrote a book on the Monarchy and dedicated it to King Francis I of France as soon as he had ascended to the throne. In the preface, he writes: that he had already been drawn into the most important affairs under three kings, Louis XI, Charles VIII, and Louis XII.

It was believed that a man of such age, of such exceptional experience, who held so much prestige and was endowed with so much learning, would be more fit than all others to gather the strayed Waldensians <term>Waldensians: a medieval spiritual movement often persecuted as heretics by the Roman Church</term> back into the bosom of the orthodox Roman Church. So that he might better approach them and have the opportunity to either lead them back or completely root them out, he was promoted from Bishop of Marseille to Archbishop of Turin. This Archbishop first wrote a book addressed to them, which I myself have among my collection of books, and which can also be found almost in its entirety in Jacques Cappel's <note>original: "Jacobi Cappels"</note> treatise on the doctrine of the Waldensians, printed at Sedan in 1618. While the Apostles desired nothing of their own in this world, one sees these men, on the contrary, coveting everything, and striving after their neighbor's goods and property more greedily than the heathens. To that end, they not only enjoy wielding the sword themselves, but also know how to masterfully persuade other princes and Christian peoples to do so. The Apostles took up the office of the Spirit for the salvation of souls only upon the prior command and inspiration of God; these men, however, seize their spiritual offices either through money or force. The favor and goodwill of the powerful on earth, which they know how to draw to themselves very craftily through their artifice, must serve them so that they may satisfy their lusts, enrich themselves and their kin, and live magnificently and in joy with the world. That former way of life <note>referring to the Apostles</note> was a constant state of waking, praying, and fasting; they moved from one place to another and shied away from no labor nor danger if only they could win souls; these men spend their time merely in idleness, gluttony, and carousing, and other works of darkness. Just as those had received the grace and gift of God for free, they shared it again for free, and said to him who wished to buy it: *May you be damned with your money* <note>original: "daß du verdamt seyst mit deinem Gelde" — a reference to Peter's rebuke of Simon Magus in Acts 8:20</note>. > "Fol. 63. They believe nothing of Purgatory, but rather direct the souls of their deceased either straight to Heaven or to Hell. Thus, in their opinion, offerings for the dead only benefit the living.

<margin>Invocation of the Saints</margin>
> "Fol. 70. They claim that the Saints in Heaven do not hear our prayers and know nothing of the service with which we honor them: their bodies lie in death and decay, while their spirits are so far removed from us that they can neither hear nor see us. They also teach that the Saints do not pray for us, and consequently, we have no need to call upon them for their intercession: they are so consumed by heavenly joy and blessedness that they no longer think of us or concern themselves with us.

> "Fol. 74. To work on Feast Days <note>Holy days of obligation</note> is nothing evil.

<margin>Fasting</margin>
> "Fol. 78. They observe neither the season of Lent nor the fast days ordained by the Church, but eat meat as they please.

<margin>The teaching of the Waldensians is based on God's Word.</margin>
> "Fol. 83. On the other hand, they wish to know nothing of the Decrees <note>referring to Papal decrees or Canon Law</note>, the legends of the Saints, and so forth. We believe in one **GOD**, in three persons: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. We believe that the Son of **God** took upon Himself our flesh and blood, was baptized in the **Jordan**, fasted in the desert, and proclaimed salvation to us. He died, was buried, descended into hell, rose again from the dead on the third day, and ascended into heaven. On the day of Pentecost, He sent the Comforter, the Holy Spirit, and shall come again on the Last Day to judge the living and the dead, and all people shall be resurrected. We are also convinced that we must confess with our mouths what we believe in our hearts. We believe that whoever does not eat the body of Christ and drink His blood cannot be saved, and so forth. They finally conclude with the words: *If anything more could be shown to us through the Gospels or the Epistles, we would believe and confess it.* <note>original: "Si quid amplius posset nobis ostendi per Evangelia, vel Epistolas, illud crederemus & confiteremus"</note>

### I. B. 18. C. Testimonies of the Adversaries

speaking of those who settled in Merindol, Cabrieres, and other regions of Provence from the valleys, and spread out powerfully, but were finally almost entirely eradicated again by the crusades instigated by the Popes, he writes: that after the Parliament of Turin sent the President of St. Julian, along with the teacher de Ecclesia <note>likely a reference to a specific theologian or legal official</note>, into the valleys against them in the year 1560, they made it known to them through their submitted Confession of Faith how they taught no other doctrine than that contained in the Old and New Testaments and in the Apostles' Creed; also that they believed in no other sacraments than those which the Savior Christ JESUS himself instituted, and through the faithful use of which they were made partakers of all his gifts, benefits, riches, and heavenly treasures: they thereby accept the conclusions of the four general councils, namely those of Nicaea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon: they believe that the secular government is ordained by God, and that everyone who fears God must be subject to it, and cannot throw its yoke from their neck without rising up against God: they have received this doctrine from their ancestors: if anyone could convince them of something better from the Word of God, and thoroughly demonstrate some errors to them, they are willing and ready to desist from them, and to be most boundly grateful to those who will lead them onto a more correct path.

# Concerning the Doctrine of the Waldensians

->on the teachings of the Waldensians.<-

to say: They believe in **God**, the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; one universal Christian Church; that the blood of **Jesus** Christ cleanses us from all our sins; that one must call upon the Father for the sake of the merit of His Son; that one must confess sins to **God**, do good works, obey the teachers who preach the Word of **God**, be subject to the authorities, and pay them tribute and taxes, etc. Instead, it is commonly only said: They believe in no saints; they reject the Roman Church, purgatory, the invocation of saints, auricular confession <note>The practice of private confession to a priest</note>, the merit of works, and works of supererogation <note>original: "Wercke der Uebergebühr" — deeds performed beyond what God requires, believed in Catholic theology to be transferable to others</note> which benefit others; they obey neither the **Pope** nor the clergy, etc.

<margin>They are persecuted not for what they believe, but for what they do not believe.</margin>
And so they are persecuted and condemned not because of their faith, but because of their "unbelief." But it cannot be otherwise; for how could one persecute them with fire and sword for the certain articles of their faith, since one pretends to hold the same opinion as they do in those matters, and the **Pope** might even boast of believing exactly what they believe? Or, if one wishes to condemn them for the sake of faith, one burdens them with such opinions—in order to persuade the common man—for which they actually have the greatest abhorrence. For example, it must be said: **God** is the author of sin; the **Lord Jesus** despaired on the cross; in view of eternal election <note>original: "Gnaden-Wahl" — the theological concept of predestination</note> it is all the same whether one is pious or godless; good works, confession, and penance are of no use; they despise the saints, and even the holy Mother of **God**, etc. And yet these are the very main points against which they testified so vehemently in the conclusion of their Confession of Faith, which they published as recently as the year 1655, and which was already cited by us above.

# I. B. 19. C. Refutation of those who [claim] the Waldensians

## The Nineteenth Chapter.

### Refutation of those who wish to derive the Waldensians from the ancient Arians, Manichaeans, Cathars, and others.

Since we have hitherto justified the doctrine of the Waldensians, both through the testimony of their adversaries and through their own confessions: it seems, to be sure, somewhat superfluous to dwell much longer on the refutation of those who have wished to present them to the world as heretics, and have particularly concerned themselves with demonstrating that they were nothing other than remnants of the ancient Arians <note>Followers of Arius (4th century), who denied the full divinity of Christ.</note>, Manichaeans <note>A dualistic religion from the 3rd century that saw the world as a struggle between light and dark.</note>, and Cathars <note>A medieval sect (often called Albigensians) known for asceticism and dualism; the name comes from the Greek for "pure."</note>, many of whom consider these to be one and the same. Meanwhile, as this opinion remains quite firmly rooted to this very day among many, even among the Reformed <note>Protestant denominations following the Calvinist tradition.</note>, as I have been able to perceive myself from various otherwise brave and learned men, who must have either found in the second part of *Hoveden’s* <note>Roger of Hoveden, a 12th-century English chronicler.</note> Annals from the year 1176 that he mixes the Waldensians, Arians, and Manichaeans together and makes only one sect out of them; or allowed themselves to be deceived by *Jacobus de Riberia* <note>James of Ribera, a 16th-century Spanish inquisitor and historian.</note>, who in his collection of the history of *Toulouse* pretends that they were remnants of the sect of the Arians, which had propagated among them from one generation to the next; or blindly followed *Petrus Vallis-Cernaii* <note>Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay, a 13th-century monk who wrote a history of the Albigensian Crusade.</note>, who in the second chapter of his history presents them as disciples of *Origen* <note>An early Christian theologian (3rd century) whose complex views on the soul were later deemed controversial.</note>: or allowed themselves to be led further astray by other historians who, either out of ignorance or even out of malice, wished to turn them into heretics, but by that very act simultaneously brought to light the most powerful proof of their antiquity: So it will indeed be worth the effort that I seek to bring such people to other and better thoughts in this matter as well.

# Concerning the attempt to derive them from the ancient Arians, etc.

<margin>Testimony of Nicolas Bertrand.</margin>
In order to avoid introducing anything suspicious here, I wish first to refer the reader to Nicolas Bertrand’s *History of Toulouse*. There, on the back of the ninth leaf, he writes in defense of the Count of Toulouse—who sided with the Waldensians or Albigensians (as those from Provence were called), and whom some sought to forcibly label an Arian <note>Arianism was an early Christian heresy that denied the full divinity of Christ; here, the term is used as a smear to justify persecution.</note>. Bertrand demonstrates that this slander was falsely imposed upon him merely by his enemies. For, he writes in that place: *He had many princes and magnates who were envious of him by reason of his virtue and power; since he could be conquered by no one, they therefore imputed heresy to him.* <note>original: "habebat multos Principes atque magnates ratione Virtutis & Potentiæ invidos, quum a nemine vinci posset, ideo hæresiu imputabant"</note> Because many princes and lords hated him for his virtue and might, and could not otherwise harm him, they went so far as to make him out to be a heretic.

<margin>Guillaume Paradin.</margin>
Guillaume Paradin assures us in the second book of his *Annals of Burgundy*, published at Lyon in the year 1566, under the entry for the year 1209 (pages 241 and 248), that he has seen from other credible historians that the Albigensians completely rejected the vices and errors falsely attributed to them. He notes they were maliciously accused, yet they convincingly demonstrated their total innocence regarding everything laid to their charge—except for one single thing: namely, that they had perhaps been somewhat too vehement in their zeal against the sins and the wicked lives of the clergy.

<margin>Du Haillan.</margin>
The verdict of Lord Haillan <note>Bernard de Girard, Seigneur du Haillan (c. 1535–1610), a prominent French historian.</note> is also very fitting here. # I. B. 19. C. Refutation of those who [call] the Waldensians [Manichaeans]

<margin>Clever reasons why the Waldensians were called Manichaeans.</margin>
This same Reinerus <note>Reinerus Saccho (c. 1200–1259), a Dominican inquisitor and former Cathar who wrote extensively against heretical groups.</note> provides yet another reason why they were called Manichaeans: For, he says in the fifth chapter, page 87, they reject the state of marriage and say that all sexual intercourse, without the purpose of procreating children, is a mortal sin. Certainly a "fine" reason to call them Manichaeans, since one does not even blame a pagan when he says:

->Wine should only quench thirst; nourishing Venus <note>original: "Venus alma"; a poetic reference to sexual love or procreation.</note> is sufficient for creating offspring; it is harmful to leap beyond these boundaries.<-

The wine should only satisfy thirst, and intercourse should be restricted to the procreation of children: it is harmful to cross the boundaries in the former as well as in the latter. Thus, the Empress Zenobia <note>Third-century Queen of the Palmyrene Empire, known for her chastity and intellect.</note> is also praised because she no longer allowed her husband near her as soon as she noticed she was pregnant. However, I do not cite this because I wish to censure all chaste intercourse or reject the moderate use of wine: but only to bring the innocence and simplicity of the Waldensians, and conversely the malice of their adversaries, more clearly to light. For since the latter knew of nothing else to charge the former with as sin and heresy, they had to take refuge in such accusations and burden them with things of which they must certainly admit that those who can keep them, and are still in a position to keep them, are to be praised.

# ...wanting to derive them from the ancient Arians, etc.

They could no longer bear to witness the luxury, gluttony, and pride which Constantine had helped provide to this Sylvester <note>Pope Sylvester I (r. 314–335 AD), whom legend claims received the "Donation of Constantine," granting the Papacy vast worldly power.</note>, and simultaneously to the entire Church. # Apostolic Succession and Descent

One who considers this well, and is willing to place what belongs to the system of doctrine upon the scales of the Scripture and the ancient Fathers <note>The "Church Fathers" refers to influential Christian theologians of the first few centuries.</note> without particular prejudice, will indisputably be convinced that at that time, idolatry did not yet sit upon the throne, and the pillars of truth still stood firm and unmoved. Indeed, it can be asserted with complete certainty that at that time—I will not say merely in all of Europe and the West, but anywhere in the whole world—not a single person, let alone an entire congregation, could have been found who could rightly have been called Papist <note>A historical, often polemical term for Roman Catholics, implying primary loyalty to the Pope.</note>; or who would have taught those doctrines which the Roman Church introduced in the following ages, and has since endeavored to maintain and propagate with fire and sword.

It is not necessary to dwell long upon this, or to demonstrate with many reasons that the Roman decrees—which moved the Waldensians <note>A medieval spiritual movement that sought to return to the simplicity of the early church; they were often persecuted as heretics by Rome.</note> to depart from this Church—were still completely unknown up to that time. # Apostolic Succession and Lineage

Just as the ignorant <note>referring to Caiaphas in the Gospel of John 11:50</note> prophesied the truth of Christ—that it were better for one man to be put to death for the people—so too did **Gregory** the Great, Bishop of Rome, prophesy not incorrectly when he sought to refute the opinion of **John**, Bishop of **Constantinople**. (John believed that because this city was then the seat of both the **Western** and **Eastern** Empires, he could also bear the title of a universal bishop of all Christendom). In doing so, Gregory publicly used these words among others: That whoever should once presume to claim this title for himself must necessarily be either the **Antichrist**, or at least his forerunner. And this is exactly what his successor **Boniface** did in the aforementioned century, when—through the help and advancement of the cruel tyrant and parricide **Phocas**, who like a second **Shimei** <note>A biblical figure who cursed King David; here used to denote a traitor</note> murdered his lord, Emperor **Maurice**, in order to seize the Empire for himself—he declared the See of the Roman Church to be the head of all Christian churches, <note>original: "sedem Ecclesiæ Romanæ Caput omnium Ecclesiarum"</note> just as the city of Rome itself was declared the head of the entire salutary life, which previously had been **Constantinople** on account of the Imperial seat being located there. These are not our words, but the words of **Bede** in his book *On the Six Ages of the World*, **Paul the Deacon** in *Roman Affairs* book 15 and *History of the Lombards* book 4, chapter 14, **Pomponius Laetus** in his *Compendium of Roman History*, and many other famous historians.

# Of Apostolic Succession and Descent.

A great bishop <note>Referring to Claudius of Turin (died c. 827), who opposed the use of images and the authority of the Pope.</note> set himself with such zeal against the abuses that had been introduced into the Roman Church during the 8th century and up until the beginning of the 9th. He did this, moreover, in the second and most prominent commercial city of France <note>Lyon</note>, which was situated so near to the borders of *Provence*, *Languedoc*, and our valleys, and was to be regarded as the largest and sole warehouse for all goods passing through France. There, he knew how to maintain the Evangelical truth with such steadfastness, pure and clear. Is it not likely that this holy seed remained in store even into the 10th century, and was the very same that afterwards, in the 11th and 12th centuries, grew so magnificently and even to the point of astonishment in all the surrounding lands? And after it had been fully watered through the preaching of the Divine Word and the exceptional zeal of *Peter Waldo* <note>original: "Petri Baldo"</note>, or rather *Valdensis*, did it not bear such excellent fruit? We shall also see in the sequel that as soon as he began to preach in this famous city, all the public squares became too narrow to hold the innumerable multitude of his listeners and disciples; these subsequently spread themselves as so many good shepherds and true Evangelical teachers throughout all *Europe*, and even into a part of *Asia*.

Thus one also finds in the biography of *Louis the Pious* <note>original: "Ludewigs des Gütigen"</note>, published by *P. Pithou* <note>Pierre Pithou (1539–1596), a French lawyer and scholar.</note>, that when Pope *Gregory* IV threatened to excommunicate the Emperor along with all his bishops, the latter publicly opposed him. They would by no means submit to the Papal obstinacy, but instead declared: That in the event he should venture to do such a thing, they would in turn regard and hold him as one who was himself excommunicated. Indeed, in the French Annals, also published by this same *Pithou*, one reads under the year 863 an excellent letter which *Gunther*, Archbishop of Cologne, and *Theutgaud*— <note>Theutgaud was the Archbishop of Trier; they were deposed by the Pope for supporting the divorce of Lothair II.</note>

We exclude you from this communion by virtue of your own judgment; because whoever does not keep the commandments of the Apostles, dishonors the divine laws, and sins outrageously against the dearly accepted canons <note>Ecclesiastical rules or laws</note>, must be an Anathema <note>original: "Anathema"; a formal curse or excommunication</note>, as you are. Know, therefore, that we no longer belong to you or your clergy, and you have no reason to boast of us any further."

<margin>4. Especially in Italy and Piedmont.</margin>

# Apostolic Succession and Lineage

Since they have always maintained the pure doctrine of the Holy Scriptures and the ancient orthodox churches in an unadulterated form, they have never ceased to voluntarily reject everything that others have sought to impose upon them. One need only look at the complaints which they sent not only to the Pope in Rome, but also—which is well worth noting—to the Eastern Churches. An irrefutable testimony of this is provided by that beautiful letter which all the bishops in Italy wrote to all the Eastern Patriarchs. It is addressed to the Patriarch of Constantinople, Photius <note>Photius the Great (c. 810–893), a central figure in the conflict between Eastern and Western Christianity</note>, 
<margin>Testimony of Baronius <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), a Catholic cardinal and historian known for his "Annales Ecclesiastici"</note></margin>
and is cited by Baronius in his Annals, where one hears the aforementioned Patriarchs speaking thus:

> We have received a synodal letter from Italy, in which the inhabitants there complain about their own Bishop <note>Referring here to the Pope in Rome</note> and accuse him of a gruesome multitude of wickednesses and vices: among other things, they cite the excessive power that he arrogates to himself over them, and they beg us for the protection of their churches with many tears: *a synodal letter was brought to us from the regions of Italy, containing six hundred evils and crimes, concerning which those who inhabit Italy [complain] against their own Bishop, especially regarding his tyranny, etc.* <note>original: "ex partibus Italiæ Synodica Epistola ad nos allata est, sexcenta continens mala & delicta, de quibus adversus proprium ipsorum Episcopum illi qui Italiam incolunt, maxime de tyrannide &c."</note>

It is therefore so far from the truth that all of Italy should have accepted the innovations that the Popes sought to introduce at that time; rather, one finds entire assemblies of bishops and other clergy who opposed them, and this continued even until toward the end of the ninth century.

# The Twenty-First Chapter.

->Claudius, Archbishop of Turin and in the Valleys, publicly departs from the Pope and the communion of the Roman Church at the end of the eighth century.<-

It has indeed been demonstrated and proven more than sufficiently in the preceding pages that, despite the Roman Church and the Pope exerting every effort to scatter all kinds of superstitious doctrines, there were nevertheless found—even up until the end of the 9th century—many churches, indeed great provinces and kingdoms, which not only did not accept them, but rather opposed them with all zeal and emphasis. This was done in such a way that these doctrines could never be forced upon them, no matter how the Pope in Rome may have wished to arrange it. Thus, the prophecy we read in the Revelation of John was fulfilled: that there would always remain souls who would not worship the beast, nor his image, and would not receive his mark on their forehead and on their hand, so that they could neither buy nor sell, but on the contrary would be most cruelly persecuted and deprived of all freedom to associate with others, until a thousand years should be completed, at which time the dragon, the old serpent, which is the devil, should be released again. <note>A reference to Revelation 20, interpreting the medieval period as the time of the dragon's binding or release.</note> Accordingly, we praise here the incomprehensible wisdom and admirable providence of the Most High, who not only knew how to maintain at all times a multitude of such faithful witnesses who earnestly and zealously resisted the "Son of Perdition" <note>original: "Kinde des Verderbens"; a biblical title for the Antichrist</note> after he had fully revealed himself: but also willed from time to time to awaken men who spoke out with an open mouth against the Antichrist from the very moment he was, so to speak, born and brought idolatry <term>idolatry: the worship of images or icons, a central point of contention for Claudius</term> into the world with him.

# I. B. 21. C. Of Archbishop Claudius

"I do this even now, and I will not cease to do it with all my strength, as long as God grants me His grace to do so. For since it is expressly stated: **You shall not make for yourself any image or any likeness, whether of that which is above in heaven, or that which is below on earth,** etc. <note>Exodus 20:4</note>, this is by no means to be understood only as the likenesses of foreign gods, but generally of all and every heavenly creature.

"Those against whom we have undertaken to defend the Church of God make this conclusion: if you paint the images of Peter, Paul, Jupiter, Mercury, or others on the wall or elsewhere, these paintings are neither gods, nor apostles, nor men. Thus the name is changed, and yet the error remains at all times one and the same: if one had to worship them, surely it would have to happen while they were alive, rather than under such images as you are accustomed to present—namely, of irrational animals, or at least (what cannot be denied) of stone or wood, which has neither life, nor sensation, nor understanding. Now, if one is not even to revere or worship the work of God's hands <note>referring to nature or living beings</note>, how much less then that which only human hands have made, in order to perform a service to the one whose likeness is thereby represented? But if that image which you worship is not God, why then do you fall down before it, and lie like a prisoner at the feet of an absurd and disguised earthly being? But everyone who reveres something—be it a visible image or another creature in heaven or on earth, be it spiritual or physical—and performs a service to it: he serves it and honors it instead of God, and expects from it the salvation which he is to seek from God alone. Consequently, such a person belongs to those of whom Paul says: **that they honored and served the creature more than the Creator.**" <note>original: "daß sie das Geschöpfe mehr geehret und ihm gedienet, denn dem Schöpfer." This very same confession is found almost word for word in another discourse he held for the priests, which was translated from English into Latin and thereafter into German, and was also printed by order of Wulfstan, the Bishop of York <note>original: "eboracensischen Bischofs"</note>.

# The Twenty-Third Chapter.
## Concerning the Revelation of the Antichrist in the 11th Century.

From everything that has been discussed thus far, one can now very easily draw the conclusion that since Satan was still bound until the eleventh century <note>The author refers to the millenarian belief that Satan was bound for a thousand years after Christ's first coming</note> and was not yet permitted to deceive all the inhabitants of the earth collectively, the Antichrist was also not yet fully revealed. It was still free for anyone to either accept or reject the errors creeping into the Church as they wished. Thus, the churches in the valleys could very well have maintained the pure Apostolic truth, even if they had not yet so solemnly separated themselves from the communion of the Roman Church. 

However, since we know with complete certainty that such a separation actually occurred in the eighth century—when they not only departed from Rome in the manner cited above, but also steadfastly denounced the Roman doctrine as superstitious, false, and idolatrous, and proclaimed the Popes to be by no means Apostolic, but rather like the Scribes and Pharisees sitting in the seat of Moses—we are continually more and more strengthened in this conclusion. That this was actually their faith in the 8th century, and that they remained steadfast in it through the 9th and 10th centuries, has been sufficiently confirmed to us by the aforementioned irrefutable testimony of a prominent writer of the Roman Church, Aurelius Rorencus. He was himself a member of the Great Council <term>for the extirpation of heretics</term> <note>original: "de extirpandis hæreticis"</note>, a native of the valleys, and a co-regent of the Valley of Lucerne. He made it his particular business to work on this matter, specifically in two books, one of which he wrote to Turin and the other to Rome, both of which were published with the approval of the clergy in Turin.

# I. B. 24. C. Concerning the State of the Church

**Berengarius** <note>Berengarius of Tours (c. 999–1088), a theologian who famously disputed the real presence of Christ in the Eucharist.</note> found himself compelled to recant his teachings: nevertheless, he remained steadfast in them until his end, as **Ussher** <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh and a noted scholar.</note> reports in the place cited above: and **Peña** <note>Francisco Peña (c. 1540–1612), a canon lawyer who edited the 'Directorium Inquisitorum'.</note> writes at the end of Commentary 31 on the second part of the *Directory of Inquisitors*: <note>original Latin: "Berengarium nunquam conversum a prima sententia"</note> *Berengarius was never truly converted from his first opinion,* even though he had solemnly recanted it. Whoever desires more testimonies regarding the constancy of this **Berengarius** should read **Baronius's** *Annals*, Volume 11 for the year 1085, and **P. # I. B. 24. C. On the State of the Churches

Peter of Vaux-de-Cernay <note>original: "Petrus Valsernensis," a 13th-century Cistercian monk and chronicler of the Albigensian Crusade</note> in the preface to his history of the Albigensians, and Davity <note>Pierre Davity, a prolific 17th-century French writer</note> at the cited location, have noted this. Therefore, they call the former by the name of the latter, and the latter by the name of the former, as it suits them, and condemn both together under this designation. 

Since, however, at that time nothing was yet known of Peter Waldo of Lyon, let this be taken as a new and strong proof—and added to what we have already recalled when we spoke of this Waldo, who lived at the same time as Abbot Berengarius <note>Berengar of Tours (c. 999–1088), a theologian who disputed the nature of the Eucharist.</note>, and of which we have already dealt in the second chapter of this book with a detailed indication of the true origin of their name—that this name by no means originates from this Waldo. Rather, they received the name Waldensians, *Valdenses*, *Valdensi*, according to their local language, from "valleys" <note>original: "Thälern"</note>; for the word Waldensian in that language means as much as an inhabitant of a valley. Furthermore, the entire population of all those valleys lying between the Alps—not only toward Piedmont but also toward France—have held the same faith and doctrine from ancient times.

For the full confirmation of this truth, let the kind reader further note the following: according to the chronology of Genebrard <note>Gilbert Génébrard (1535–1597), a French Benedictine exegete and historian.</note> and other proven Catholic historians, Saint Bernard was placed among the number of the saints by Pope Alexander III in the year 1165, twelve years after his death. # I. B. 25. C. Concerning Peter Waldo of Lyon

<margin>The Waldensians received their name from the valleys, and not from this Waldo.</margin>

The author of the book titled *The State of the Churches* confirms this very point when he says on page 336: After Waldo and his followers were driven out of Lyon, a portion of them turned toward Lombardy (in which the valleys of Piedmont are situated), and from there spread throughout all of Italy and Sicily. This is clearly stated in the *Book of Martyrs* in the description of the cruel persecution at Merindol and Cabrières, where it says: That they had come from Piedmont in former times and settled in Provence and the regions of Merindol, Cabrières, and thereabouts. When Henricus Pantaleon, in his history of martyrs published in Basel by Nicolaus Brylinger in the year 1563, cited the opinion of Jean Crespin and others regarding the massacre carried out against the Albigensians at Merindol in the year 1545, he says: *a Ducentis ferme Annis a Pedemontio in Provintiam profecti erant* <note>original: "a Ducentis ferme Annis a Pedemontio in Provintiam profecti erant"</note>, they had come from Piedmont to Provence nearly 200 years prior. The *French Church History*, volume 1, page 35, states the same.

The Archbishop of *Lyon*, an enemy and persecutor of the *Waldensians*, achieves nothing against them.

The latter did not fail to immediately excommunicate *Waldo* and all those who held with him, and gave so much emphasis to the persecution that the Archbishop had already begun against them, that they were forced to depart from *Lyon* and vacate the city. ### I. B. 26. C. Regarding the Antiquity of the Waldensians

...to stop the mouths of those who maliciously abuse the words of **Tertullian** <note>An early Christian author (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) often cited by both Catholics and Protestants regarding the origins of the church</note> in his treatise *The Prescription Against Heretics* <note>original: "de praescriptione contra Haereticos"</note>, and who cannot stop spitting these mocking questions in our faces: *Who are you? From where have you come? Where have you been hiding for so long?* <note>original: "Quis estis vos? unde venistis? ubi tamdiu latuistis?"</note>

<margin>1. From their own writings.</margin>
I shall draw the first thorough proof of this important truth from the Waldensians' own writings, though I will look more at their content than the time in which they were written. The language they use therein shall convince us whether they speak the tongue of Ashdod or of the Jews <note>A biblical reference to Nehemiah 13:24; the author is asking if their speech sounds like "foreign" heretics or the "pure" people of God</note>—that is, whether they speak as the seed of Abraham. I will primarily make use of those writings which they publicly presented to the great and high-ranking figures of the world on every occasion when they had to deal with them, and show how they always appealed to their antiquity in those documents, without anyone ever raising an objection against it.

<margin>2. From the writings of the Protestants.</margin>
The second proof will be provided to me by the most distinguished teachers and historians among the Protestants. Their testimonies shall demonstrate that they were truly convinced of the pure antiquity of these people; and we shall hear them praise and glorify God, who knew how to preserve this small, smoldering wick <note>A reference to Isaiah 42:3, symbolizing a faith that, while nearly extinguished, was kept alive by God</note> in such a wondrous way: so that in following times, almost all Reformed and Protestant churches throughout Europe were able to light their torches from it, some in an indirect and some in a direct manner.

<margin>3. From the testimonies of their own adversaries.</margin>
The third and final proof, which is intended to decide and settle everything completely, shall be so significant that it shall forever shut the mouth of **Cerberus** <note>The multi-headed dog from Greek mythology that guards the underworld; here used to represent the fierce and relentless critics of the Waldensian faith</note> himself, so that he can never again bite these poor believers, nor even bark at them. I shall seek this proof in the multitude of the most important testimonies and statements of their worst enemies and adversaries, and even the ecclesiastical judges, or so-called Inquisitors <note>Officials of the Catholic Church appointed to root out and punish heresy</note>...

### ...from their own writings.

...let [their enemies] speak for themselves—those who were destined only to completely root out this remnant of the "little flock" of Jesus <note>A biblical reference to Luke 12:32, often used by persecuted minority groups to describe themselves</note> and to entirely vanish their memory from the earth. One can see as early as the sixth line that this work was composed in the year 1100, and consequently at the beginning of the 12th century. The content and the writing style within it are perfectly Apostolic: all kinds of vices are punished most severely, while all Christian virtues are depicted most beautifully and recommended most emphatically. The reading of the Divine Word is presented therein as a primary duty for all people. The worship of the only true God—with the total exclusion of all other creatures—the patient endurance under all kinds of "crosses" and suffering, and the careful avoidance of false prophets and all errors are most strictly enjoined.
