### I. B. 26. C. On the Antiquity of the Waldensians

...[the poem, *The Noble Lesson*] depicts [the Church's corruption] in the most natural, life-like colors, and portrays the forgiveness of sins granted by priests for money <note>indulgences</note> as a most abominable new invention of the Antichrist. All of this is done in a way that clearly teaches us that they have abhorred Roman decrees at all times, and never accepted any other teachings than those which the Lord JESUS himself and his Apostles taught—teachings which have come to them, so to speak, from one hand to the other, and have been passed down unchanged from father to son. This is sufficient to relieve me of the effort of proving in more detail that the Waldensians (who were already called by that name in the cited writing) by no means received this name from a certain Peter Waldo <note>original: "Petro Waldo," a 12th-century merchant often credited as the founder of the Waldensians</note>; much less did they receive their doctrine from him, which they testify was already ancient and Apostolic back then, and with which they already defended themselves so powerfully against the modern inventions and decrees of the Popes in the year 1100.

<margin>On the Antichrist.</margin>
The incomparable treatise *On the Antichrist*, which is likewise found in its full context in the same book regarding the doctrine of the ancient Waldensians, and which is dated to the year 1120—consequently fifty years before this Peter Waldo lived—lends a hand to the preceding proof. If one considers this with just a little reflection, one will find, to the point of conviction, with what magnificent armor the believers of God were already equipped at that time against the new doctrines and errors of the Popish <note>original: "päbstischen," a historical term for the Roman Catholic Church</note> Church.

### I. B. 26. C. On the Antiquity of the Waldensians

People went further, and finally turned these blessedly departed into half-gods, or at the very least into intercessors and mediators between GOD and man, to whom one must first direct one's prayer. And it is against this that this writing is directed, in which this new teaching, *The new Intercessions introduced by the man of Sin* <note>original: "Las novas Interceſſions entermena per l'homme de Peccà"</note>, is presented and rejected as a new kind of prayer that the man of sin introduced into the Church of GOD. 

Now, it is more than sufficiently known to all those who have looked even a little into Church history that this superstitious doctrine developed in the sixth century under **Gregory the Great**, Bishop of Rome, and crept into the Latin Church; that from that time on, not only were all already introduced innovations publicly confirmed—since a wretched beginning had been made especially in the Greek churches since the year 476—but many new ones were added. It was at that time that they began to make little "godlings" out of the saints, to consecrate churches to them, to celebrate special feast days, and other such things. 

Furthermore, while the invocation of saints had previously been introduced only here and there, and the largest and best part of the Church had still vehemently opposed it, efforts were now made to make it universal. The aforementioned **Gregory** was the first who had the Blessed Virgin **Mary** placed in the Litany <term>Litany: a form of prayer consisting of a series of petitions recited by the clergy with fixed responses from the congregation</term>, thereby giving cause for the same honor to be gradually bestowed upon the remaining saints in the following times; so that by the eighth century, almost all Northern <note>The original German "mitternächtische" (midnight) was a common archaic term for "Northern."</note> churches were infected by this impurity. 

From this, the conclusion follows naturally that this little work, which the Waldensians wrote soon after the beginning [of these practices] against this new doctrine, must necessarily be much older than the one written against the **Antichrist**. But be that as it may, one sees from the content and the manner of its presentation that their only concern was to [preserve] the doctrine of **JESUS** and his A- <note>The text cuts off here; the catchword "postel" indicates the word is "Apostles."</note>

In the year 1603, the Waldensians in the valleys of Meano and Mattie—near Susa and also in Piedmont—who at all times stood as one man with the other valleys, made a similar representation to the Duke of Savoy, **Charles Emmanuel** <note>Charles Emmanuel I (1562–1630), known as "the Great," who frequently vacillated between tolerating and persecuting the Waldensians depending on his political needs.</note>. Truly, if they had wished to challenge this truth, they would have had to be far more cunning than all the state officials of the elder **Emmanuel Philibert** <note>Emmanuel Philibert (1528–1580), Duke of Savoy, known as "Ironhead," who regained his lands after the Treaty of Cateau-Cambrésis in 1559.</note>—one of the most astute Dukes to ever rule **Savoy**—put together. In the third chapter of the following second book, we will cite in its full context the beautiful and remarkable letter written by the poor **Waldensians** <note>A medieval Christian movement that predated the Protestant Reformation and survived in the Alpine valleys of Piedmont.</note> in the year 1559 to this, their sovereign prince. In it, they use, among others, the following words: "May your Highness graciously consider that the religion to which we profess is not a work of our hands, or as some falsely claim, only recently invented; rather, it is the very same that our fathers, grandfathers, great-grandfathers, and great-great-grandfathers—indeed all our ancestors from the most ancient times—have professed; yes, it is a religion taught by all holy martyrs and witnesses of the truth, sealed with their blood long before us, and in a word, the teaching of the **Apostles** and **Prophets** themselves. If anyone is capable of proving otherwise to us, we are willing and ready, etc."

Would a lord such as this Duke, or all those who were deemed worthy to be in his presence, ever have tolerated such a bold challenge from such poor people if the state officials or the clever clergy, with all their sophistication, had been capable of concocting anything to counter it?

I. B. 27. C. On the Antiquity of the Waldensians

# The Twenty-Seventh Chapter.

## Testimonies regarding the antiquity of the Waldensians, and the inhabitants of the valleys of Piedmont, from the writings of their fellow believers.

<margin>Testimonies of the Protestants.</margin>
Given so many convincing arguments for the actual antiquity of the **Waldensians**, and since they themselves have proven their true **Apostolic succession** <note>original: "Apostolische Folge"; the claim that their church lineage traces back directly to the Apostles, bypassing the Roman Catholic hierarchy.</note> as clear as day: it is then no wonder that we find that those who followed their faith—including the most prominent teachers and historians among them—recognize them as a **mother of all Reformed Churches**. They are compelled to admire and praise the divine wisdom and mercy by which this lowly **smoldering wick** <note>original: "geringscheinende Docht"; a biblical allusion to Isaiah 42:3, signifying a faith that was nearly extinguished by persecution but kept alive by God.</note> remained glowing in the midst of so many storms and tempests in a most wonderful manner. This **holy seed**, which was destined to bear such glorious fruit in the world once more, could never be choked out by the many weeds that the enemy sowed among the pure wheat from time to time while men slept.

<margin>1. Robertus Olivetanus.</margin>
Among all testimonies of this kind, we rightly grant the first place here to that which was provided by **Robertus Olivetanus** <note>Pierre Robert Olivétan (c. 1506–1538), a cousin of John Calvin and a key figure in the French Reformation.</note>. This distinguished and pious man translated the Bible entirely and faithfully into the **French language** for the very first time at the expense of the Waldensians in Piedmont, and had it printed in **Neuchâtel**, Switzerland, in the year 1537. I say "entirely" with great care: for although the Waldensians in previous times and for several hundred years had possessed the **New Testament** as well as several books of the **Old Testament**—namely the **Books of Moses**, the **Psalter**, the **Proverbs of Solomon**, and the **Book of Job**—in their homes and assemblies, they still lacked all the rest. And even though they previously had some old written

In the preface which this pious **Olivetanus** placed before the said Bible, he first thanks **God**, who ignited the light of the Gospel among the Waldensians—or, which is the same to him, among the inhabitants of the Alps—near the time of the Apostles and their immediate successors, and has let it remain bright in this Goshen <note>A biblical reference to the Land of Goshen, where the Israelites had light while the rest of Egypt was in darkness; used here to describe the Valleys as a sanctuary of truth.</note> until now. Since he himself was one of their most prominent teachers, he was able to provide the most reliable report of their circumstances, and we therefore cite his own words here: "These poor people," he says, "have constantly had cause to rejoice in the heavenly treasure of truth, as it is contained in the Holy Scriptures, and which was so very abundantly shared with them by the Apostles of our **Lord Jesus Christ**." # I. B. 27. C. On the Antiquity of the Waldensians

...that they are the true remnants of the very first true Christian Church. For it is well known and certain enough that almighty **GOD**, according to His inscrutable providence, knew how to preserve them in such a way amidst so many storms that for many hundreds of years already they have shaken the world, which had been led astray by the cunning maneuvers of the Roman Popes; and that although almost the entire **West** <note>original: *Occident*</note> had unfortunately submitted to the **Antichrist** <note>In Reformation-era polemics, the "Antichrist" was a common epithet for the Papacy.</note>, it was nevertheless never possible for him, despite all the persecutions he stirred up against them, to gather them into the number of his idolatrous worshippers and admirers of his tyranny. To this very day, in defiance of the devil and all his satanic efforts, they still have their churches there, and these remain, even up to the present hour, in the most beautiful and flourishing condition, both in terms of doctrine and conduct. I am speaking here specifically of the valleys located in the **Alps**, belonging partly to the King of **France** and partly to the Duke of **Savoy**. It is beyond description what pains these lords took from time to time, at the prompting of the Popes, to root out these people: who, otherwise due to their extreme poverty, need fear no thieves or murderers, and who, for the sake of their pious and blameless conduct, were held dear and worthy by all men, whereby they always successfully deflected and put to shame the thousands of false accusations and slanders brought against them.

<margin>See Sleidanus.</margin>
**Sleidanus** <note>Johannes Sleidanus (1506–1556), a famous historian and diplomat known for his detailed chronicles of the Reformation movement.</note>, a very famous historian whom all scholars throughout **Europe** applaud, and upon whose exceptional scholarship and faithfulness members of other churches themselves rely, has [written] many books on spiritual and secular histories...

<summary>This page argues that the Waldensians represent the original, uncorrupted Christian Church, preserved by God through centuries of Papal persecution in the Alpine valleys of France and Savoy. It cites the historian Sleidanus as a scholarly authority on their enduring and blameless character despite their poverty.</summary>

<header>from the writings of their fellow believers.</header>

...written. When he deals with Emperor Charles V, and in the 16th chapter also comes to the Waldensians, he gives them the testimony on page 534 that they have resisted the Popes from all times and have kept their religion pure and clear. <term>By ancient custom, they in no way recognize the Roman Pontiff, and have always held a purer religion</term> <note>original Latin: "Hi vetusta consuetudine Pontificem Romanum nequaquam agnoscunt, & puriorem semper habuerunt Religionem."</note>. Here, this great scholar himself knows of no specific time to name when they began to no longer recognize the Roman Pope, but instead uses only the unrestricted expression: <term>by ancient custom</term> <note>original Latin: "vetusta consuetudine"</note>, meaning from times of old.

<margin>4. Rudiger and Illyricus.</margin>
Thus, Esron Rudiger, in his book <term>A Brief Narrative of the Churches of the Brethren in Bohemia</term> <note>original Latin: "Narratiuncula de Ecclesiis Fratrum in Bohemia"</note>, also knows of no specific time to determine the beginning of the Waldensians, but instead frankly offers only the following confession regarding them: <term>The Waldensians precede our origin by at least two hundred and forty years</term> <note>original Latin: "Valdenses ad minimum ducentis quadraginta Annis originem nostrum antecedunt"</note>. The Waldensians are at the very least two hundred and forty years older than we are; he is speaking of the **Hussites** <note>Followers of Jan Hus, a Czech reformer who preceded Martin Luther.</note> or disciples of the well-known **Jan Hus**. Since it was already approaching the end of the thirteenth century when a part of **Bohemia** threw the Roman yoke from its neck, and it is stated here that the Waldensians had already existed in their current constitution for more than two hundred and forty years prior, it necessarily follows that they must have existed at least by the beginning of the eleventh century, and thus eighty years before **Peter Waldo of Lyon** <note>The author is attempting to prove that the Waldensians were not founded by Peter Waldo in the 1170s, but existed long before him, making them a "true" ancient church.</note>. It is also remarkable that **Illyricus** <note>Matthias Flacius Illyricus (1520–1575), a Lutheran reformer and historian.</note>, in the 19th book of his *Catalog of the Witnesses of the Truth*, says that Jan Hus and **Jerome of Prague** did nothing more than restore the doctrine of the Waldensians—or rather, the Gospel of Jesus Christ—and that **Wycliffe** <note>John Wycliffe, the 14th-century English reformer.</note> provided them with the occasion and opportunity for this. He stated shortly before that Wycliffe lived during the time of **Nicholas of Lyra**, consequently around the year 1322.

<header>I. B. 27. C. On the Antiquity of the Waldensians</header>
<meta>catchword: bishop</meta>

<margin>J. Comenius.</margin>
The venerable, learned, and God-fearing *Comenius* <note>Johannes Amos Comenius (1592–1670), a famous Czech philosopher and the last bishop of the Unity of the Brethren before its near extinction during the Counter-Reformation</note>, who was the sole survivor among the Reformed bishops who had the good fortune to escape the Bohemian persecutions, has recorded the history thereof, just as he diligently drew it from the yearbooks and chronicles of this land, which he snatched from the flames in quite a miraculous way and still preserves in *Amsterdam*; and he writes therein on the 70th and following pages, among other things, this remarkable event:

<margin>Their doctrine dates back to the time of Constantine.</margin>
> The believers in Bohemia and Moravia, who had broken away from the fellowship of the Papists and Calixtines <note>A moderate Hussite group that insisted on receiving "the chalice" (wine) during communion, unlike the Catholic practice of the time which reserved it for priests</note>, had chosen three teachers among themselves, but were very troubled regarding their formal consecration into church service. However, when they heard that Waldensians were located on the borders of Moravia and Austria, they resolved—to relieve their own consciences and those of their people of all worry and doubt, both now and for the future—to send one of their preachers, *Michael of Žamberk* <note>original: "Michael Zambergium"</note>, who had previously been ordained by the Roman Bishop himself, along with two others, to report to the Waldensians how they were faring, and primarily to seek counsel on how best to arrange their affairs under the current circumstances. Here they met a certain Waldensian bishop named *Stephen* <note>original: "Stephanus"</note>, who, to please them, summoned another bishop and various other clergy, with whose assistance he clearly showed these delegates from Bohemia and Moravia that his doctrine and that of the other Waldensians had been as it was since the time of *Constantine* <note>original: "Constantini," referring to the Roman Emperor Constantine the Great, implying a lineage back to the 4th century</note>; he then explained their articles of faith to them piece by piece, and thereafter recounted the many cruel persecutions that he and his fellow believers had endured in Italy and France. When all this had occurred, the said bishop

<summary>This page cites the historian and bishop Comenius to argue that the Waldensian lineage and doctrine date back to the time of Emperor Constantine. It recounts a meeting between Bohemian reformers and a Waldensian bishop named Stephen to establish a legitimate, ancient succession for their ministry.</summary>

...bishop Stephanus, with the inclusion of the other three aforementioned clergymen, granted them the formal call to the preaching office, ordained them, and blessed them with the laying on of hands. At the same time, he authorized them to likewise empower others in the future to lead such an office. From that time on, the believers in Bohemia and Moravia always desired and sought the opportunity to be more closely united with the aforementioned Waldensians, and for that reason, they were afterwards themselves called Waldensians. On the 75th page, he confirms once more that the churches in Bohemia as well as in Moravia have never denied that they received both the power of the laying on of hands and the outward succession from the Waldensians. And so, not only do the Waldensians themselves claim that their doctrine already existed in the fourth century—at which time Constantine the Great lived—but the Bohemians and Moravians also recognize this and have no objections against this antiquity.

<margin>
6. From the French Church History. Those in Provence come from the valleys.
</margin>
The *History of the Reformed Churches in France*, called "of the Three Hammers" <note>This likely refers to a specific 16th-century historical work, possibly Jean Crespin’s *Histoire des Martyrs*, which was printed in various editions in Antwerp; "Three Hammers" may refer to a printer's mark or a specific volume subtitle</note>, printed in Antwerp in 1558, likewise speaks in the first part, page 35, of their antiquity, and says:

> The Waldensians have, from time immemorial, resisted the abuses of the Roman Church, and God has protected them against all the fury of their enemies in such a way that they were able to continually maintain themselves in the valleys of Piedmont. From there, they later dispersed, and about 270 years ago <note>Counting back from the 1558 publication date, this would place their arrival in Provence around the late 13th century</note> moved into the regions of Provence, especially to Merindol, Cabrières, Lourmarin, etc.;

and further down it says:

> as far as their religion is concerned, they have never accepted the papal decrees.

If they have now, as it is stated here, never accepted the papal decrees, then it follows of itself that they must have [separated] from the Roman Church immediately...

<page-num>454</page-num>
# I. B. 27. C. On the Antiquity of the Waldensians

...must have separated themselves when the [Roman Church] began to force upon them such innovations that were diametrically opposed to Holy Scripture; consequently, they never had any need to renounce errors that they had never accepted in the first place.

<margin>7. Amiraldi.</margin>
This very point is made by the renowned Amiraldi <note>Moïse Amyraut (1596–1664), a highly influential French Protestant theologian at the Academy of Saumur</note>, famous for his learned writings, former preacher and teacher of theology at Saumur. In a sermon on Romans 10:15, he initially discusses the ignorance, errors, and superstition that prevailed in the times of Luther, Calvin, and those who carried out the work of the Reformation before them, and then adds:

> And you know, my beloved brothers, how universal this great blindness was then throughout all Europe; only one small corner was still to be found in the world, hidden deep in the valleys of the Alps and among the rocky mountains of Provence, where the Gospel of Christ was able to preserve itself in purity and clarity.

<margin>8. Drelincourt.</margin>
The well-known Drelincourt <note>Charles Drelincourt (1595–1669), a prominent French Reformed minister in Paris known for his polemical and devotional works</note> writes similarly in the second of his *Intimate Conversations*: "Finally," it says there, "there have been such faithful Christians in the Piedmontese valleys from time immemorial who never at any time accepted the Roman decrees, nor shared in their gross errors." This even compelled a certain Italian monk named Belvedere <note>Andrea Belvedere, an author and member of the Jesuit order who wrote polemics against the Waldensians</note>, in his *Report to the Congregation for the Propagation of the Faith* <note>original: "Relation alle Congregatione de Propaganda Fide"</note> printed in Turin in the year 1630, to say straight out that these people have been "heretics" at all times. But what are "heretics" to those Catholic gentlemen other than people who hold solely to the doctrine of the Apostles and will not allow themselves to be turned away from the simplicity and purity of their faith?

<margin>9. Pantaleon.</margin>
Henricus Pantaleon <note>Heinrich Pantaleon (1522–1595), a physician and historian from Basel</note>, Ordinary Physician <term>Physicus ordinarius: a state-appointed or official physician for a city or region</term> at Basel, repeats this in more detail in Book 5 of *On Things Done in the Church* <note>original: "Rerum in Ecclesia gestarum"</note>,

<summary>This page cites various 16th and 17th-century authorities, including Moïse Amyraut and Charles Drelincourt, to argue that the Waldensians preserved the pure Gospel in the Alpine valleys since ancient times, never succumbing to Roman Catholic "innovations."
